This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of function space known as the spectral Barron space, we establish that the convergence rate of the generalization error is not influenced by the dimensionality $d$. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of this premise through a new estimate that demonstrates the ground state's smoothness in the specified function space, achieved through a proof utilizing a fixed-point approach grounded in the Krein-Rutman theorem. Ultimately, we verify the validity of the assumptions underlying our findings through an examination of specific scenarios. This research provides the first theoretical evidence for the effectiveness of neural networks in calculating quantum many-body physics quantities. The findings, presented as a research report, have significant implications for the application of these networks in kinetic quantum gas models. The associated code can be accessed via the link provided. Additionally, we have included a summary of the research in English. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/wangxj25/sde_barron. A French version of the research is also available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.00105.

This study explores the ability of two-layer neural networks to calculate the ground state of a $d$-dimensional quantum gas governed by the Schrödinger equation. Assuming that the ground state can be found within a specific function space, we demonstrate that the convergence rate of the generalization error is dimension-independent. To verify the assumptions underlying our findings, we prove that the ground state can be found within this function space through a fixed-point approach grounded in the Krein-Rutman theorem. This research provides the first theoretical evidence for the effectiveness of neural networks in calculating complex quantum many-body physics quantities. The intricacy of the human nervous system makes studying simpler organisms, such as C. Elegans, more manageable. With well-documented behaviour and structure information, C. Elegans serves as an ideal model to explore neural activity simulations. Traditional approaches using empirical data often fail to identify underlying neural patterns due to overlapping activity in multiple neurons. In an attempt to model these complex neural interactions, researchers introduced a novel model - the C. Elegans Neural Activity Model - based on observed neural co-activations in the worm's neurons. This neural model accurately replicates the co-activation patterns observed in the experiment and generates viable simulations of C. Elegans' sensory responses. Successful simulations of the worm's robust responses to multiple stimuli demonstrate the effectiveness of this neural model, revealing that neural coordination can produce robust and dynamic patterns of coordinated neuron groups. This C. Elegans Neural Activity Model also facilitates the exploration of neuron pairing possibilities, ultimately leading to the development of an algorithm to determine these pairings, which are subsequently used to design experiments to optimize neuron activation. In addition, researchers discovered that robust neuron group activations can emerge from large numbers of randomized neurons, providing new insights into neural patterning and the dynamics of coordinated neuron groups. The C. Elegans Neural Activity Model, being an generative model, differs from traditional predictive models like recurrent neural networks, thus offering a unique perspective in the field of computational neuroscience. The model has been made publicly available at [www.circuits.caucaus.com](http://www.circuits.caucaus.com). In an effort to promote open neuroscience, we've shared our data and the model under an open-source framework, encouraging further studies on C. Elegans' neural activity using the model. By publishing the C. Elegans Neural Activity Model, researchers can leverage it as a generative model to investigate coordinated neuron groups, ultimately shedding light on biological neural mechanisms within the human brain. In an effort to promote open neuroscience, we've shared our data and the model and have invited fellow researchers to explore C. Elegans' neural activity using the model. By publishing the C. The paper establishes global solvability and scattering in the energy space $H^1_a(\mathbb R^3)$ for all initial conditions in the defocusing scenario, whereas for the focusing scenario, it proves scattering for data below a threshold by leveraging a virial/Morawetz method. As a consequence, it resolves an open question posed by Li and Zhang regarding the existence of blow-up solutions in this model. Investigating orbital resonances enables the restriction of planetary properties in compact systems. The early K-type star K2-138, hosting six planets, particularly five proposed to be in a prolonged chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances, has undergone extensive analysis with multiple reports of potential resonant configurations through simulations. By running 1000-1000 orbital configuration simulations for each possible arrangement, our study aimed to identify the most likely planetary configuration, especially focusing on the most consistent resonant configuration and the associated uncertainties. Following preliminary analyses based on existing publications, our results indicate that the planets likely experience no resonances, whereas numerous simulations (around 75%) support a chain of 3:2 resonances, consistent with planets C and F, and potentially planets D and E, respectively. Due to significant uncertainties, the potential involvement of planets B and G in resonant configurations could not be confidently determined. Theoretical models suggest that the expected resonant zone following planetary migration should span the planetary configurations that exhibit mean motion resonances, leading us to infer that the planets likely fell short of reaching the predicted resonant zone due to differences in the planets' and host star's properties compared to theoretical models. The required additional mass to trigger resonances, making the system similar to other ultracool dwarfs, could alter our understanding of the resulting orbital evolution. Consequently, if future observations confirm the predicted orbital configuration, it may be interpreted as indicative of delayed or incomplete migration. Moreover, if the proposed resonant configuration is correct, it would make K2-138 the sixth known system featuring a prolonged chain of resonances and would make it the fifth system experiencing mean motion resonances involving five planets, changing our comprehension of planetary migration in such compact systems. A set of experiments utilized the STM instrument, employing a probe tip to investigate sample surfaces by tracking tunnelling currents. These studies included (1) utilizing STM to map the atomic structure of Highly Oriented Pyrolytic Graphite's (HOPG) surface to calculate its lattice constant, (2) employing STS mode to quantify the work functions of gold and HOPG samples, and (3) examining how the Local Density of States (LDOS) of gold, graphite, and Silicon samples changed with respect to varying bias voltages. Experimental results yielded a lattice constant of 0.27 nm for HOPG, and work functions of 0.7 and 0.5 eV for gold and graphite, respectively. However, work functions of 4.4 eV for gold and 4.9 eV for graphite were found to differ significantly from established literature values. Moreover, gold displayed a positive Local Density of States (LDOS), peaked at approximately 4.25 eV, while graphite showed the opposite, peaking at about 2.85 eV, and silicon had a higher LDOS than both, peaking at 4.9 eV. Possible explanations for the discrepancies between our results and literature values for work functions and LDOS are provided. These discrepancies may be attributed to a variety of factors, such as air-exposed surfaces, contamination with substances like MoS2 and SiOx, and the influence of the STM tip. These factors can cause significant issues, and experiments should be conducted while considering their implications. Furthermore, LDOS measurements may be affected by how energy states are combined, and thus it's crucial to understand the underlying physics behind obtained data. These issues highlight the need for further optimization of sample and tip preparation, along with the integration of phase-sensitive detection, in order to refine the STM instrument and tunnelling processes. Such capabilities will greatly enhance the instrument's utility in a wide range of fields. These experiments also demonstrated that STS mode can successfully quantify the local work functions of materials. A new class of rotating black brane solutions, including all possible rotational parameters, have been constructed in an arbitrary number of dimensions. These rotating black branes are flat in topology at their horizons, yet due to the influence of the dilaton field, they do not conform to either flat or (anti)-de Sitter asymptotic behaviors. We've analyzed their physical properties by applying a method that uses the counterterm, which was inspired by AdS/CFT correspondence. A small-step operational semantics breaks down computation into discrete, indivisible steps. 
The definition of such semantics for programming languages typically relies on well-defined notions of reduction and substitution. 
This paper proposes an automated method of constructing small-step operational semantics from high-level specification statements that define reduction and substitution processes. 
This method translates the semantics into a form suitable for automated verification and further transforms it into alpha-equivalence normal form. 
To demonstrate its effectiveness, the method was applied to a lambda-calculus with parallel evaluation and the obtained specification was verified in Isabelle/HOL. 
For comparison, the paper also presents a traditional, step-by-step construction of lambda-calculus semantics and highlights the differences between the two approaches. 
The proposed method was further used to automate the definition of semantics for lambda-calculi with parallel evaluation, for which the specification and alpha-normal form were directly derived, and for localized name evaluation, for which the definition was reconstructed in normal form and the specification was computed. 
Finally, the paper examines an existing, established implementation of a small-step lambda-calculus evaluator and shows that it adheres to the specifications generated by the automated method. 
All developed materials, including Isabelle/HOL proofs and code, were made publicly available on https://github.com/TarsDane/step-to-spec.

Additionally, we establish that minimal polynomials based on cosine values do not yield factorizations for certain Chebyshev polynomial variants of the fifth and sixth kinds. The evidence presented involves a study of the degree of these minimal polynomials. The advantages and limitations of multicast beamforming for millimeter-wave systems have received little attention despite their potential for creating extensive indoor coverage areas. To gauge the benefits of this technology in practice, we analyzed the performance of multicast beamforming with millimeter-wave communication in an open environment, covering topics such as transmission methods and practical implementation. Our study reveals that multicast beamforming significantly decreases spectral efficiency when there are multiple designated recipients for the same transmission, whereas traditional point-to-point beamforming has a negligible negative impact. Consequently, we suggest utilizing a hybrid approach that combines point-to-point and multicast beamforming methods to maximize system efficiency. We also designed an efficient hybrid transmission method, incorporating multiple types of phase shifters and large antenna arrays, to minimize implementation costs. Our study provides comprehensive analysis of antenna coupling capabilities, transmission power, and complexity requirements. Our findings show that this new hybrid transmission method achieves optimal performance and reduces power consumption by approximately 4 dB compared to pure beamforming methods. Moreover, we developed an algorithm to combine multiple types of phase shifters, reducing complexity by as much as 90\%. Finally, we designed a practical implementation plan for millimeter-wave multicast beamforming systems, taking into account real-world constraints to ensure feasibility. Our study demonstrates that these new technologies can provide extensive indoor coverage while minimizing implementation costs, making them a suitable choice for next-generation wireless communication systems. Furthermore, our investigation also sheds light on potential research directions for millimeter-wave communication in the near future. The outcomes of this study are made available in an open-source format to facilitate future research in this domain. A moving dielectric medium can alter the path of light traveling through it, a phenomenon termed the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect. The induced deviation in the path is directly proportional to the velocity of the medium. Our investigation documents a previously unreported instance of the optical drag effect where the path deviation remains proportional to the medium's velocity but is oriented in a direction counter to the medium's motion. To observe this anomalous effect, we conducted an optical drag experiment under the conditions of electromagnetic transparency and monitored the shift from typical optical drag to zero drag and ultimately the anomalous effect through adjustments to two-photon detuning. Our results demonstrate a connection to the phenomenon of electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT), as well as a possible connection to Einstein's relativistic theory, with the anomalous effect suggesting a need to reevaluate the definition of optical drag and its connection to the medium's drag coefficient. Additionally, this discovery opens new avenues for studying this phenomenon and its relationships using a diverse range of techniques. Furthermore, we identify and propose a method to identify potential locations on Earth for observing this anomalous effect. Our findings hold promising implications for leveraging optical drag to measure minute changes in gravitational fields and precision science, as well as to develop advanced systems for force detection. The research also involves the development of an analytical framework for forcing effects in moving medium systems, which finds application in this discovery. Our work presents a significant advancement at the intersection of optics and relativistic physics. The research provides a model for predicting forcing effects in similar conditions and could influence the development of advanced systems for force detection, ultimately yielding valuable insights and test methods for evaluating the forcing effect itself. This paper introduces an exact calculation method for worst-case scenario parameter realization in robust optimization problems involving uncertain binary or categorical data. Existing exact algorithms for these problems are computationally resource-intensive, partly due to their increased complexity following reformulation of the problem, and partly due to unknown bounds for decision-independent variables. In contrast, we suggest a Lagrangian dual approach that avoids these issues, which can be easily integrated into existing algorithms. This method is particularly tailored to scenarios where binary parameters activate or deactivate constraints, which is commonly encountered in various applications. We discuss possible extensions to scenarios with limited recourse or integer variables and provide numerical results demonstrating notable computational advantages over existing methods. This approach is currently applied in a MATLAB tool, dualdecpair, which is open-source and available for download at https://github.com/LiE-orchestra/DualDebair.

The development of pattern extraction algorithms helps gain valuable insights into ever-growing datasets by translating recurring data configurations into simplified representations. However, the rapid advancement of pattern extraction algorithms lags behind the limited accessibility to diverse test datasets, which hinders the validation of novel algorithmic approaches. In this research, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 9,772 patterns, derived from 2,530 examples, 1,677 of which are original and the rest obtained through duplication, is introduced. This dataset covers a range of inherent and artificial patterns, including those from real-world applications and artificially generated examples with varying characteristics. Furthermore, the dataset includes an unusual collection of patterns featuring extensive and frequent exceptions. In addition to the dataset, the results of a series of experiments examining state-of-the-art pattern extraction algorithms are provided, evaluating their performance on various types of patterns. This investigation aims to promote transparency within the pattern extraction research field, highlighting inconsistencies in many algorithmic improvements and encouraging the development of more robust evaluation methods. Moreover, the results show that even widely-used algorithms often struggle with exceptional patterns, and often fail to meet the requirements for real-world applications. Consequently, the dataset and corresponding analysis are made available to the public through an online repository at https://github.com/PatternAnalytics/PatternAnalytics/tree/main/datasets/exception_patterns. Additionally, the results of a new algorithm, ApOp, are presented, demonstrating its capability to adapt to diverse pattern distributions by incorporating user-defined parameters. In contrast to traditional algorithms, ApOp employs a strategy of identifying and extracting distinct sub-configurations within each data instance, rather than searching for an all-inclusive solution. This approach uniquely positions ApOp to tackle patterns featuring extensive and frequent exceptions. We present an integrated multi-grating system fabricated using CMOS technology that enhances light coupling between input optical signals and optical dipole traps on chip. This design utilizes a specific pattern of alternating refractive indices within the silicon material to redirect input light into a desired path, effectively increasing the efficiency of light transfer and reducing waste. In our experiment, this silicon structure combines with a micro-optic assembly to create an optical dipole trap with a wavelength of 780 nm, and is used to capture single Rubidium atoms. The resulting optical dipole trap has a diameter of approximately 1.6 μm and an intensity peak of 2.48 x 10^3 W/m^2. In comparison to a conventional wedge-based input coupler, our silicon structure achieves an enhancement factor of 19.5 for optical dipole trap formation and exhibits improved light transfer efficiency with a minimum input coupling efficiency threshold of 12%. Additionally, this design shows an impressive input-to-output transmission loss of less than -0.5 dB. The development of this silicon structure offers a compact and efficient solution for developing optical traps on chip, and has significant potential for various applications including quantum information processing, atomic clocks, and quantum metrology, as well as being used as a building block for future optical sensors and traps. Furthermore, this technology can also be employed for creating optical traps for quantum cooling of non-autonomous atoms as well. The design rules used for creating this device are also explained along with a potential approach for scaling up the structure, and further discussions on existing design challenges and potential solutions are discussed. Furthermore, this technology can also be used for creating optical traps for single atoms as well as collective trapping of atoms in case of future applications. The design rules used for creating this device are also outlined along with a potential approach for scaling up the structure, and further discussions on existing design challenges and potential solutions are presented. We have discovered that neural networks trained with an explicit robustness constraint in the spectral domain do not necessarily become resilient to adversarial attacks. In contrast, neural ODEs, which inherit the differentiability of their underlying functions, demonstrate a inherent capacity for withstanding such attacks. In fact, this differentiability often overloads the model to the point of complete performance degradation. By interpreting neural ODEs in the context of adversarial attacks, this study provides a theoretical framework for understanding robustness and generalization in deep learning models, thereby refuting a previous assumption that neural ODEs exhibit enhanced robustness. Our work also involves reconstructing neural ODEs from a robustly trained network, which in turn demonstrates weakened adversarial robustness after the reconstruction process. In a broader sense, this study offers an alternative approach to interpreting neural networks, which may hold significance for various applications. In addition, this research provides initial insights into neural ODEs, which have yet to be well-understood. Our experiments and code are publicly available at https://github.com/22-IT/Robustness_of_Neural_ODEs. Research on top tagging has advanced rapidly due to the top quark's substantial role in studying physics that goes beyond the standard model. Recent studies have found that machine learning techniques have improved tagging methods, enabling more accurate distinctions between top quark events and similar background events such as $t\bar{t}$-jet events. We explored the application of unsupervised graph-based methods to develop an effective top tagging strategy, utilizing the association between an event's particles and a set of predefined top quark decay modes as the foundation for this study. By utilizing LHC top quark event data simulated with MadGraph5_madWeb, we tested and compared the effectiveness of top tagging using the C4, Normalized Low Energy (NLE), and Graph Unrolled Neural Network (GUNN) methods. Unsupervised graph-based methods revealed top quark decay graph substructures that aligned with our prior expectations. Additionally, we evaluated the effectiveness of the GUNN and C4 algorithms in top quark event selection, determined the top quark identification efficiency, and assessed their ability to reject $t\bar{t}$-jet events. Surprisingly, we found that graphs built from an event's charged particles were better than those built from all particles, and that tagging efficiency was maximized at a false positive rate of 10\%. At this false positive rate, the GUNN method exhibited a 20\% increase in top quark identification efficiency over the C4 method, resulting in a top quark identification efficiency of 51.3\% and a $t\bar{t}$-jet rejection factor of 115 in fully leptonic top quark events. Furthermore, we identified the top quark decay distribution of the event particles as the primary characteristic that differentiates signal from background for all considered top quark decay modes. Finally, we outlined a possible implementation strategy for these graph-based tagging variables in a standard set of physics events. We expect these variables to be incorporated into the CMFV model simulation in the coming years, enabling further research into their application in analyzing physics beyond the standard model. This paper addresses challenges in the spatiotemporal predictive learning approach, known as ST-PL, that uses short observed sequences to forecast future frames and is widely applicable. One of the significant obstacles in this area is identifying meaningful spatiotemporal features, and excessive variation among successive frames exacerbates long-term forecasting difficulties. The main goal of this research is to improve the forecast accuracy by reinforcing the connection between short-term and long-term models and enhancing feature extraction within the framework. We introduce a novel feature extraction method called LST-Net, which breaks down a given frame into independent components and combines them with future frame predictions through a prediction-transformation process. The transformed features are then fed into the prediction model, and our findings indicate enhanced frame forecasting, and statistical analysis demonstrate increased model reliability by reinforcing relationships between short-term and long-term models. The proposed approach achieves a 2.0 dB improvement in PSNR and 0.2 in SSIM on the NTSG dataset, and 1.1 dB improvement in PSNR and 0.1 in SSIM on the K400 dataset, corresponding to an increase of approximately 50% and 10% respectively. This study focuses on polar codes received with carrier interference and explores permutation decoding as a strategy to simplify the process of finding the closest codeword. We establish that permutations resulting in cyclic shifts are sufficient for decoding polar codes, and we also determine which subcodes within [Z/2nZ] are suitable for transmission using polar codes, based on a given permutation. To implement permutation decoding in practice, we use a truncated version of the Brute Force Search algorithm, and we also present a method for recovering the transmission order of a received polar code, based on a given permutation. We perform comprehensive analysis of the error rate of permutation-based decoding, compared to the standard Brute Force Decoding approach. We show that, given a received vector of length n, the error rate of permutation-based decoding is at most n times the error rate of Brute Force Decoding. We use this finding to estimate the error rate of permutation-based decoding for a given received vector. Notably, the error rate of the standard Brute Force Decoding algorithm is essentially the same as the error rate of the List Viterbi decoder. Generating realistic synthetic cells can greatly benefit from efficient cell representation. Current methods using voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches can only approximate cell shapes, thereby compromising synthesis accuracy. We present a novel approach relying on level sets of signed distance functions to model cell structures. This technique not only speeds up anisotropic voxel generation but also facilitates the creation of signed distance functions from voxel sets and polygon meshes. Additionally, our method allows for the synthesis of novel cells by traversing a constructed space of generated cells. The efficiency and versatility of our approach enable the synthesis of cells at unprecedented resolution using high-end graphics processing units. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in the field of digital pathology by modeling red blood cells and cancer cell shapes based on histology images. For voxel and polygon mesh conversions, our method significantly outperforms existing libraries while reducing their running times by one to three orders of magnitude. We create over 1 billion synthetic red blood cells and thousands of cell shapes from histology images, producing a total of 1.2 billion cells. The accompanying video shows our approach in action, and additional results can be found at: https://levelset.github.io/cells. We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one flow field configuration to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator of order zero and one in space, revealing enhancements in intensity and diffusion associated with transition rates. We apply the operator of order one to study diffusion in stratified turbulence and verify that it generates a factorizing tensor product structure. This structural property enables the use of tensor product structure even when the underlying Markov process is approximated numerically. We demonstrate the efficiency of the tensor product structure approach by simulating both exact and approximate stochastic advection problems. For a two-tracer system in flow fields with two distinct states, we show that the factorizing structure leads to exact and approximate transport operators that match in intensity and diffusion but differ in inner structures. This discovery implies that numerical approximations in lower-order tensor components do not affect diffusion properties, but can impact intensity. Moreover, we verify that factorizing structure preserves two-tracer correlations while their sum is conserved. This conservation property is responsible for the exactness of transport operators in tensor product structure. In closure theory, this finding implies that models based on tensor product structure do not introduce additional transport effects beyond diffusion, even when the underlying Markov process is approximated numerically. We further apply the exact transport operator to optimize two-tracer closure models and verify its efficacy. In certain flow fields with approximations, we show that models optimized according to sum of inner structures perform better than those optimized according to diffusion properties or intensity. We believe this counter-intuitive result is due to the model optimal in intensity being sub-optimal in diffusion, and inversely, the model optimal in diffusion being sub-optimal in intensity. We conclude that tensor product structure offers exactness and efficiency in turbulent transport, and additional structure beyond diffusion may not be beneficial. Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within a specified boundary. Our method effectively bounds the expected R\'enyi divergence between interdependent data sets, revealing the trade-off between expected privacy loss and interference deviation limitation. Our approach is applicable to various conditional distributions and can handle a range of dependence levels. As an extension, we introduce a statistical test to assess whether observed data dependencies align with assumed assumptions of the guard zone system. The framework's utility and effectiveness are illustrated through a Monte Carlo simulation and a real-world application involving monitoring air quality in Los Angeles. This research provides an essential framework for analyzing the relationship between collected data sets, offering valuable insights for designers of safe systems and facilitating empirical studies of system limitations. By leveraging these findings, users can make more informed decisions about location data disclosure. The framework's availability in form of open-source code enables researchers and practitioners to utilize it for various location anonymization purposes. With the rise of devices equipped with GPS and sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, and beacons that can track various human activity markers, the potential sources of dependent location data are continually expanding. As an example, sharing locations along with corresponding road conditions or weather could lead to noticeable correlations. Similarly, disclosing GPS and sensor data can reveal substantial interdependencies. Our framework's generality allows it to be applied to safeguarding dependent data in various fields including social, medical, and psychological research. In the near future, employing our framework to safeguard dependent data on heart readings, cancer data, or social network information over short periods of time may become a pressing need. Future research can utilize our framework as a fundamental approach and develop novel extensions to tackle real-world challenges in safeguarding dependent data. Lastly, designers of safe systems can utilize the expected deviation limitation metric to establish guard zones that effectively minimize privacy losses in real-world settings. As an example, urban authorities can utilize the metric to determine optimal guard zone sizes to maintain privacy while introducing new services that combine multiple locations. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, including a combination of 3T and 7T magnetic field strengths. Our findings demonstrate that commonly observed network structures are consistent across sites, and we effectively removed age-related effects from our connectivity measures. In addition, our analysis identified notable individual and group differences, specifically in the default mode network, left dorsal attention network, and left frontal cortex. Our results confirm that our sample size is sufficient to accurately estimate the underlying structure of our connectivity data. Our research provides essential insights to inform the design of future multisite research projects. Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the positive electron-phonon interaction and the negative electron-electron interaction - yields a predictable trend in the isotope effect coefficient as a function of pressure. However, incorporating the variable density of states enhances our understanding of both interactions and improves agreement with experiments, particularly at high pressures, suggesting the importance of its range dependence. Furthermore, we investigated how the variable scattering lifetime influences the energy-range dependence of the density of states, particularly at high pressures, and found that it remains consistent with experiments, despite some deviations at low energies. The approach presented here can also be applied to other superconducting materials, such as PH4, and may lead to improved predictions of superconducting properties. The methodology used in this study is capable of handling complex materials and interactions, and may be adapted for simulations, offering a valuable tool for optimizing materials designed for superconducting applications. This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. Conventional motion planning methods utilizing map-based global planners face limitations in dynamic settings, as they rely on outdated static environment maps that are often inaccurate. This research focuses on developing a focal set map representation to facilitate motion planning in car racing, an inherently dynamic environment. A novel constraint optimization method is proposed for generating the spatial boundaries, taking into account instantaneous sensor data and a priori environmental information. The resulting focal set map is integrated with a behavioral system to generate spatial boundaries for safety-critical areas, as demonstrated in a functional implementation. The technique is successfully validated through its integration with a human-driven game controller, enabling a fully autonomous racing simulation with safety-critical bounds. Evaluation results demonstrate that, with this spatial boundaries technique, players can drive more aggressively, yielding higher lap times, while the system ensures safe driving in critical areas with up to a 9% reduction in Euclidean distance. Comprehensive videos and code for the proposed method are available on https://github.com/GT-RAI/SafeFocalSets. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera position estimation process is proposed, starting with a point-based initialization, followed by optimizing camera positions and surfel parameters. A camera network is established by defining each camera's pose relative to previously estimated positions. Evaluation of this method, as demonstrated by testing with the TUM dataset, demonstrates comparable performance to that of block-wise surfel mapping at both intragram and interframe levels. Moreover, this method successfully achieves substantial reduction in both keyframe count and runtime without compromising results. Furthermore, this method is successfully applied to large-scale datasets such as KITTLZ3D, AirSim, and CarScene, achieving 70% reduction in keyframes and only a 0.6% drop in interframe accuracy. Consequently, this technique significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of efficiency. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve. Eventually, this work is extended to show that the rational function semifield of a tropical surface also has a finite set of generators over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of another tropical surface through a harmonic morphism. All proofs rely heavily on a previously established algorithm to test if a harmonic mapping is surjective. The algorithm's extension to tropical surfaces is also provided. The paper's work is eventually applied by deriving a finite set of generators over the real numbers with maximum and addition operations, thus solving a long-standing open problem first introduced by Thuong Nguyen. Furthermore, it is shown that additive integrals of coefficients of points within a polyedral convex set that satisfy additive linear equations also have a finite set of generators over the real numbers with maximum and addition operations, thus solving another long-standing open problem first introduced by Stefanos Athanasiadis. Lastly, the paper's work is applied by deriving recursive relationships of additive linear combinations for additive integrals of coefficients of points within a polyedral convex set that satisfy additive linear equations, thus solving yet another long-standing open problem first introduced by Stefanos Athanasiadis. We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) maps to the second ordered Vassiliev cohomology group w2(X). We've also successfully extended Gassels result that positively solved Fox-Hatchers conjecture, by further showing that the integral of any 1-cocycle over any long knots 1-cycles generates a non-trivial, higher order Vassiliev invariant. We've specifically found an example of a 14th order Vassiliev invariant, having originated from integrating a 1-cocycle with a long knot's 1-cycles. We've also produced a specific analytical expression for a three order Vassiliev invariant, by integrating an arbitrary 1-cocycle with a long knots 1-cycles. This produced an expression that matches Millets description of a specific three order Vassiliev invariant. This research introduces two modifications for enhancing the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem.
Originally built using Gabidulin codes within the McEliece framework, Loidreau's system is now subject to a new type of attack.
We utilize the learning to rank (LTR) method to create public keys, replacing the traditional learning to rank (LTR) public key with a matrix product of low-rank matrices.
In our first modification, we utilize the vector product instead of the matrix product.
In our second modification, we combine the vector product with rank metric short vector problem (RMSVP) problems to decode the ciphertext.
We conduct comprehensive analysis and test the new modifications with various parameters, comparing their performance in terms of size, decryption efficiency, key size, and resistance against the Faulstapler attack. The results showcase that our modifications yield exceptional results when using the matrix product and exceptional to moderate results when using the RMSVP decoding. Notably, we discover a trade-off between the RMSVP decoding method and the fault attack resistance – the RMSVP method offers fault attack resistance but fails to provide it when incorporating RMSVP decoding method. This research showcases a thorough investigation of modifying an existing cryptosystem to enhance its security against known attacks. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train one collective model without exchanging sensitive information. To protect against snoopers, participants in this system collaborate on a training model by sharing processed data. Two primary FL variants exist, which differ based on how participants contribute. Horizontal FL is based on combining datasets with the same structure, while Vertical FL is based on uniting datasets with the same objective but differing attributes. We specifically investigate a two-party VFL scenario where two entities, aiming to expand their customer bases, are willing to share their data for mutual benefits. This research presents an attacker model where two entities decide on the shared attributes and the training method, without revealing their choice to each other, to potentially steal as much information as possible from their counterparts. In return, we propose an attacker model where the stalwart party exploits the confidence and model predictions from the compromising party to reveal useful information of the former. This research presents an experimental evaluation of an attacker model where the compromising party attempts to steal information of the stalwart party. To prevent such breaches, we suggest implementing token transfer protocols, which limit an entity's ability to sell its customers' data. Specifically, TokenFT is a protocol, which enforces a token-based system, where an entity can only purchase data following a predefined transaction; TokenFTFT is a protocol, which enables an entity to transfer tokens only after the initial transaction has been completed. Both token transfer protocols significantly limit an entity's ability to steal information of the stalwart party. Moreover, TokenFT also provides stalwart parties with the option to revoke previously shared data at any moment. Finally, we validate the practical application of our research through an econometric analysis, which shows token transfer protocols can increase revenue for both parties in case of a successful transaction. In return, our research highlights token transfer protocols as a viable solution to enhance data sharing collaboration in case of horizontal and vertical FL applications. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling approaches have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by selecting only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we introduce InfogGNN, an enhanced pseudo-labeling framework specifically designed for GNNs operating under a scarcity of labels. The framework initially identifies informative pseudo-labels through a confidence-based filter before incorporating them into the model training, utilizing a weighted loss function that distinguishes between actual and pseudo-labels. This study introduces the first fully verified methods for privately learning decision trees in a hierarchical manner across a network of devices, each with limited storage capacity. We developed two distributed approaches that ensure privacy by controlling data access and apply it to learning decision trees. Both methods use a two-step process: first, we create a decision tree based on aggregated data; second, we refine the tree with individual device data. Despite facing significant storage constraints, our methods successfully learn decision trees without compromising privacy, and in a practical sense, our proposed algorithms can learn decision trees with up to 16 nodes using 256MB of storage and 5 seconds of computation. When tested on sample data from the OpenIris dataset, our methods achieved accurate results, and by using a technique called data compression, our proposed algorithms can learn decision trees with up to 512 nodes while still ensuring privacy. This breakthrough enables applications such as parallel tree-based classification to be executed privately for the first time. We verified that the steps of our algorithm are secure by providing formal security proof, and we conducted extensive testing across a network of machines to verify that the steps are side-free and robust against real-world applications. Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our algorithm by comparing its performance to an unprivate method using the OpenIris dataset and evaluating metrics such as accuracy, false positive and negative rates, and information overhead. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting mini-batches of data. When working in distributed environments, communication avoidance strategies aim to minimize the amount of data transmitted between machines. Although utilizing parameter pruning can help reduce communication, the recycled gradients generated during unpruned computations still need to be transmitted. Consequently, significant bandwidth can still be wasted on computing and transmitting recycled but unnecessary gradients. This paper proposes an algorithm called Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD) to prevent the computation and transmission of unnecessary recycled gradients. By integrating the communication-avoiding principle from Communication-Avoiding Distributed Stochastic Gradient Method (CAD-SGDM), CA-SGD achieves its objective. The method has been compared with traditional SGD through hardware testing and has demonstrated substantial communication reduction - the communication savings of the algorithm were verified on AMD EPYC 7702VH and NVIDIA A100 GPUs, where CA-SGD incurs 87.5% and 85.7% less communication compared to SGD, specifically translating to 73.1% and 69.6% less execution time in the presence of 100 GiB and 100 GiB of active and 100 GiB of cold memory conditions respectively. Additionally, the algorithm was shown to outperform SGD on memory-constrained hardware during training of the Light-weight Deep Fisher Linear Model (LDFL) for image classification. Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computing cross-correlations given traditional architectures, where the computational demand increases exponentially with the number of antennas involved. Traditional architectures, requiring O(N^2) computations for real-time data analysis, might be surpassed by FFT-correlators, capable of producing identical results through higher-dimensional Fourier transformations. Nonetheless, fft-correlators require substantial modifications to incorporate classical sampling theory, where data is initially sampled below the Nyquist rate along specific dimensions, usually with ratios greater than one, making Fourier transformations invalid in these dimensions. This paper presents a new fft-correlator architecture, bypassing the necessity for fft-correlators, as the Fourier transformation is valid when sampling rates exceed one in all dimensions. Leveraging the underlying Fourier transformations, this architecture successfully computes correlations with a computational complexity of O(N log N). Compared to the fft-correlator, this design reduces real-time data analysis costs by factors of 3 to 4, bringing the computational expenses on par with traditional architectures. Despite this efficiency, our fft-correlator design still incurs a penalty, with the system's overall sampling rate being approximately 3 to 4 times higher than traditional architectures, meaning the data volume needs to be amplified before Fourier transformations can be reapplied, thus increasing the storage and online analysis costs. Consequently, this design will specifically benefit radio interferometry experiments requiring real-time data analysis, storage, and online processing, as it successfully mitigates the previously identified bottlenecks, a substantial sample rate increase. With further advancements and optimizations, we aim to make the Fourier transformation valid in all dimensions, making the fft-correlator design obsolete and the new architecture the sole available option. We further apply convex optimization techniques to achieve a substantial reduction in the overall sample rate, making the fft-correlator design obsolete and the new architecture the sole available option. Finally, this design is validated by applying it to real-time data analysis in radio interferometry, as it successfully correlates 30 seconds of live data from five antennas within 3 seconds. The new architecture, specifically designed for the BigBoost project, can be accessed at https://bigboost-rw.codeplex.com. During live testing, we identified minor inefficiencies, leading to the new open-source library Xylinx at https://xylinc.codeplex.com. We establish that any hypergraph can be viewed as a composition of hypergraphs formed by a common tensor-based operation. We also obtain results on the spectra of hypergraphs by applying our tensor-based method, and demonstrate its utility by constructing cospectral hypergraph pairs for adjacency, Laplacian, and normalized Laplacian matrices. Furthermore, we show how to use hypergraph tensors to encode interactions between networks and derive conditions under which a hypergraph can be completely decomposed into smaller components. We maintain that the widely-adopted categorical time model is flawed and has a tendency to produce biased estimates. We utilize simulated data to compare the performance of four models with different time representations: continuous, categorical with equal partitions, categorical with adaptive equal partitions, and categorical with intervals varying by the size of the previous interval. We find that the continuous time model yields the most accurate results but comes with computational complexities. In contrast, the categorical models exhibit discrepancies when evaluating models, with the equal partition methods exhibiting poor accuracy, particularly when evaluating models, but producing more consistent estimates than the variable partition method which typically yields the most inconsistent results. We suggest employing the variable partition method for its relative efficiency and accuracy while acknowledging the drawbacks. We provide R code for implementing these methods to facilitate comparison and allow users to make an informed decision based on our findings. Additionally, this method can be applied to other research areas tracking change over time. We advocate for the use of continuous time in modeling, but acknowledge the variable partition method's potential advantages. Since the variable partition method is more readily analyzed with continuous models than the equal partition method, we propose using continuous models followed by post-hoc analysis using the variable partition method. Post-hoc analysis can be performed through the implementation of a step-wise algorithm. We have developed software in R that allows users to replicate our results and make an informed decision between the different time models. The variable partition method has the advantage of being suitable for modeling with an unknown number of time intervals and an uneven distribution of disease progression among subjects. We provide an original solution to handle the estimation of model parameters with time varying by size. We suggest comparing the performance of the three categorical models and the continuous model and selecting the variable partition method when accurate estimation is the primary concern. In cases requiring a trade-off between estimation and computation, the equal partition method may be a viable alternative. We discuss potential limitations and outline avenues for future research aimed at addressing these challenges. We propose integrating the variable partition method into common analysis software to facilitate its widespread adoption among researchers and clinicians. However, these efforts have met with limited success, as none have led to undecidability proofs for the regular functions generated. This paper contributes to this line of research by defining a new family of Church encodings for polyregular functions, providing explicit algorithms, and revealing that this system is uncomputable. To validate the new family, we established a formalization of its definitions and calculations within the Coq proof assistant and verified its completeness, leveraging the regular proof assistant method.

We demonstrate the new Church encodings' potential by mapping them to (i) nondeterministic weak alternating automata with polynomial alternation, (ii) alternating automata with two alternations, and (iii) regular two-way automata. Furthermore, we show that this mapping allows us to prove undecidability for the regular two-way functions with a polynomial time and space complexity bounds limit. Additionally, we prove the new Church encodings' independence from specific choice mechanisms, such as explicit, intensional, and explicit intensional methods.

Apart from undecidability proofs, this paper offers a precise method to calculate the size of Church encodings for polyregular functions over a given alphabet. We establish a recursive formula that determines, based on a given polyregular function over a specific alphabet, the minimum number required to encode it over the same alphabet. We further introduce a representation mechanism for polyregular functions that allows for size evaluations, even in the absence of a explicit structure representation. We validate the size evaluations through Coq's automated proof checking process.

We further introduce a new mapping from nondeterministic finite automata to Church encodings for polyregular functions, providing explicit algorithms and evaluating their size according to the new formula.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our method develops a data-driven strategy for distributing robot trajectories after training a deep learning network to navigate safely. By utilizing a distributionally robust approach, our method ensures safety by limiting the impact of novel and unforeseen robot states, providing a more secure navigation system for complex environments. We test our approach using a large-scale dataset and demonstrate that it outperforms existing methods by significantly reducing unsafe trajectories, with nearly 45% of previously calculated paths now considered hazardous. Notably, our method achieves this by leveraging the representation power of a deep neural network to identify and mitigate risks, with little impact on the overall number of possible trajectories. As a result, our method provides a more secure yet conservative navigation system with a substantial reduction in the number of possible trajectories, resulting in a significant time complexity decrease of over 50% compared to the original model's computational demands. We analyze the performance of our method using a scalable mathematical framework and show that our approach converges to an optimal solution. Furthermore, our approach's safety guarantees are based on optimal solution properties and a robustness measure that accounts for uncertainty, with the potential to extend this approach to other data-driven applications. We validate our findings by comparing our method against state-of-the-art approaches for data-driven safe navigation and robust policy optimization. The proposed approach is currently applicable to planar navigation but can be extended to multi-dimensional spaces, offering vast potential for real-world applications in robotics and beyond. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as enhanced social divisions and amplified hostility. Consequently, researchers have proposed a multitude of hate speech detection approaches, with deep learning models demonstrating exceptional performance in identifying hate content from online postings. Nevertheless, existing hate speech data is scarce, and researchers often struggle to develop reliable hate speech classification models when working with limited data resources. Active learning techniques address this challenge by selectively opting for labeled data from an unlabeled dataset. In this study, we employed a variety of deep learning models and active learning strategies to explore their effectiveness for hate speech classification across three distinct datasets. We observed that active learning-based methods outperformed random sampling, and models utilizing visual or mixed input outperformed those processing only textual data. We examined the impact of active learning techniques on model performance and assessed the influence of dataset and the specific hate speech dataset being utilized. We analyzed the variability in active learning-based approaches and evaluated the efficacy of different distance metrics while utilizing diverse deep learning models for hate speech classification. The findings of this study are presented in an open-access report. The study's implementation, data, code, and results are publicly available for review at https://github.com/nextml-bons/active-learning-ml. Furthermore, we share our custom-hatched dataset, active-learning-based data sampling code, and model training code at https://github.com/nextml-bons/DSL-ML. We also share our code using an open-source repository at https://github.com/ali-622/ASRC2022. We have also submitted a poster based on this research which can be found at https://doi.org/10.1109/ASRC2022.00000. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. These mean field equations will serve as a valuable tool for researchers to gain insights into neural networks. They allow for a quick evaluation of how altering network characteristics, such as degree distribution or width, might impact the complex dynamics of large neural networks. Furthermore, they enable an approximation of the maximum allowable variation in degree distribution while maintaining a stable collective rhythm in inhibitory networks. Similarly, in gap junction coupled networks, it is possible to determine the degree distribution width range that initiates collective oscillations. We have demonstrated that these theories can predict certain biologically relevant features of neural networks, potentially opening up new areas of exploration. As an example of their applicability, it has been observed that in biologically realistic excitatory networks, the upper limit of out-degree distribution width that keeps excitatory neurons below threshold (positive) bias is around 0.69, which corresponds to approximately two standard deviations in out-degree distribution. The timely detection of COVID-19 remains a significant research priority, offering potential advantages in the early prevention of disease spread and the lightening of healthcare burdens. With the advent of machine learning capable of analyzing data from diverse sensing modalities, research has been actively explored. This study proposes an end-to-end deep learning approach, merging Multi-Sensor Information Fusion and Progressive Multi-Stage, to develop a real-time cough sound classification system for COVID-19 detection. The designed system aggregates multi-layered information from Raw Wave, Mel Spectrogram, and Continuous PCEN images for COVID-19 identification. Evaluation on a multi-center dataset has yielded a recall rate of 93.75% and AUC of 99.25%, solidifying its ranking as the top-performing method. Moreover, the system boasts real-time efficiency, with processing times below 30ms for individual sounds and under 100ms for consecutive sounds. Code and dataset are available at: \url{https://github/CoughSoundCOVID19}. A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we develop methods to assess the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions in various wireless communication systems, focusing on a binary classification model. We evaluate GNN performance in both unencoded and encoded systems, then propose a framework to quantify prediction uncertainty and robustness metrics, including the optimal decoding strategy and information theoretic lower bounds. We present simulation results demonstrating GNN robustness under random and Rayleigh fading noise using Geometric GNN and GCN models. These findings underscore the significance of robustness in GNN-based communication systems and suggest the use of GNN models incorporating channel information for superior communication outcomes. The proposed framework is adaptable to various wireless systems and can be leveraged in multiple applications to inform optimal design and protocol strategies. Overall, our study provides a solid foundation for using GNN-based approaches in wireless communication systems. Furthermore, our work motivates further research into GNN-based communication systems, including the exploration of more advanced GNN models and channel coding techniques. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate transformation. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of benchmarks, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100. For example, on the ImageNet dataset, our approach compresses a ResNet-50 model into a 2x efficient ResNet-26, achieved in just 0.25x of the original parameters, while maintaining their respective test accuracies. The source code for InDistill is available at https://github.com/nielslee/Indistill. Interestingly, the model reveals that unevenly distributed grazing can, in some instances, prevent self-destroying feedback loops that can lead to the collapse of the ecosystem. In such systems, areas with more vegetation tend to experience greater grazing pressure, however, this pressure ultimately serves to protect the ecosystem as a whole by limiting the spread of critical thresholds that would lead to irreversible degradation. In systems where grazing is uniformly distributed, this safeguard no longer applies, and the model suggests that local fluctuations in grazing resistance can significantly impact the likelihood of irreversible ecosystem collapse, with more resilient grazing areas acting as key buffers against catastrophic system failures. In contrast, uniformly distributed grazing presses the ecosystem against critical thresholds, leading to a heightened likelihood of irreversible collapse. A python-based program, ipie, is presented for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations.  The program is written in a modular and object-oriented manner for ease of use and adaptability.  It utilizes NumPy and PyAlPS for efficient numerical operations and data output.  Baseline results are demonstrated for a hydrogen molecule and compare favorably to established methods, showcasing a 25x speed advantage when combined with NWChem.  Variations of the program are also discussed that leverage openfors to accelerate simulations through distributed computing.  The ipie package is available for download on the GitHub repository "python-afqmc/nosqexample" and includes additional guidance on its use.  Further discussion and implementation details can be found at https://github.com/free-chem-phys/hipie.  Research supported by the NASA Astrobiology Institute's Theory Program (C. D. J). The goal is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on knowledge of the distribution of item preferences or intermediary participation rates, and to ensure that buyers can discover the best strategy despite the unknown distribution of item preferences. To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity chains, and training transformer models to predict these chains, and subsequently generate summaries conditioned on them. In our experiments, which included pre-training and fine-tuning with the planning objective, we found that incorporating entity chains led to better summarization performance and entity accuracy on four diverse datasets. Notably, this method outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of Rouge metrics for the XSum and SAMSum datasets. Furthermore, our findings indicate that incorporating entity chains allows for more effective hallucination control, and we were able to identify cases where model hallucination can be positively assessed. The code and data are publicly available on our GitHub repository.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the importance of understanding entrainment patterns in conversations. To measure this synchronization accurately, we developed an advanced method combining long-term memory dynamics and complex network analysis to track changes in conversational pairs as interactions unfold. Through this approach, we can pinpoint significant changes in social bonding processes and uncover new insights into the underlying mechanisms driving entrainment. To illustrate the power of our method, we examined conversations between pairs of individuals with varying levels of mental resonance during discussions, revealing statistically significant correlations with measures of emotional intelligence and face perception skills. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that individual differences in mental resonance could be detected as early as 5-7 minutes into the conversation. Additionally, we explored the entrainment dynamics at an intra-individual level within each conversation and discovered that mental resonance consistently fluctuated in synchronized patterns, even among individuals who engaged in fewer face-to-face interactions. Notably, this intra-conversational entrainment showed a strong correlation with overall mental resonance levels, suggesting that understanding the synchronization dynamics at both individual and conversation levels is crucial for comprehending the underlying mechanisms of entrainment. With further modifications to accommodate non-stationary conditions, our method enables the identification of meaningful patterns in short datasets and holds promise for real-world applications in human-computer interaction settings. To facilitate replication and foster community development, we make our code and data openly available. We anticipate that our approach will facilitate new insights into the social bonding processes and increase our understanding of the intricate entwining of individual and group synchronization dynamics. Ultimately, this knowledge will enable the design of more effective strategies to increase trust and cooperation in human-computer interactions. In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact-related issues in marine ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This research focuses on a specific scenario involving a 2D marine ice sheet with a grounding line, though the approach can be extended to other contact issues like subglacial cavitation. A primary challenge arises from the analysis due to ice's nonlinear rheology, the implementation of a power-law based friction boundary condition, and the presence of rigid modes in velocity space, resulting in a semicoercive variational inequality. To tackle this complexity, a mixed formulation is explored that incorporates a Lagrange multiplier, followed by a finite element approximation analysis. This research derives error estimates by employing a specially constructed projection operator to account for rigid modes, leveraging a Korn-type inequality, under the assumption that certain conditions on this operator hold. To conclude, numerical simulations are conducted to validate the analysis and offer insights into marine ice dynamics. These simulations cover a range of scenarios, including a linearized model involving a power-law friction boundary and a study on how the iterative process converges in time. Results from the analysis suggest that the model needs around seven iterations to reach convergence over a 3500-year span for a power value of n=5. To explore n=5, n=10, and n=20 scenarios, the model was run over 3500 years, yielding a series of convergence maps that could be crucial in investigating marine ice dynamics. These maps show that in the steepest descent method, the model reaches convergence on rigid modes in a relatively short period for high-n values, while convergence on velocity and stress took longer. On the other hand, the convergence time for stress components was found to increase with the power value n. Notably, the model reached convergence on stress components over 3500 years for n=5 in the snapshot-triangle-based mass-transfert algorithm, whereas this time frame was insufficient for n=10, n=20 power values. In a second set of numerical simulations using a full year's data, the model was run over 365 days with a time step of 30 days for 20,000 mass transfer iterations. Results showed mass transfer convergence over 20,000 iterations with a time-dependent trend that could be crucial in investigating marine ice dynamics. On the other hand, the model was found to reach convergence in around seven iterations in the snapshot-triangle-based mass-transfert algorithm, yielding a series of convergence maps that could be essential in exploring marine ice dynamics.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. Furthermore, the mass of outflowing gas detected in our study exceeds the amount that could be fully resolved by current state-of-the-art instruments, suggesting that future studies of more distant and more massive galaxies will be essential to understanding the role of outflows in cosmic processes. For the first time, we directly observed how outflows affect the movement of gas within a galaxy, finding that outflows can either have little to no effect, or in some cases, can actually help regulate the rotation of galaxies by dissipating some of the gas that contributes to rotational motion. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of fluctuations was accounted for, this observation made sense, revealing that initial anisotropy and its fluctuations play a crucial role in shaping final triangular flow results. Additionally, we observed in 200 GeV Au+Au collisions that initial geometric flow and fluctuations contribute nearly equally to final elliptic flow. Predictions for 60 GeV Au+Cu collisions were also generated, offering a reference for future experiments. The research is expected to contribute to an understanding of the initial conditions through experimental measurements in various collisions. Our proposed testbed, SyROF, is designed to facilitate the development of
cooperative robot systems, making it easily accessible for both undergraduate
and graduate students to implement robotic swarms in a timely manner. To achieve
this goal, we developed SyROF, an innovative testbed that features a user-friendly,
high-level programming environment supporting the Timed Input/Output Automata
(TIOA) paradigm. This versatile tool boasts the following distinctive features: 
1) An efficient synchronization mechanism to coordinate robotic actions, 
2) A membership verification system with built-in failure detection, and 
3) A transparent, common knowledge sharing platform. To streamline development,
we created a library containing various utility functions and adapted existing
algorithms for the testbed. Additionally, we conducted experiments utilizing a 10-
robot swarm to demonstrate its capabilities, presenting both success and failure
scenarios as case studies. Our assessment of SyROF highlighted its numerous benefits,
including its simplicity, extensivity, and flexibility. We highly recommend SyROF for
instructional purposes due to its proven effectiveness in various robotic swarm
applications, even with the presence of common knowledge sharing limitations. 
Ultimately, SyROF can serve as an invaluable teaching tool, serving as an efficient
means to introduce undergraduate students to the design of robust, cooperative robot
systems and help them efficiently develop their first robotic swarm project. This

depth estimation from unlabeled videos to gain depth information for tasks
that don't need it (like ours), and then uses this information to speed up
training and improve results for segmentation tasks. Unlike other approaches,
ours doesn't require adjusting the architecture of the network or using special
layers with new parameters. Instead, we use the features produced by a network
that was previously trained on labeled data and use these to make new images from
depth data, and then train on those images along with the original images. Our
method works well, cutting the time it takes to get good results from hundreds of
hours to just dozens of hours, with results that are comparable in our tests on

$$\mathcal{P}:= \{p\in \mathcal{H}(\mathbb{D})\text{ such that }|p(z)|<1\text{ for all }z\in\mathbb{D}\}.$$
Bohr's inequality states that there must exist a real number $r\in (0,1)$ for which the following inequality holds:

$$\left|\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n z^n\right|\leq 1\text{ for all }z\in\mathbb{D}.$$
This means that the power series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n z^n$ converges within the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. We aim to find a minimum value of $r$, denoted by $r_0$, such that $r\geq r_0$ satisfies Bohr's inequality. Bohr's inequality has been generalized in various functional settings including normed linear spaces and Banach spaces.
