However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from time bias in evaluations, as systems favor searching areas evaluated earlier in the process. This time-related bias can be categorized into two main concepts - static time bias, which affects the entire population equally, and dynamic time bias, which varies among individuals. Our main objective is to investigate how this bias influences search performance in parallel computing environments. A comprehensive study involved evaluating the impact of both static and dynamic time bias on the search performance in a given function minimization task. We also explored strategies to counter these biases, focusing on using uniform selection pressure and recalculation of fitness distances. Search performance was evaluated on computationally demanding tasks, which we defined as high-computational-cost (HiCC) functions. We discovered that Asynchronous PEAs with static time bias exhibit a trade-off between efficiency and search performance. We found that incorporating uniform selection pressure or adjusting the selection pressure to maintain uniformity do not yield notable improvements in search performance. On the other hand, Asynchronous PEAs with dynamic time bias show a trade-off between population size and search performance. We observed that incorporating uniform fitness distance recalculations accelerates the algorithm's search. Notably, a combination of both strategies - uniform selection pressure and fitness distance recalculation - does not enhance search performance or efficiency. Our research indicates that Asynchronous PEAs with static and dynamic time bias have a negative impact on population size, influencing the Asynchronous PEA's search performance. We conclude that Asynchronous PEAs with static and dynamic time bias restrict the Asynchronous PEA's population size choices, imposing limitations on the Asynchronous PEA's search performance. We recommend increasing the population size to counter the time bias effects, albeit limited by hardware constraints such as Central Processing Unit (CPU) architecture. A practical application of our research is to Asynchronous Parallel Genetic Algorithms (APGAs) where selecting parents based on rank and linear fitness scaling can counter the time bias effects, maintaining a larger population size. Furthermore, a comparative analysis between Asynchronous PEAs with static and dynamic time bias shows that the latter yields better search performance at equivalent computational costs. These light components were categorized as being stellar in nature. Analyzing the event through Nankai's lens-light model, researchers were able to determine that seven out of eight stellar components possessed similar masses and revealed a distinct relationship between mass and flux within the lens system. Although initial calculations indicated a planet-host mass ratio consistent with the expected power-law trend, uncertainties surrounding the planet's mass made it challenging to determine the host star's mass. Fortunately, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434's peculiar light curve displayed a significant "hump" mid-curve, ultimately allowing researchers to resolve the planet-star mass ratio and derive a precise star-planet mass ratio of $0.17 \pm 0.03$. Notably, this value lies near the point of significant change in the planet-host mass-ratio power-law and may serve as a reference point for future refinement of the power-law trend. OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 represents the first micro-lensing event to identify a cold super-Earth in the Galactic field with a star-planet mass ratio consistent with the expected value for the lower mass end of the planet-host mass-ratio power-law. The new data point may influence Nussbaum et al.'s (2010) finding that more massive planets tend to reside in more massive host stars by demonstrating that this relationship could be shifted towards lower stellar masses. Moreover, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434's unique properties may provide significant constraints on the model used in the analysis if identified as a system located near the Galactic center. The OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 super-Earth is a type of "Jovians," which have masses ranging from sub-Earths to Neptunes, and constitutes the majority of planets in our galaxy, particularly in the habitable zones of lower-mass stars. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new results about their dynamics, including information on periodic points and the recurrence properties of certain points. Ultimately, our analysis leads to a formulation of questions regarding the dynamics of beta-transformations with holes, which are not immediately resolvable using existing techniques. We also illustrate how to construct KMS maps for other types of holes beyond zero, offering a foundation for further exploration. The methods employed in this study combine recent developments in KMS maps theory with the understanding of beta-transformations dynamics, highlighting a fruitful approach to investigating the dynamics of beta-transformations with holes. Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors but encountered difficulties with information loss during non-maximum suppression and the multitasking nature of anchor-based object detection. To address this issue, we developed Token-wise Uncertainty Estimation for Object Detection (TUEOD), a novel method for object detection that integrates uncertainty estimation. TUEOD employs a modified convolutional neural network with an uncertainty prediction module and confidence filtering block to generate token-wise uncertainty maps, eliminating information loss and leveraging efficient architecture design. By adopting a self-supervised loss function, TUEOD optimizes token-wise uncertainty maps to accurately reflect a detection model's performance. We evaluated TUEOD using the widely used MS COCO dataset and discovered that it can improve detection accuracy by calculating uncertainty metrics. Furthermore, we analyzed TUEOD's robustness using naturally noisy images from the NOISE CoCo and SAD datasets and found that it can reduce detection errors. We also found that an ensemble of models with varying token-wise uncertainty levels achieves enhanced performance on MS COCO and ImageNet. Overall, TUEOD enhances the output predictions of a detection model, increases robustness, and offers more efficient resource allocation during system design. The code for TUEOD is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Byungsooo-Seo/TUEOD. expressivity in CNN architectures. First, a basic network architecture is created 
with optimal expressivity, followed by a process of strategic expansion where 
new trainable parameters are strategically placed to further increase expressivity 
before final fine-tuning. In comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods, 
ArchiT surpasses their performance levels at multiple benchmark points, as well as 
achieves enhanced generalization at larger parameter counts, while also ensuring 
transparency in its results by adhering to the PAC-Bayes bound principle. Several 
key insights into ArchiT's operation are explored, including observations that 
expressive networks often result in reduced generalization, and alongside overfitting 
and overregularization, there exists an inverse relationship between expressivity and 
generalization abilities. Furthermore, our research indicates that for deep networks 
specially, a network's ability to achieve optimal generalization is heavily dependent 
on the specific placement of expanded parameters. This discovery is reminiscent of 
research findings from previous decades, as well as recent research focusing on 
Spatial Attention Residual Networks, as highlighted in our study. Lastly, our 
research identifies key differences between theoretically optimal architectures and those 
designed via reinforcement learning on challenging benchmark games such as Dino.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models primarily operate within local neighborhoods. To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness. Our method is built on two core components - the first enables the construction of equitable neighborhoods for any node in a graph and the second allows adaptation to accommodate specific data constraints. Notably, while numerous studies have explored link prediction, we delve into fair link classification as part of the graph representation learning task. Through comprehensive evaluations, we showcase the effectiveness of our neighborhood fairness framework across multiple graph machine learning tasks and observe improved accuracy alongside enhanced fairness metrics. Additionally, we provide insight into the nature vs. noise distribution in graph representation learning, aiding in understanding when neighborhood fairness is feasible. Moreover, we develop a method to incrementally train models while maintaining fairness in the unlabelled part of the graph, as well as propose a metric to measure fairness in the labelled subset by attributing bias to the unlabelled subset. All our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashishgupta9/Neighborhood-Fairness. Moreover, we contribute our work to the domain under review via a research proposition presenting novel findings that challenge established assumptions as well as offer practical solutions to existing problems in fair learning. To establish the generalizability of our results, we perform a second review focusing on key extensions and real-world applications of the neighborhood fairness framework in Section 7. This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  For each method, we provide implementing algorithms and demonstrate the convergence of these methods using an iterative scheme.  Further analysis involves assessing the accuracy of resulting approximations by comparing them to exact solutions obtained through Exact Numerical Integration.  Finally, we provide approximate analytical representations of kinetic models for Michaelis-Menten type reactions, facilitating further analysis and examination of these models.  For more details on Exact Numerical Integration, refer to [2].  We conclude by presenting a brief overview of reversible enzyme reactions and their corresponding kinetic models.  For further information, refer to [1].  We have also made available in the online Support Material section: the MATLAB code for implementing these methods and a detailed analysis of the Homoturbation Perturbation Method, including a discussion of its applicability and limitations.  Additionally, we provide an examination of the Equilibrium Approximation, a simplification of kinetic models for reversible reactions, based on the results obtained from Exact Numerical Integration and Approximate Analytical Solutions.  Finally, as an alternative to the Simple Iteration Method, we present an Approximate Analytical Solution derived via the Optimal Iteration Technique from [3]. Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, by replacing words with alternative choices in parallel corpora, selecting points to replace either randomly or with sequence-to-sequence models, to boost the efficiency of CS NLP systems. The effectiveness of these data augmentation methods on neural machine translation models is evaluated in two aspects: the optimum amount of CS words to replace and the performance comparison with the best existing CS datasets in dialectal AR-EN translation. The experiments reveal that data augmentation can enhance the performance of open-source neural MT models and that the best outcome is achieved by replacing 50% of words in each sentence, utilizing a simple CS-AR-EN model for data augmentation, and that the developed approach can increase the performance by 1.5-2.0 BLEU points. Additionally, this study suggests that including CS words from the gold standard parallel corpus, rather than using a trained model, yields a 0.25-0.75 BLEU points improvement. The research also finds that the developed data augmentation method is cost-efficient as it only requires a small number of CS sentences for training and can produce a considerable amount of CS data, 5-10 times the original size of the CS dataset, without needing CS alignment information. In various scientific applications, data is processed using complex hexahedral grids, which are often the preferred choice for numerical computations. However, verifying the accuracy of these grids is a labor-intensive process, especially for large-scale grids. Our research presents an efficient method for validating the precise transformation of hexahedral grids through the open source pyleps library. Utilizing the elastic registration algorithm, which is highly effective in robust parameter estimation, enables seamless transformation mapping. Furthermore, we leverage the properties of hexahedral elements to minimize artificial nodes, thereby reducing the computational requirements. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in processing a standard grid from the GRIDS test collection. Consequently, we derive a precise evolution equation to assess discretization errors in numerical simulations. Ultimately, we outline potential applications and future directions for integrating this method with the GRIDS test collection. Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions, like the existence of a finite-dimensional policy space.
However, in reality, policies often have infinite dimensions, making way for a few
reliable theoretical approaches. These models often come with faster solution derivation
times, but guarantee optimal results only under specific, possibly unrealistic conditions
related to the nature of the Q-function. This research presents a novel method that
exploits a Q-function's lipschitz continuity to reduce the dimensionality of the policy
space and find a closer-to-optimal policy within a limited budget of sample data.
Experimental results demonstrate the efficiency of this approach, especially in terms of
policy dimensionality, and offer up several potential variants for further investigation. 
Additionally, the method can be applied to continuous action spaces with some modifications. 
It's worth noting that this research focuses solely on partial reinforcement learning tasks. 
Therefore, the method's suitability for tasks involving continuous rewards remains to be properly evaluated. 
Before this approach can be considered reliable, several conditions must be thoroughly tested.
To begin with, the assumption of a finite Q-function lipschitz continuity should be examined.
Furthermore, the method's dependence on the Q-function's smoothness makes it incompatible
with a key reinforcement learning property known as the Bellman equation's lipschitz continuity.
This research attempts to address these limitations by exploring possible Q-function
modifications and the condition's implications for reinforcement learning. A thorough
analysis of the method's implications for conservation, the presence of optimal stationary
policies, and the growth rate of the policy space is also presented. A related issue is
raised regarding implicit lower bounds on the required sample data amount for accurate
policy derivation. To to set the stage for the method's implementation, several key
reinforcement learning concepts are defined, including the definitions of stationary policies,
continuous action spaces, Lipschitz continuity, and finite-dimensional spaces. A brief
review of the related literature is presented, highlighting approaches such as linear Q-function
parameter generation and policy gradient methods. A discussion of the method's potential
applications and related research areas is presented, including imitation learning, policy
derivation from several known policies, matrix analysis, Markov decision processes, linear
programming, policy search, policy optimization, reinforcement learning types, stochastic
optimization, state and action discretization, stochastic processes, stochastic programming,
transfer learning, variational auto-encoder, and continuous reinforcement learning tasks.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal boundaries or by the similarity between categories as measured against a common space. In our study, we employed classification-based measures to assess animacy recognition following unilateral LTL MEG-compatible lesions to TC. The results demonstrated that both types of lesions disrupted ventral TC, including the lateral occipital complex, from facilitating animacy classification. In contrast, damage to the parahippocampal cortex had no impact on animacy classification performance. These findings imply that the ventral TC, particularly its lateral occipital component, plays a crucial role in animacy recognition, consistent with theories proposing that animacy is a basic feature across visual objects. Furthermore, animacy was recognized equally well for human and non-human objects, suggesting that the recognition of animacy is rooted in understanding the presence of life. The implications of these findings are discussed in terms of their contributions to theories attempting to explain priming of animal concepts from visual stimuli. In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed transfer empowerment as a method that quantifies the influence between the actions of individual agents and aims to guide MARL agents toward developing reactive approaches. Three simulated cooperation scenarios confirm our hypothesis that this approach leads to improved performance in multi-agent settings, making transfer empowerment a promising principle for enhancing the effectiveness of MARL coordination through increased reactivity to partner behaviors. The corresponding source code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/harbor-ml/marlst. Additionally, we examine the relationship between our definition of transfer empowerment and existing measures of influence within the context of individual agents, revealing key differences and similarities that highlight the unique properties and applications of these concepts. Interestingly, we discover a specific instance where the transfer empowerment of MARL agents differs fundamentally from that of their single-agent counterparts, ultimately contributing to a deeper comprehension of the interactions and dependencies between agents in cooperative tasks. The numerical evaluations we conducted also shed light on the specific characteristics of MARL settings that facilitate the effective transfer empowerment of MARL agents, including tasks requiring coordination and limited action spaces. We observe a corresponding decrease in the effectiveness of these agents in settings that do not meet these criteria, further illustrating their limited applicability. Overall, our approach provides valuable insights into understanding and quantifying influence within the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, while highlighting potential limitations and applied constraints of our findings. The question of whether this principle can be used to enhance communication among MARL agents remains an open and intriguing area of inquiry. As a result, this knowledge can potentially be adapted for use in human-mate team settings, facilitating collaboration and information exchange between members. The empirical findings presented confirm our hypothesis that this principle can be effectively used in such environments, leading to enhanced performance in both cooperative and competitive settings. The effectiveness of this approach was also found to be influenced by factors including team size, level of required cooperation, and available training resources. The presence of these variables makes it challenging to pinpoint a single optimal configuration for the use of transfer empowerment in MARL settings, thereby emphasizing the need for further research into the effective integration of this principle within various teamwork scenarios. We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. By
enabling the identification of similarities between visual materials, our technology
can be applied to various real-world contexts, including monitoring and controlling
the progression of art pieces, predicting the durability of construction materials,
and sorting waste. To create MatSim, we collaborated with a group of participants
to generate a vast collection of 2D and 3D visual materials, paired with manual
descriptions and similarity ratings. We developed an innovative method to train
our model, which achieves state-of-the-art performance in similarity and transition
classification. Additionally, we developed two cutting-edge approaches for
classifying the sequential progression of materials and predicting the degradation of
3D printing objects based on visual appearances alone. Our research and dataset
are now publicly available, enabling further research into the transformation of
materials and encouraging innovative applications of computer vision. The MatSim
dataset can be accessed at https://matsim-dataset.github.io. This research was
supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) grant 1921196. Please note,
the MatSim dataset contains a substantial collection of data and complies with all
relevant rules and regulations, including those related to copyright, intellectual
property, and the avoidance of images containing explicit or objectionable content. 
We utilize synthetic 2D and 3D materials in the MatSim dataset generated from
rendering engines, and we also include data with explicit content to facilitate
research on the removal of such images from databases and the handling of
objectionable content, as detailed in Section 10 of the MatSim dataset. 
We respect existing copyrights and intellectual properties and refrain from
including data from books, academic papers, and other sources, to prevent
copyright infringement and preserve academic integrity. 
We prioritize research-only purposes and collect data from participants who are
capable of providing informed consent for data collection and processing. 
We understand and adhere to the principles of double-blind reviewing as outlined
in the program committee charter and the MatSim dataset policy on author
information. 
We respect the privacy of our dataset contributors, consisting of 2D and 3D
material creators, similarity raters, and synthetic data generators, and
endeavor to remove identifiable information from the dataset. 
We strive to ensure fairness, as outlined in the MatSim dataset policy on
fairness.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of iterative relaxation, we employ a global optimization technique using a Transformer architecture. By substituting local feature descriptors with learned, compact vectors that preserve detail and texture information, we enhance prediction performance in feature matching. Experimental results indicate a significant 22% increase in R@1 and 40% in R@10 indices compared to traditional approaches, with notable success in low-texture areas, where our approach outperforms traditional methods by 55%. Moreover, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on Image Retrieval benchmarks, including BING and ROBUST, while significantly reducing the needed training data to 5% of the original amount through our distinct feature encoding technique. We also derive a shortcut to directly compute feature similarity from patch-level representations, avoiding the usual iterative process and achieving a 2x speedup. Based on this idea, we develop a lightweight object detection system by iteratively refining a single prediction. We further demonstrate the unique capability of our feature matching method to outperform other detectors in knee cases, where existing systems fail. We make our code and trained models available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/10YearsOfGPU/learnedmatching. We plan to further utilize this approach for object detection and image retrieval tasks. A related manuscript with full details is submitted to a top Vision conference in 2023. This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which consumers selfishly aim to minimize their energy bills by scheduling their energy usage in advance. To effectively persuade these consumers to use less energy during peak hours and fairly compensate them, we developed a novel billing scheme that instantiates real-time energy usage charges. Initially, we define an aggregative game to simulate how these consumers strategically interact with one another. By employing variational inequality theory, we identify the circumstances under which the game's equilibrium exists and is unique. To address a situation in which a central control system processes and distributes current load data to consumers, we devised an iterative algorithm with provable convergence that enables these consumers to achieve equilibrium through shared load information. Moreover, in settings where there is no central control, we proposed an information-sharing protocol allowing connected consumers to achieve equilibrium by exchanging their estimated usage data with neighboring consumers. This protocol was analyzed, and it was demonstrated that its implementation results in a stable equilibrium. Furthermore, in a network where a central control system is present, we examined an optimal pricing strategy and proved its existence and uniqueness using our established variational inequality framework. Results from simulation experiments conducted using IEEE test nodes and real-world data from the Irish All-Island Demand-Driven Market revealed a substantial (35.74 percent) decrease in peak-hour energy usage following implementation of our proposed scheme. This reduction was comparable to that resulting from current billing methods in Ireland. In addition, simulation experiments conducted on a graph comprising 200 nodes and 500 edges showed that our proposed scheme effectively reduced congestion on the smart grid. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness relies heavily on the suitability of the chosen kernel. The'm-ar-K-FastICA' approach generates a suitable kernel for ICA based on a specific data subspace, taking advantage of the arcsinh $\equiv \int_{0}^{\infty} \cos(\theta)\sinh(\theta)d\theta$ property to produce independent components from potentially correlated data. By utilizing a constant of proportionality ($m$) that enables scaling to non-linear manifolds, the approach addresses cases where sources may have varied relationships. The'm-ar-K-FastICA' algorithm was developed and tested on different domains, including a synthetic dataset that produced impressive results - it successfully extracted 4 independent components from 7 mixed components with $m=1.5$. The method was also applied to real-world medical data from Electronic Health Records, focusing on asthma patients who were treated with inhaled steroids. Using simulated benchmark data,'m-ar-K-FastICA' outperformed other common feature extraction methods like PCA and ICA when predicting asthma symptoms, including when only a small number of features were selected. In comparison to the widely-used ICA implementation in scikit-learn, the approach produced extracted features that were more relevant to predicting asthma symptoms. Overall,'m-ar-K-FastICA' emerged as a superior feature extraction method in this particular application. The source code for the'm-ar-K-FastICA' approach is available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/omarzakaria/m-ar-K-FastICA. The study also utilized data from the Ohio Medicaid for Asthma Project ('OMAP'), including EMR data from over 14,000 asthma patients who were treated with inhaled steroids. We extend the concept of effective vertex functions to develop multi-body theories for both non-Hermitian and Hermitian systems, yielding a series of solvable orders. We derive the all-orders result for 2-photon scattering using a perturbative approach, matching our findings with a non-perturbative method for exact results. Additionally, we apply the multi-body approach to phenomena such as m-photon transmission spectra with irregular patterns, and Hermitian m-photon scattering with odd parity symmetry. We also show that the multi-body approach can encompass the effects of non-Markovian decay, previously treated as a rate equation, by examining the end-time behavior of the multi-body approach in the long-time limit.

Optimal distributed controller design under communication limitations can be
complicated unless certain system structure conditions, like sparsity or
decoupling, are established. Drawing from graph signal processing principles, we
reframe a basic distributed control problem as a optimization task involving
path-based graph filters. This observation leads us to define Graph Symmetric
Systems, which encompass a subset of systems with subject to structural
decoupling conditions. For Graph Symmetric Systems, we develop a standardized
approach for designing near-optimal distributed controllers via formulaic
derivation. Additionally, we derive specific distributed control strategies for
four fundamental distributed parameter systems, which are among the most common
cases encountered in engineering. Our research offers a unified framework for
these common control systems and provides parametric control formulas, which
can be computed in polynomial time. We demonstrate that these controllers
exhibit optimal closed-loop performance when the system is Graph Symmetric and
satisfies certain condition related to the resistance distance matrix. Specifically,
this means that Graph Symmetric Systems with a resistance matrix satisfying the
Feller condition enable the derivation of optimal controllers for dynamic systems. 
This research offers the first general solution to distributed optimal controller
design for a broad class of control systems under communication limitations. For
the general case, we establish a comprehensive analysis of the design's
computational complexity and optimality, which depends on the system's
configuration and communication topology. Ultimately, this work showcases the
power of linear system representation and graph theoretical properties in
optimal distributed control design. The findings presented provide concrete
answers to the following questions: (1) Which systems allow for the derivation of
optimal controllers through standard design methods? (2) Which systems ensure
the derived controllers yield the best possible closed-loop performance? (3)
What system characteristics ensure the existence of optimal controllers with
arbitrarily small communication bandwidth. The research conducted was presented at
the 2021 American Control Conference. The corresponding code for executing the
research findings can be accessed at https://github.com/GraciaL/Graph-Symmetric-Systems. 
This work has been accepted for publication in the journal IEEE Transactions on
Automatic Control. A expanded version of the research, which includes additional
analytical findings, is available under the title "Graph Signal Processing for
Distributed Control: Graph Symmetric Systems and Structural Systems". The
research conducted was performed within the AutoGraph: Graphs for Control Systems
project, which is supported by the grant ANR

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing, a search method that interacts with the neural network to optimize the retrieval and accuracy of copied images. Active indexing achieves this by selectively discarding parts of the vector that are unlikely to contain valuable information, thereby improving the precision of image retrieval and cutting retrieval time by 10-50% through a more efficient comparison process. Moreover, active indexing enhances the precision of image copy detection and maximizes the detection rate of relevant images. This technology is now commercially deployed in a mobile app. Active indexing can be applied across neural networks and other machine learning systems, and its utility is not limited to image search; it can be used in a wide range of deep learning-based vector search applications, including automatic speech and text recognition and classification. This paper outlines active indexing, its motivations, benefits, and use cases, and provides a comparative analysis of its performance with existing, top techniques in the field of image search algorithms. All sources and documentation for this paper are publicly available on GitHub under https://github.com/appliedmachinelearning/ams-100nec/tree/master/100nec/100nec. A live demonstration of active indexing can be seen at http://100nec.com. Active indexing has significant potential to improve the precision and speed of image search algorithms, and its applications extend beyond image search to include deep learning-based systems such as automatic speech and text recognition and classification. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each mention. However, the common approach to acquire gold standards involves labor-intensive human annotations, making it impractical for widespread applications. In this research, FG-NET is modeled as a hyperbolic embedding task, leveraging the hyperbolic space's property that distances accurately model hierarchical relationships. Initial experiments were conducted on the Subtree Node Labeling dataset, producing promising results. However, the proposed method was not directly applicable to more complex datasets like TAC 2021. To address this, FG-NET was framed as a multi-label classification task using BERT and Bounded Context Matching, achieving a 71.3% macro average F1-score without prior knowledge. Furthermore, the proposed method reached state-of-the-art performance when incorporating previous benchmarks. Our analysis highlighted issues with TAC 2021 data labeling and proposed a new development pipeline. The code and model have been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ashishsingh160/FG-NET. This research demonstrates the potential of the hyperbolic space to effectively model FG-NET data, underscoring the need to revisit existing datasets to ensure their integrity in producing reliable results. Additionally, the hyperbolic space offers a valuable framework, making FG-NET easier to model and potentially increasing its popularity. Based on our analysis, we recommend splitting the FG-NET task into sub-tasks, such as initial entity detection and typing, to be handled by separate models. The proposed multi-task approach allows the models to be at least as effective as single-task models, offering improved performance. Ultimately, the multi-task approach, aided by the hyperbolic space, demonstrates considerable potential in enhancing FG-NET models. Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely relies on load balancing, and virtualization enables this by using a proactive approach to prevent server overload. This involves predicting and addressing potential problems before they cause issues, and comparing the effectiveness of different methods is challenging without actual data.  Existing research has focused on either migrating virtual machines based on load and resource allocation, but the load balancing mechanism is usually reactive, and the entire system is treated as a single unit. 

We introduce a method of proactive load balancing that considers future loads when allocating virtual machines, and to address the system's finite size, we also introduce a new concept called Prepartition. This involves initially dividing the system into sections based on expected loads, and assigning virtual machines to the corresponding sections based on their load requirements. 

This approach, combined with reactive migration, enhances load balancing and reduces the costs of disk migration. We compare the effectiveness of our method, Prepartition, with traditional load balancing in terms of disk migration costs, and our results show that it achieves better balance with the same migration costs, and leads to a 15% cost reduction when accompanied by 20-30% fewer disk migrations.

To evaluate the computational efficiency of our method, we analyzed its time complexity and found that it is comparable to other load balancing methods, and takes an average of 100 milliseconds to allocate a virtual machine.

This study examines the ability of EvoCrash, a stack-based crash reproducer, in comparing to JCHARMING, a technique for automatically crashing and reproducing faults in software systems.  We use two applications, Kaluza-Zeit and JFreeChart, for our comparison, selecting failures from JCHARMING that could be replicated as stack-based failures and feeding these to EvoCrash for crash generation.  Our results reveal that EvoCrash successfully created crashes in both programs using five-minute time frames, similar to JCHARMING in six applications with over fifty unique crashes per program.  Our evaluation shows that approximately 87.5% of JCHARMING crashes matched EvoCrash's crashes.  Furthermore, we discovered that 75.6% of EvoCrash crashes were present in JCHARMING's dataset prior to model learning.  Our investigation into the source of non-matching crashes following EvoCrash suggest that EvoCrash may be missing certain anomalies in program behavior due to its reliance on normal program execution data in learning its models.  To rectify this shortcoming, we developed an EvoCrash modification where it is trained using crashes in addition to normal program behavior, resulting in 85% match in crashes between EvoCrash and JCHARMING.  Our study demonstrates potential synergies between JCHARMING and EvoCrash in enhancing software testing and validation processes.  Ultimately, based on our findings, we propose a novel, synergistic approach for utilizing EvoCrash and JCHARMING in conjunction to facilitate software exploration and testing, which we term the E^2 approach.  Under the E^2 approach, we evaluate a novel, more effective form of symbolic exploration called Z3 exploration that leverages the capabilities of Z3.  Our results show that the E^2 approach can increase the number of unique failures in Kaluza-Zeit by 42% over EvoCrash and JCHARMING, offering a valuable addition to software testing and validation tools.  Our exploration and crash dataset for Kaluza-Zeit and JFreeChart are publicly accessible at https://github.com/yasdasan/E1. Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for certain spin models with global spin rotations symmetries, focusing on group theoretical methods for triangular and kagome lattices. These regular magnetic orders hold significance as potential ground states for various spin models, making them prime candidates for study. Using the Artin generator formulation, we have employed a systematic approach to determining the toric code spectra and other related lattice models, applying the same methodology to these spin models. Our analysis for the triangular and kagome lattices is comprehensive, encompassing all possible regular magnetic orders, regardless of band numbering. For each configuration, we have explicitly calculated the corresponding Wilson lines, enabling the computation of the RMO spectra. Our findings confirm that no nontrivial regular magnetic orders exist for spin-1/2 models on these lattices, contradicting a recent claim stating otherwise for the triangular lattice. Furthermore, we have explored spin-1 models on the triangular and kagome lattices, determining the effects of degeneracy on the RMO spectra and identifying a nontrivial regular magnetic order for the spin-1 triangular lattice, which cannot be achieved by spin-1/2 models. Our work enhances the understanding of the RMO framework, broadening its applications and insights into spin models. Moreover, we have discovered a novel connection between the failure of a dual map in certain regular magnetic orders and the presence of unphysical constant modes in the dual lattice, which emerges from enforcing symmetry conditions. Our findings are significant in the context of developing a systematic approach to studying spin models, particularly those with global spin rotations symmetry, through group theoretical methods. The three-dimensional versions of these lattice models remain unexplored but are sure to pose even more compelling challenges and questions. Our study lays the groundwork for investigating the regular magnetic order for general lattice configurations, opening up opportunities for further research in the RMO framework. The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented. Furthermore, we outline the process of particle creation and how it results in the generation of matter's initial density gradient prior to the onset of radiation-dominated era. In addition, we discuss the physical process of adiabatic perturbation and the stochastic realization of inflation, which relies on random sampling within the causally disconnected horizon, pre-existing in the super-horizon field state. A novel, straightforward approach for stochastic inflation is proposed, where we consider two types of stochastic operators: within the Hubble radius, and outside it, with the condition of causal separation. This approach yields stochastic inflation with minimal inside influence from the outside world, without relying on any specific Hamiltonian representation and without causing violations of unitarity, which are typically requirements for this type of study. By applying this approach to two models, the linear and quadratic potential inflation, we use numerical sampling to illustrate how one can use an operator that is outside the Hamiltonian representation to introduce randomness into the system, which could be crucial for understanding the random causal influence of pre-existing super-horizon fields on the adiabatic perturbations of interest in current and future CMB experiments. The derivation of perturbation equations for quadratic potential inflation is presented in detail, including how one can use an e-folding clock to create these perturbations. The newly introduced method could have significant implications for research into stochastic cosmological processes, potentially uncovering unknown cosmic history, field dynamics or external influences, which may exist outside our current understanding. The code used for numerical analysis in this study is provided in Ref. [40]. The numerical analysis presented in this study focuses on an inflationary model, which could have been previously overlooked in the literature due to the lack of required mathematical tools to derive perturbation equations for this model. The FNAL muon magnetic moment measurement also displays a $4.2\sigma$ discrepancy. In an effort to resolve the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2), we have investigated the type-X two Higgs doublet model. Our analysis focused on the area in the type-X 2HDM parameter space that is consistent with the muon (g-2) and W boson mass measurements, and our results show that it can explain the anomalies while meeting ongoing electroweak data requirements. To validate our results, we examined the type-X 2HFD model's decays of the charged Higgs and heavy neutral scalar into muon pairs, and our findings were compared with recent CMS searches. In addition, our results for the type-X 2HFD model's constraints from muon (g-2) measurements are provided. Our study shows that for certain choices of the type-X 2HFD decay modes, the anomalies in both the W boson and muon (g-2) can be explained by considering a common source of new physics. Ultimately, our results may lead to the cancellation of one or both discrepancies if both observed anomalies have the same origin. Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, occurs when two individuals adjust their communication patterns to coordinate with each other, either subtly or significantly. To understand this adaptive coordination process, researchers are focusing on the automatic detection of acoustic characteristics that reflect the speakers' natural speech patterns. To this end, a new method using pre-trained Transformer models has been developed to identify speaker-specific features from paired speech inputs. The proposed multi-head self-attention architecture, based on the BERT model, can automatically identify patterns unique to each speaker that were previously defined through human annotation. The optimized model, known as the Entrainment Detection model (EDet), achieves high accuracy in detecting entrainment signals, even when the interaction duration is as short as 2 seconds. The model performs comparably to human experts in evaluating entrainment, evaluating pairs of individuals engaging in synchronized conversations. The analysis revealed that the speaker-specific features identified by the Transformer models contribute significantly to entrainment detection. The study provides new insights into how entrainment is perceived through acoustic features and sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of adaptive coordination in human communication. The research opens up new avenues for using AI to detect and analyze social interaction signals from spoken language, enabling more in-depth understanding of entrainment processes. analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Vue.js web technologies to build engaging,
interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, and diagnostic diagrams,
such as BPT diagrams generated from spectroscopic analysis. Leveraging client-side
processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining panning, zooming,
and data filtering capabilities on the client-side also enables seamless navigation.

visualization database that links user submissions to underlying analysis data.
Lastly, we outline potential future improvements for further development.

Many current domain adaptation techniques, however, are yet to achieve satisfactory performance when dealing with large-scale and real-world distribution mismatches. To address this issue, we propose a novel method that leverages semi-supervised learning and adversarial learning known as semi-supervised mutual enhancement. This approach combines the benefits of semi-supervised and adversarial learning to achieve more robust domain adaptation in cases of limited labeled data. Experimental results on notable benchmarks like Waymo and KITTI and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach. This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in time-projection chamber technology for dark matter exploration. Characteristic signals within these TPCs facilitate detector component identification, allowing the visualization and analysis of signal patterns to determine detector performance. An innovative Domain-informed Neural Network architecture surpasses traditional multilayer perceptron models in localized signal prediction, offering improved accuracy and faster training compared to traditional neural network methods. Furthermore, analysis reveals that this novel network's findings align with expected detector operations, as evidenced by active and passive radioactive decay analysis. Active decay shows the network accurately identifying electron paths even at low electron energies of approximately 0.38 MeV or less. This research examines the impact of disorder on the correlation between bulk and edge states in two-dimensional topological insulators of higher order. We specifically focus on samples with elliptical shape, exhibiting hinge states protected by non-symmetry, and find that disorder can't destroy these hinge states. Additionally, we find that bulk edge correspondence persists even with the disorder applied uniformly in elliptical samples. However, when the disorder is tailored to break specific symmetries, it can lead to a phase change in a finite portion of the sample while maintaining the hinge states. This topological phase change is influenced by the ratio of elliptical radius to hole radius, exhibiting topological robustness. We also identify another type of topology, defined by a donut-shaped sample, exhibiting both bulk and edge states. This donut sample displays a similar response to disorder, maintaining the topological robustness. We utilize the topological robustness of corner states as a reference point to develop a metric for measuring symmetry breaking in a finite system. This metric allows the detection of symmetry breaking in a finite system through analysis of bulk edge correspondence. We further propose an experimental method, observing signals from corner states that have remained unchanged despite the disorder, resulting from the total reflection of corner states at a flat band. This method can be applied across various systems without altering the Hamiltonian. This research provides a new approach to studying topological insulators and developing novel devices based on robust corner states. Furthermore, the development of a metric for measuring symmetry breaking in a finite system can serve as an essential tool across multiple fields. Recent searches for supersymmetry at the classical level have not provided any conclusive signs of new physics. In response, the CMS is implementing specialized searches aimed at more complex and precise supersymmetry scenarios. This contribution will focus on three new searches using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS detector between 2016 and 2018: a heavy gluino search involving the decay of heavy neutralinos and resulting in boosted $ZZ$ boson pairs, a search for supersymmetry compression in final states dominated by soft tau leptons, and an investigation of compressed, long-lived charginos in lightweight gravoaxial chargino-neutralino pair decays, characterized by unconventional tracks and non-physics signatures. These analyses are part of a broader effort to study the diversity of supersymmetry models, which will increase our understanding of the superspectrum. Furthermore, the results will be presented in terms of simplified models, revealing valuable insights into the properties of heavy particles. In addition, the development of machine learning and unstructured data algorithms has significantly enhanced the detection capabilities of these new searches by enabling efficient sifting through complex data. By incorporating advanced data analysis techniques, we are exploring the limits of detectability for a wide range of supersymmetry models, which will soon encompass models with natural supersymmetry, leading to more comprehensive findings. At the time of submission, the data analysis results yield lower limits on the mass of supersymmetric particles, with further results anticipated from the findings of Run-2's data analysis, including LHC results from 2015-2019, which are set to be presented at the Moriond QCD conference in March 2019. In addition, the analysis findings will be shared with theoretical physicists for further study, offering a valuable platform for discussion between experimental and theoretical researchers. Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate reproduction of view-dependent phenomena by densely sampling a scene's views, yet these phenomena are often overlooked in existing geometry-based rendering methods. The model LFRAN, proposed in this work, utilizes a four-dimensional light field representation to replicate the appearance of densely viewed scenes. Notably, LFRAN leverages the four-dimensional representation's inherent spatial and temporal consistency to represent arbitrary view-dependent effects, thereby expanding the traditional light field framework's representation power. Through optimal alignment of geometric features, LFRAN also enables precise reconstruction of view-invariant scene structures. The model further replicates occlusion and ambient lighting across views using two-dimensional occlusion and ambient maps. Comprehensive evaluations on real-world and synthetic datasets reveal that LFRAN surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in reproducing densely viewed scenes with significant view-dependent phenomena. Specifically, LFRAN surpasses existing models in replicating geometric details, occlusion, and ambient lighting. A key advantage of LFRAN is the substantial decrease in required input views for realistic novel view synthesis compared to previous approaches. The model also yields minimal view-dependent distortions and signification accuracy boosts with fewer input views, making it a valuable addition to previous work. A user-friendly, web-based demo of LFRAN is available at: https://shirikawa.github.io/LFRAN/. The source code and trained models have been deposited on https://github.com/shirikawa/LFRAN. This probabilistic solution provides a general framework for solving boundary value problems through random sampling, with the presented example being a circular sector with a boundary consisting of equilateral triangles and circles. Finally, we illustrate random vortex dynamics as a real-time simulation in an interactive web browser, allowing for the exploration of various interfaces and initial conditions. The state of system's sampling involves gathering data on a specific correlation function derived from sampling another function, essentially applying a second round of probability sampling. Research has demonstrated a relationship between this process and the system's mode expansion, revealing that the system's initial state can be fully reconstructed by accessing all modes for specific states. Our study focuses on boson sampling, specifically a non-degenerate, multi-mode system based on laser propagation, to optimize for highest entropy. To achieve this, we calculate the maximum entropy and determine it linearly proportional to the number of used modes. Furthermore, we examine mode coupling in an $LC$ circuit driven by coherent laser pulses and observe strong coupling between certain modes. The system's ability to reach the maximum allowed entropy depends on the strength of this coupling, specifically how it affects the distribution of path intensities. Our analysis also enables the recovery of the system's initial state, an outcome only possible with the coupled mode configuration, an effect entirely caused by using multiple modes. Our work highlights the complexity of reaching the system's initial state due to the influence of mode coupling. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for boson sampling and the realization of high-entropy states. Our work sets the foundation for exploring the influence of specific coupling on path intensities and phase space distribution, an area we plan to investigate in a future study. We present a novel technique, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), which leverages parallel processing for real-time predictions. By incorporating temporal information into the topographic mapping of massive datasets, SGTM-TT enables fast and accurate predictions. We've successfully tested SGTM-TT across various synthetic and real-world scenarios, including the prediction of microbial populations under environmental changes conditions. Its high predictive accuracy makes it a suitable tool for applications like predicting the dynamics of microbial populations, detecting rare cells, and performing other complex predictions. Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies to achieve long-term goals in various tasks, often characterized by temporal disconnection. A novel neural reinforcement learning method uses a recurrent neural network to process sequential data, incorporating past experiences into the policy to boost expected outcomes. The method presented in this study enhances this approach by increasing its information intake from the environment, resulting in higher long-term rewards. The modified algorithm not only improves performance but also reduces variance in its performance metrics, such as expected return and standard deviation. We examine two variants of this technique: one that combines policy and value network weights and another that separates them, observing better performance with the combined approach in common benchmark tests. We also analyze the method's capacity to learn from examples through comparative studies with random walk baselines and other reinforcement learning methods. Theoretical analysis suggests that the rate at which the algorithm's performance improves is directly related to the amount of available data. To validate this prediction, we perform a test where we simulate multiple instances of the same environment in parallel, observing better performance with the data-aggregating technique. The method's code is available online for reference. A significant limitation of this technique is its high computational demands, making it impractical for some tasks. Therefore, we discuss potential methods to make it more efficient, such as increasing the memory of the recurrent neural network and merging multiple environments to accelerate learning while minimizing variance. The potential applications of this technique extend beyond reinforcement learning, potentially benefiting other supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. A significant unexplored area of research is extending this technique to online learning scenarios, where the algorithm must be able to adapt to changes in the environment over time. We identify a method to make the technique suitable for online learning, involving regular training sessions with frozen networks to preserve knowledge between sessions. The theoretical analysis of this technique raises further questions about performance decay, which we investigate through a comparative study of different techniques to preserve performance across multiple sessions. The method presented in this study represents an essential step towards answering these questions and addressing the significant challenge of online reinforcement learning. The technique's adaptability to different reward structures, such as episodic and continuous rewards, makes it applicable to a wide range of real-world reinforcement learning tasks. In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D convolutional networks.  However, we believe that understanding an action involves also considering its context - objects and individuals within a video scene - so we've developed a novel framework integrating self-attention and graph convolutional networks to better model context dependencies.  This approach, using context information derived from object detection, has yielded impressive results in action localization with a significant reduction in 'false positives', even when using lighter object detection outputs.  We've supported our method's effectiveness with successful applications in generic action detection and a new task we've introduced - distinguishing between aggressive and non-aggressive actions based on observed object interactions.  Action localization codes are now available on the GhpyTorch repository at https://github.com/dvpham/AggroLoc.  We've contributed a new dataset for aggressive forecasting - a dataset for aggressive action detection, which we'll make public at a later time due to ethical considerations.  Our work has been presented at ICCV 2019 in Ericeira, Portugal.  We've demonstrated that integrating context information leads to better end-to-end performance in multi-scale object detection and action localization.  We've also shown that distinguishing between aggressive and non-aggressive actions is feasible given context information, which we've often omitted in previous studies.  We argue that distinguishing between aggressive and non-aggressive actions is a challenging task that has been undersized in previous studies - we've focused on predicting binary outcomes rather than continuous aggressive scores.  We've also found that context information enhances predictive power - we've achieved a significant 19.2% increase in accuracy based on a grid search, adding context information, regardless of the graph convolutional network's structure.  We've also carried out ablation studies to investigate the effect of graph size and position on end-to-end performance.  We've discovered that spatiotemporal action detection benefits from context information, albeit to a varying extent based on action type - we've achieved a 5% increase in mAP for actions involving group interactions but only a 1% increase for individual actions.  We've also found that context information benefits forecasting - we've achieved a significant 6.3% increase in average precision for aggressive forecasting.  We've also conducted a study to assess the impact of object detection quality on action localization and discovered that spatiotemporal action detection benefits from object detection to a significant extent. This new map has facilitated a breakthrough understanding of the UV luminosity properties across the complex. Researchers discovered that the diffuse UV radiation in the area can be attributed to the absorption of Lyman continuum radiation from nearby quasars and blazars, based on simulations using the SKY3D framework. However, the absorption lines in the spectrum, primarily stemming from H I in interstellar media, enhance the apparent luminosity by about two-fold. Moreover, the estimated total luminosity of the galaxy continuum in the area is approximately 10^6 L⊙, which is comparable to the contribution made by young star-forming regions in the complex, as observed in the far-ultraviolet band. Ultimately, the observed UV properties across the complex may be shaped by the interplay between the distribution of Lyman-continuum sources and young star-forming regions, and this interaction needs to be accounted for in the predictions of UV radiation across the complex. Therefore, a revised prediction is needed with the inclusion of Lyman continuum absorption and recognition of its impact on the UV background radiation. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, successfully applying it to a scenario where players make sequential decisions based on an evolving, non-stationary state space. In contrast to classical computing, which experiences increasing bottlenecks with growing datasets, our quantum approach leads to faster learning and reduced computation time as the dataset size increases. Nonetheless, our findings indicate that achieving stable clusters at the cost of minimal error depends on a delicate balance of quantum resource allocation, particularly the number of measurements, ancilla qubits, and training samples. This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in videos by employing object persistence principles. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects throughout a video, even when they are obscured, covered or carried by other objects. Currently prevalent deep learning based methods exhibit spatiotemporal biases when applied to video-based reasoning problems. We introduce a model named Hopper that employs a multi-hop transformer to deduce object persistence in videos by iteratively skipping key frames to accurately predict the final location of the target object, given both video content and localization information. Furthermore, our proposed model benefits from using a contrastive loss to counter spatiotemporal biases. Evaluating Hopper on widely used video-based reasoning datasets indicates its superiority over current prevailing methods. We demonstrate Hopper's effectiveness across various object persistence tasks and configure it to solve an example test video. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear functions. This new algorithm uniquely estimates expert parameters through an analysis of the cross-moment tensor between inputs and outputs. While it still necessitates an EM algorithm to recover gating parameters, the proposed approach simplifies this process and significantly improves convergence compared to existing methods, leading to enhanced performance on both simulated and real-world data sets when compared to standard baselines. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that learning the first-order cross-moment tensor is sufficient for accurately recovering the underlying MoE model parameters. This finding offers a promising framework for tackling other demanding learning problems. The paper provides a comprehensive framework that combines theoretical insights into learning MoE models with a new algorithm capable of consistently estimating its parameters for a wide range of non-linear functions. It also presents an alternative volume-scan algorithm for recovering gating parameters, an approach that can be applied even in scenarios where output moments are unavailable. Experiments were conducted using a combination of simulated and real data sets, including the MNIST dataset developed by DBertini et al. in 2011. The results reveal that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms existing baselines on a large number of these data sets. The paper concludes by illustrating the efficacy of the proposed algorithm on the Stanford Visual Learning Assistant (SVEA) by demonstrating its ability to separate distinct visual attributes like shape, color, and texture. This study offers a promising framework that can be applied to other complex learning problems, potentially leading to novel applications in visual information extraction. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. A potential explanation for this phenomenon could be a very light, electromagnetically interacting pseudoscalar field, which must be protected from the effects of gravity. We demonstrate that a certain upper limit on the gravitational disruption of global symmetries would be required for this scenario to be feasible. Such a bound would have far-reaching implications, influencing the development of theories of quantum gravity as well as numerous models in particle physics. We derive a straightforward model-independent constraint for the gravitational disruption of global symmetries. Although primarily obtained by eliminating the primordial tensor mode, our bound could also be relevant to theories with dark matter that exceed the present epoch's kinetic scale. Furthermore, we illustrate that gravity in asymptotically safe quantum gravity cannot significantly disrupt global symmetries, provided a certain condition is met. This condition is randomly sampled from a probability distribution, which is equivalent to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ constraints. Consequently, we obtain a lower bound for the QGR scale, which stands at around one Gigaelectronvolt. Ultimately, we find that maintaining global symmetries in quantum gravity may be possible across a wide range of scales, from the electroweak scale to the Planck scale. Such findings have significant implications for numerous models in particle physics as well as the theory of asymptotically free quantum chromodynamics. As a side note, we show that globally symmetric non-commutative geometry is consistent with this bound. Consequently, the gauge field instantons can be incorporated into this bound, which in turn may help to resolve the matter-antimatter asymmetry problem in the early universe. Lastly, we find that maintaining global symmetries in the early universe may have prevented it from reaching a series of widely-known singularity types, including the Hartle-Hawking singularity. This finding could have far-reaching implications for cosmology. This capability is referred to as domain transferability. This research investigates why the transferability of pre-trained DNNs often declines as they are processed further down stream. Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems, where the traditional perception of a service - executing a specific function with a defined outcome - is shifting towards a more nuanced understanding: a service is an operation that can be viewed from the consumer's perspective. As a result, services are classified into procedures and relations, with procedures delivering explicit results and relations not providing any feedback or return values. Furthermore, services can be considered as part of larger, composite relations. To facilitate service composition, novel concepts are introduced: operations that consume relations as inputs and produce relational results; relations that can exist in multiple states (active, finished); and mechanisms allowing for state-based management of relations. An formal algebra is defined to describe the behavior of relations, including union, restriction, and selection operations that enable service composition. To address issues related to error handling, the concept of selective union is introduced, effectively handling cases where operations either succeed or fail (but not both). A formal algebraic framework for composing services as relations has potential to enhance current service orchestration techniques, and is intended to offer a foundation for future compositions at higher abstraction levels. 

Key Words: Service-oriented Computing, Service Abstraction, Service Composition, Service Reconciliation.

Conversely, this new framework accurately predicts the AI system's performance in the new environment. The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was a significant innovation in entropy encoding developed by Duda, revolutionizing data compression by surpassing the capabilities of arithmetic and Huffman coding. Despite its optimality being studied by Duda et al., the asymptotic redundancy of ANS, relative to entropy, remained unclear. This paper provides a precise bound on the redundancy for the table-based ANS (tANS), the most prevalent variant, and reveals that tANS encoders can be improved by initiating sequences of prefix codes instead of Duda's method. Specifically, we demonstrate that tANS encoders using this initialization approach yield optimal prefixes with zero redundancy. This improvement not only reduces redundancy but also eliminates instances of negative redundancy, thereby making tANS more efficient. To validate this optimization, we have developed a software tool to simulate tANS encoders and decoders, which are available for research purposes. This research also sets the foundation for exploring the conditions under which tANS can achieve zero redundancy in practice. Furthermore, we propose a general framework called Asymmetric Prefix Codes (APC), which encompasses both ANS and a broader class of codes, thereby providing valuable insights into their optical and structural limitations. Additionally, APC provides a framework for optimizing the conditions under which lower bounded redundancy is achieved in ANS. This research is consequently discussed in terms of its implications for the optimal entropy encoding of data. The paper is accompanied by supplementary code at https://github.com/AdityaPR/AsymmetricPrefixCodes. A previous version of this paper was presented at the Data Compression Conference 2022. A related investigation into the optimal segmentation strategies for ANS is conducted in a companion study, thereby confirming the results by providing multiple proofs and use cases. This research is further validated through a study on the optimal segmentation techniques for ANS, which is described in a companion paper titled Optimal ANS Segmentation. A theoretical analysis of ANS's ability to achieve zero redundancy under certain conditions is also conducted in a follow-up publication titled Achieving Zero Redundancy in ANS. A final investigation into the optimal initialization approach for tANS encoders is carried out in a follow-up paper titled Optimal tANS Initialization. A comprehensive review of APC's structure, comprising a more general code framework, is presented in a follow-up publication titled Asymmetric Prefix Codes: A Comprehensive Framework. Over the past thirty years, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze intricate systems. This research aims to compare their effectiveness by using a simplified metric to measure system complexity. By applying the complexity metric to simulate a variety of scenarios, such as Hebbian learning in simple neural networks, it can predict the evolution of these systems. To validate the application of the complexity metric to neural networks, simulations of two types of learning algorithms, Hebbian and Hebbian contrastive, were conducted. These simulations involved fully-connected networks with random weights, which showed that the complexity metric correctly identified and mirrored the known behaviors of these systems as their weights evolved over time. Next, the complexity metric was used to analyze the dynamics of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) over time. To do this, it was observed how the complexity of RNNs changed as they were trained using Hebbian and contrastive Hebbian learning algorithms. This research demonstrated that the expected increases in system complexity, corresponding to breakthroughs in problem-solving and the adaptation of stable patterns within the networks, were accurately forecasted by the metric. Furthermore, the complexity metric was used to examine the unique characteristics of RNNs, known as bottle-neck structures, which facilitate the flow of information within these systems. This research showed that the expected growth of information flow through these structures, linked with increases in system complexity, was accurately forecasted by the metric. Overall, it was determined that the simplicity of the metric, rooted in the fundamental principles of information theory, makes it a valuable tool for analyzing the dynamics of neural systems. As such, it has the potential to further our understanding of how these systems solve problems and adapt over time. Moreover, it is hoped that the metric may also be applied to other intricate systems, beyond neural networks, to gain insights into their behavior. In addition, it is suggested that the metric may also be used as a guide to aid in developing algorithms that efficiently use resources, such as the case with Hebbian learning algorithms, which often achieve their goals through efficient use of resources. Finally, it is hoped that the metric may also be used as a tool to help identify unique characteristics of algorithmic patterns within these systems, which may otherwise remain unknown. To enable this, we developed an affordable, easy-to-set up optical sensor on each robot that can detect diverse hand gestures in real-time. Our experiments, comprising both simulated and real-world tests with 10m x 10m areas, have successfully demonstrated the feasibility of this approach. Our robots, which are enabled with general kinematic motion capabilities, can be controlled to move locally. In our experiments, we examined the accuracy of the optical sensor in detecting different hand gestures while the robots are in motion. Our vision is that this technology can enable a person to easily control a large robot swarm with minimal training, thus reducing costs. In the near future, we aim to explore ways to improve the robot motion model and increase the optical sensor's recognition capabilities. Additionally, we aim to investigate methods for efficiently encoding different hand gestures and optimizing the leader-follower strategy in the robot swarm. This research can be further extended to investigate optimal strategies for efficiently utilizing the optical sensor to detect larger numbers of gestures.
