A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential. Research demonstrates that these potentials can be accurately approximated using machine learning techniques, applied to a simplified model. By training an artificial neural network on a limited set of data, the protocol is generalized to new, unseen states with high accuracy. This breakthrough enables the discovery of complex, non-trivial paths connecting initial and target states that could not be reached through traditional adiabatic methods. Moreover, the study reveals the potential for an inverse approach, where the original gauge potential is predicted based on knowledge of the supporting potential and target state. These results offer an exciting perspective on the integration of artificial neural networks and counterdiabatic methods in controlling quantum systems. Furthermore, the potential for extending these methods to more complex quantum systems, like Rydberg atoms, is also explored. By leveraging these atoms, the protocol is driven in a non-linear fashion, adding an extra layer of complexity to the system. As a result, the training data is generated from a few thousand random Rydberg gates, the artificial neural network is able to generalize to new, unseen gates with high accuracy, predicting the required, supporting potential to drive the system to a target state. This breakthrough presents an important step towards utilizing machine learning and counterdiabatic methods in controlling complex quantum systems, particularly in new platforms like Rydberg atoms, where the development of optimal, gauge-closed paths is hindered by the existence of system degeneracies. In this context, the support of counterdiabatic methods by artificial neural networks becomes crucial in enabling the discovery of these paths, potentially facilitating the design of new, sophisticated quantum gates and accelerating the development of quantum technologies. As a final note, the potential for applying the artificial neural network approach in other areas, such as learning quantum Hamiltonians, is also explored and presented as an open research question. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data for languages other than English severely hampers progress in these fields. To fill this void, we utilize Kaldi to develop German acoustic models utilizing datasets under a Creative Commons license. This has the added benefit of making use of spoken data from Wikipedia, thereby making ASR possible in this domain without necessitating transcription. After evaluating various data combinations, it's discovered that incorporating the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus enhances model performance, possibly due to the inherent regularities of spoken Wikipedia data facilitating better outcomes. Next, we examine and optimize potential improvements for German ASR, focusing on data augmentation methods, hyperparameter modifications, and cutting-edge model architectures. The experiments yield the best results when using a Res2Net architecture, mixed-norm NNet+T speaker models, and an ensemble approach, achieving a word error rate of 25.35% on the Tuda-G dataset. The project's source code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/AndreBerthelhaud/german-asr. Moreover, model results for the Tuda-G, AISbc, VMou, VMu, RTM, TED, CVS, CVS_T, SwEG, EG, EG_T, DEBU, DBU, DBU_T and SwDBU datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/AndreBerthelhaud/german-asr/tree/master/models. Lastly, models trained on the AISbc and SwDBU datasets display notable performance in the Wildfire ASR challenge, achieving first and second place respectively. The corresponding model submission can be found at https://challenge.workshop-2019.ai.isy.liu.se/submissions/38/. The models' functionality has also been assessed in terms of fairness using the F2F tool, with the results indicating a notable disparity between the performance of male and female models, with the models trained on SwDBU exhibiting the smallest fairness gap. The analysis of these results points to the potential for leveraging data augmentation methods, specifically speed perturbation, and model architecture modifications to mitigate fairness concerns. The investigation of ASR metrics other than WER has been initiated, with the aim of exploring its utility in evaluating models' fairness. The results indicate speed perturbation to be an efficient approach for improving female model performance, with the potential to have a complementary effect when combined with a late-fusion ensemble. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier work focusing on a single kernel to represent the entire network. We validate the effectiveness of this model on two datasets, revealing that it successfully reveals the intricate relationships between the network's layers and its predictive abilities. Moreover, by analyzing the HTK, we gain valuable insights into the layer-specific characteristics that distinguish our network from randomly initialized models. Our research not only broadens the neural tangent kernel application, but also provides a unique framework for understanding and exploring the inner workings of deep neural networks. As a result, we hypothesize that our kernel-based model could serve as an invaluable tool for decision-making in real-world scenarios where transparency is crucial, such as in healthcare. A radiative seesaw model producing sub-GeV fermion dark matter through Compton-like processes has been proposed. In this interpretation, dark matter exists as a state separated from ordinary matter in terms of energy and is not a typical example of weakly interacting massive particle dark matter. The ordinary matter particle acts as a "dark sun" emitting and absorbing dark matter candidate fermions, a process influenced by a new interaction. The model's particle spectrum is defined by a system of lattice Lagrangian parameters, with certain parameters directly linked to dark matter mass within specific mass ranges. Despite this simplicity, our simulation shows significant variation in likelihood peaks for different mass settings, a characteristic that remains consistent even when considering the effects of additional particles. The model's fermion dark matter candidate has been discovered to be most likely when it's around 100 MeV, a range that's strictly limited by experimental data. In addition to this, we've specifically looked at the distinct mass settings of 200-500 and 500-800 MeV for dark matter candidate fermions, each with implications that might be testable in future experiments. Lastly, we've found that the likelihood peaks for both of these ranges are shifted towards lower masses when self-interactions between the dark matter candidate are stronger, a phenomenon that could aid in understanding the model's nature through future experiments. The model has been proposed as an example of "effective dark sun" models, a broader class of models where the dark sun's particle spectrum is entirely determined by renormalization group invariance, a concept that's also effective in generating sub-GeV dark matter candidate fermions. The model's simplicity, effectiveness, and testability make it worth further investigation. This refined model enables us to analyze the behavior of the Universe's size and density over multiple cycles. A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this potential, developing a clear hidden-variable model for it has been a challenge, making it hard to properly evaluate. In this piece, a hidden-variable model for the theory is developed and several aspects of the theory are analyzed with it. Our results indicate that many arguments supporting the theory fail when examined closely. The model itself displays superdeterministic and nonlocal properties with a quantum state, and it includes a hidden variable that contains redundant information. Using earlier analyses, our work further highlights the flaws in arguments supporting the theory. Additionally, our work shows how the theory resolves certain puzzles related to the EPR paradox. Furthermore, our work shows how the theory explains certain critical Bell correlations without relying on a conspiracy or nonlocality, instead explaining it through a hidden variable that contains redundant information. Our work does, however, show how the theory is consistent with certain experimental results that previously supported the Clifton form of the Clauser-Horne-Howard inequality. Lastly, our work shows how the theory is compatible with certain general arguments supporting the Clifton-Maccone hypothesis. Our work ultimately shows that Invariant-set theory, when turned into a hidden-variable model, loses much of its appeal as a solution to the EPR paradox. Our work further highlights the need for a more precise examination of proposed solutions to the EPR paradox. Each term in this product is based on a two by two matrix inversion. The problem is to reexpress the partition function in a form that is free from gauge dependent terms. Historically, this has been achieved through the introduction of a regularized Chern Simons theory with a coupling constant of 1/p. When approached from a mathematical standpoint, the issue revolves around finding a formula to multiply any 2 by 2 matrix of the form AB, given that A is invertible, in terms of a specific set of matrices denoted P, Q, and R. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we employ a two-step process: First, we use the Group Lasso to estimate a correlation matrix. Second, we use Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the estimated correlation matrix with a truncated singular value decomposition to introduce sparsity through the application of a soft threshold. We prove that our approach, called GrPCAr, leads to a consistent estimate of the covariance matrix. We also expand upon this method by accounting for missing data in categorical variables using maximum likelihood estimation, yielding GrPCAr.MLE. Through numerical experiments, we evaluated the performance of GrPCAr and GrPCAr.MLE and demonstrated their reliability through application to real-world data. These methods are provided in a new R package called sparseGrGroupLasso. The proposed algorithms were inspired by a previous study on GrPCAr.MLE, although this article provides a comprehensive mathematical foundation and statistical justification that surpasses the original methodology. Furthermore, the approach presented in this article offers computational efficiency improvements, specifically utilizing an iterative Hebbian algorithm for PCA and a closed-form method for Maximum Likelihood Estimation, thus enhancing both computational and memory requirements compared to the original study. As an alternative to the Hebbian algorithm, we also introduced the Generalized Power Iteration algorithm to perform PCA, ensuring the consistency of the estimates generated by GrPCAr and facilitating the derivation of statistical inference. To ensure the consistency of the estimates generated by GrPCAr, we also introduced a new method called Maximum Simulated History Bayesian Adjustment (MSHBA) for handling categorical variables with missing data, which surpasses MLE in terms of reliability. The approach presented in this article offers an additional computational advantage as it requires simulated data, thus mitigating the impact of finite sample distribution issues, and facilitating numerical experiments and assessments of empirical robustness. The MSBH method also allows for simulations to assess the empirical robustness of GrPCAr.MLE, which was previously impossible with the original Maximum Likelihood Estimation method. Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution to address these demands.  Past research has revealed the potential of lightweight hypervisors to meet the requirements of mixed criticality real-time systems.  However, the existing mixed criticality hypervisors have failed to balance the key attributes of real-time systems, which are predictability, efficiency, and steerable performance.  To address these shortcoming, T-Visor, a new hypervisor, was designed with a unique structure and can be executed in virtual mode.  By utilizing the split kernel architecture, T-Visor separates its core and peripheral processing, allowing for a balance to be found between resource consumption and functionality.  Furthermore, T-Visor's token-passing mechanism facilitates seamless communication between the core and peripheral processing.  Additionally, T-Visor supports nested virtualization, thus enabling the creation of root tasks to enhance flexibility. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus minimizing the impact of distortion. In response to this, existing panographic stitching techniques have incorporated correction mechanisms to counteract alignment flaws. Despite these efforts, the current approaches still fall short, as they rely on intensity-based correlations which are susceptible to ambiguities. To address this limitation, we examine the representation capabilities of both density and frequency representations in unraveling alignment uncertainties. Building upon this insight, we propose a novel intensity-free method for correcting camera alignment in panographic images. In this framework, we transform image clusters into spherical harmonics and use them as universal symbols to deduce the position of features within the scene. By testing our approach with realistic simulated data and actual images, we demonstrate that our method consistently achieves superior results with minimal dependence on parameter adjustments. Furthermore, we compared our technique to established correlation-based methods using real images, and through experimentation, we validated its effectiveness in reducing stitching errors by as much as 75%. By integrating our approach with a vertical axis alignment prior, we were able to successfully stitch images captured from the vertical axis. When applied to images captured from arbitrary orientations, our method yielded significant improvements in stitching accuracy, notably a 3-fold decrease in stitching errors. Ultimately, we found that our vertical axis prior outperformed even the most advanced correlation-based approaches in our experiments. In the realm of portable device-based pano-stitching, we investigated the reliance of our approach on device orientation. As expected, our results showed that our technique performed optimally along the vertical axis, while orientation drifts exceeding 30 degrees compromised the stitching quality. To mitigate this, we examined the effects of image rotation on the reliance of our approach, discovering that rotating images captured from arbitrary orientations around the vertical axis reduces their alignment uncertainty. Based on these findings, we suggest that image rotation be adopted as a best practice when stitching images captured from arbitrary orientations. Conversely, images captured with vertical axis alignment as the reference suffer minimal reliance, indicating that image rotation carries negligible drawbacks in such scenarios. Consequently, we propose that vertical axis alignment be considered the optimal capturing configuration for portable device-based pano-stitching. We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional algebra. This process involves an n-dimensional layer and an additional dimension consisting of directed paths, with corresponding multiplication rules that build upon those of the original algebra. Subsequently, we utilize this concept to create quiver algebras that are minimal of finite dimension and have a specified number of non-linear relations. Furthermore, we apply an existing method to extend the basic structure of a quiver algebra by adding a two-dimensional matrix format to its multiplication rules, before presenting a multi-layer quiver to achieve this extension. Finally, we discuss examples of minimal, two-dimensional algebra extensions with a specified number of non-linear relations. These specific examples include the algebra Al(Q, T), the algebra Al(Q, T'), and a sub-algebra Al(Q, T''), each having a unique set of properties. The algebra Al(Q, T) is an extension of the algebra Al(Q) by a given map that adheres to a pre-existing relation; the algebra Al(Q, T') is an extension of the algebra Al(Q, T) by a linear relation based on the algebra Al(Q, T); and a sub-algebra Al(Q, T') is itself an extension of the algebra Al(Q, T) but with a different set of multiplication rules, specifically in the case where T equals the n-tuple (e11, e22,..., enn). In each of the examples presented, the resulting algebra maintains a minimal, two-dimensional format. Through these examples, we demonstrate that every n-dimensional algebra with a specified number of non-linear relations can be expressed as a sub-algebra of a higher dimension (n+1) algebra Al(Q, T'), possessing the same set of properties and a specific quiver structure. In the case where T equals the n-tuple (e11, e22,..., enn), the resulting algebra Al(Q, T') is itself symmetrical. However, the current understanding of BECs relies solely on linear quantum mechanics. This work challenges this linear framework by proposing two potential sources of nonlinear effects in BEC interferometry: a nonlinearity inherent to the interaction potential and another nonlinearity stemming from the influence of nearby excited states. To address these nonlinear effects, researchers have developed an approximate method based on the distinction between rapid and slow processes, similar to the Born and Markov approximations in quantum rate equations. This method can potentially broaden the scope of quantum interferometry and information processing by enabling the exploration of nonlinear effects. This work outlines the theoretical foundation for further investigations into the use of nonlinear effects in quantum interferometry and information processing systems. While this work focuses on BECs, the proposed formalism could also be applied to other systems that rely on nonlinear quantum mechanics, such as superconducting qubits and atomic ion systems. To illustrate its relevance, researchers have discussed the potential to enhance the sensitivity of quantum interferometry by leveraging nonlinear effects, leading to notable advantages in systems with reduced atom numbers. Moreover, the principle of data protection does not seem to restrict the use of nonlinear effects in quantum interferometry and information processing, enabling better performance with less stringent requirements for coherence time, which could be beneficial for scenarios where atom loss is prevalent, such as in optical tweezers. Finally, researchers have outlined a plan to experimentally observe the Zeno effect, which can suppress the loss of coherence in interferometry, by leveraging the use of nonlinear effects to control this phenomenon through the interaction potential. By tuning the nonlinearity resulting from the interaction potential, researchers can control the rate of atom loss due to pair collisions and, consequently, adjust the rate at which the Zeno effect takes effect and adjusts the coherence time of the system. This method offers a potential means to rapidly switch quantum interference patterns on and off and to correct errors that may arise between data collection. In summary, researchers have outlined a comprehensive theoretical framework for leveraging nonlinear effects in quantum interferometry and information processing, broadening the scope and capabilities of quantum-based systems by enabling better performance, faster switching times, and increased resilience with excitation. This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. To address this, we hypothesize that the issue might be due to the overlap of quantum states, which could be resolved by increasing the dimensionality of the quantum feature space by employing a different encoding method. This hypothesis is later verified through an experiment. Due to the limited coherence time, we were unable to achieve significant benefits from the quantum circuit. However, this study highlights the potential for leveraging overlap avoidance as a performance optimization strategy for hybrid algorithms. Additionally, it emphasizes the necessity for more advanced quantum feature learning techniques to capitalize on the potential advantages of quantum computing. The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures, instrumentation flaws such as time-varying gain and pointing errors, leading to model inaccuracy in practice. When errors occur, this estimator becomes biased, causing distortions to spread across the scanning pattern through correlations in noise. A notable effect of this phenomenon is the creation of 'X' shapes surrounding strong point sources in typical scanning patterns. This paper examines why such distortion occurs and introduces both established and a new robust estimator designed to mitigate the effects of these biases, with the latter having the notable benefit of reducing the impact of strong sources' distortion into circular patterns centered on the sources. Additionally, this new estimator shares similar weights with the established MLE, making it straightforward to switch between them, with the weight of the center pixel remaining unchanged. A critical aspect of these estimators is the determination of the boundary beyond which the signal is assumed to dominate the noise. This boundary is referred to as the'signal boundary'. A key aspect of these estimators is the determination of the efficient boundary, known as the 'efficiency boundary', beyond which the signal is treated as dominant and all nearby pixels have equal weights. By leveraging the large number of observations in typical scanning patterns, this paper develops two efficient statistical tests to rapidly and reliably calculate the efficient boundary for any given map. One of these tests, the 'ratio test', is both fast to compute and straightforward to implement, while the alternative 'chi-square test' offers enhanced reliability at a minor computational cost. Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through induction. Our experiments involve training two artificial agents to accomplish a simulated robotic task (block-stacking) and demonstrate that incorporating these ideas in the inducer (simulator) design improves its performance and efficiency. This is measured by both the time it takes for the inducer to understand the teacher's objectives and the actual time it takes for the inducer to achieve these objectives. Our findings show that increasing complexity in the environment (adding new objects) strengthens the inducer's ability to correctly interpret teacher objectives, even in cases of referential ambiguity. However, the effectiveness of the inducer's learning also depends on how it itself adaptes to changes in its preferences during the learning process. When given the option to adapt, the inducer is better equipped to handle complex learning situations; however, the same option given to the learner results in decreased performance. Consequently, the timing of agent adaptability is crucial and should be considered carefully in the designd of self-adaptive learning systems. This work presents novel applications of cognitive science concepts in the context of active learning and highlights the benefits of combining principles from cognitive sciences and active learning to improve systems that interpret natural language teaching instructions. Additionally, the approach and design of our model can serve as a model evaluation framework for understanding human learning processes. This program maximizes the number of users who can receive content within a predetermined time frame, allowing the UAV to seamlessly establish communication at successive points. Moreover, we introduce a convex optimization technique and leverage sparse signal detection methods for obtaining the optimal trajectory in real-time, albeit with increased computational demands. The results revealed the UAV's ability to successfully play back streamed files, outperforming the benchmark methods. The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A new approach is introduced to determine the optimal measurement time by calculating a quantum coherence metric, known as $c_{\rm qy}$, which is derived from the Ramsey sequence's spectral density and decays according to a power-law near its central resonance. This metric serves as an indicator for measuring the spectral width at which optimal efficiency is achieved and for detecting deviations from Lorentzian lineshapes in quantum systems. Moreover, the concept of $c_{\rm qy}$ can be applied to various low-dimensional quantum systems, as exemplified by experimental results involving a spin qubit in a two-dimensional silicon array. By utilizing this approach, the efficiency of Ramsey measurements can be maximized, thereby advancing the capabilities of spin qubit magnetometry. This technique has the potential to be adapted for different types of measurements, such as those employed in atomic clocks. It is predicted that the optimal measurement time will be reached around the pre-set deadline, slightly preceding it due to the influence of the finite switch time between phases. Notably, the coherence metric provides a means to quantify and analyze the effects of various decoherence mechanisms on quantum coherence, especially those resulting in non-exponential decay patterns. By applying this approach, the main decoherence pathways in silicon quantum bits can be identified and their impact compared. Ultimately, this approach offers a versatile tool for optimizing performance in quantum measurements, identifying dominant decoherence mechanisms, and designing high-performance spin qubits. As a general principle, this approach can be applied to optimize performance in quantum measurements, and it might also be adapted for use in different types of measurements such as those employed in atomic clocks. Furthermore, the concept of $c_{\rm qy}$ can be used to monitor and analyze the effects of spin diffusion on quantum coherence by means of magnetic resonance imaging. By combining the approach with simulations, the effects of spin diffusion can be modeled and measured, and their impact on optimal measurement time determined. For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This overarching model encompasses most established algorithms for iterative problem solving, including Newton-Raphson method variants and greedy algorithms associated with convex optimization and the Perron-Frobenius operator's top eigenvector computation. Our analysis demonstrates that, given sufficient data storage, these algorithms inevitably converge to a cycle, provided that the system's initial state has sufficient precision. Furthermore, we provide a lower bound on the expected time required to converge to this cycle when starting with arbitrary initial conditions and implementing Newton-Raphson type methods. This theoremic prediction is exemplified through numerical validation. Lastly, we have also derived a probabilistic proof of convergence for a class of iterative algorithms that do not necessarily satisfy strong monotonicity, thereby broadening the applicability of this theoretical framework. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. In the variational principle of VQE, the Hamiltonian of a molecule is compared to a controlled unitary transformation of its initial state, facilitated through an ansatz circuit. This study compares two approaches to ansatz design: one applying a controlled version of the Lie-Trotter product of single-qubit rotations, utilizing qubit-excitation evolution with Pauli-X operators; the other implementing a controlled, rotated version of the Lie-Trotter product involving fermionic-excitation hopping within a Slater determinant. Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A new approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating Pareto fronts for such problems. A computational study, comparing this proposed hybrid method to non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, demonstrates its enhanced efficiency. A real-world mechanical engineering application, an optimal design of a bellows, is used for demonstration purposes. Furthermore, a publicly available test suite is employed for thorough validation of the proposed algorithm's performance. Results indicate that hybrid approach outperforms non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2 in computational time, utilizing approximately 40-70% fewer evaluations to achieve a comparable solution set. A 5-10% improvement in bellows displacement is also observed using the hybrid approach. A free and open-source C++ implementation of the proposed algorithm, named bsolve, is provided for public access. A Python-based public test suite for evaluating algorithms in solving bi-objective minimization hybrid approach problems is presented.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the Heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, the method's accuracy for integrating the Linear Transport equation is influenced by a combination of spatial and time integrations. To demonstrate the method's effectiveness, results are presented for the Heat equation, Linear Transport equation examples, which mirror those used in [A. K. Singh et al., Sci. Comput. Programm. 2018]. Interestingly, by leveraging a proper neural network architecture, the method converges to the exact solution at the same rate as the original finite volume scheme, reaffirming the importance of building upon established numerical methods. Therefore, the method proposes a novel approach to solving partial differential equations, which combines finite volume schemes with neural networks, which is easy to implement and flexible in terms of the time step size. The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase arising from this time-related entanglement between the future and past, showing that it can be effectively modelled by a $\Lambda$-system. This provides a new approach to detecting the Unruh effect, offering a different method from traditional Unruh-deWitt detectors. Due to the immense accelerations required by Unruh-deWitt detectors to trigger a response, their experimental verification remains unachieved. Conversely, we showcase that a $\Lambda$-system that is static yet time-dependent can, in principle, detect the timelike Unruh effect using modern technological capabilities. This enables the calculation of the geometric phase using quantum circuit adiabatic evolution, and we find that it is predominantly influenced by the kinetic term. Furthermore, we show that the coupling to the Unruh metric's time component is analogous to the coupling to an inertial capacitor with increasing acceleration. Consequently, the geometric phase reaches a maximum of 27.27% at an acceleration of $10^{17}\,\text{G}$, significantly surpassing the Planck scale. Lastly, we speculate that the timelike Unruh effect might be experimentally verified through simulations with superconducting qubits. These qubits, when designed as either transmon or Cooper-pair, can implement the required time-dependent $\Lambda$-system using periodic driving and magnetic field fluctuations. Their high coherence levels would facilitate a realistic simulation, bringing the Unruh effect closer to experimental validation. Current quantum technology is sufficient to detect the geometric phase arising from the timelike Unruh effect, marking the first experimental verification of this phenomenon and opening up new avenues for investigating quantum effects with accelerated particles. Nonetheless, the predictability of the Unruh effect depends on whether a timelike worldline is inhabited by a quantum field that is either massless or very lightly massive. A theoretical understanding of this predictability, though present, necessitates further investigation. Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed how a clumpy stellar wind from a companion star affects the variable X-ray binary system 2X1 R136b at different distances from its parent star, R136. Analyzing four instances between 2007 and 2008 when the wind from R136 was expected to clear, yet the X-ray binary system remained accessible within the telescope's field of view, allowed for a study of how the clumpy stellar wind impacts the variability of the system's X-ray emissions. Comparing the observed variations with theoretical models of wind-induced variations, the analysis concluded a significant correlation between the wind's density and the clump size in the stellar wind from R136. According to the analysis, the largest clumps have diameters estimated to be 0.23 AU, which is approximately 40 times smaller than the radius of the star, and the analysis also provides an estimate for the average wind clumping factor, which is around 3400. The analysis further indicates that the stellar wind from R136 may clear at a lower rate than previously anticipated for stars with masses over 40 times that of the sun due to the presence of wind clumps. Finally, the analysis provides an estimate for the density of the stellar wind from R136, which is approximately 3.9 times 10^-12 g/cm^3, and discusses potential implications for studies focused on stellar wind evolution over time. To explain observed X-ray emissions from high-mass X-ray binaries within certain star clusters like R136, future studies are recommended to account for stellar wind variations, which can lead to variations in emissions up to 100 times. Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area at the cost of the other, contradicting research highlighting the complex interactions between the two. To address this issue, we examine multiple model designs capable of tapping into rich data in the Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) dataset, parsing it alongside Universal Dependencies for high-performance results in both formats. Analyzing the effects of combining syntax and semantics parsing reveals patterns that are supported by linguistic theory at their interface. Moreover, we examine the effectiveness of joint modeling in multiple languages, discovering analogous trends in 8 languages tested. Additionally, we investigate the benefits of shared object-level features, known as salience, between syntax and semantics parsing, finding it plays a significant role in joint modeling performance. Ultimately, we conclude that joint modeling delivers better performance than isolated parsing approaches across all datasets and languages tested, underpinning the significance of joint modeling in understanding the interplay of syntax and semantics. This research marks a significant breakthrough in multiple fronts: 1) it shows joint modeling helps in performing parsing tasks efficiently in various languages; 2) it showcases the value of using datasets that merge syntax and semantics for enhanced parsing results; 3) it proves that incorporating datasets with rich object-level annotations produces better parsing outcomes; 4) it produces outstanding parsing outcomes in multiple languages, thereby becoming a new standard for parsing performance in the English and other languages context. This research will be made available online through an open-source repository, located at https://github.com/uci-NLP/joint-syntax-semantics-parsing. Moreover, the datasets used can be retrieved from https://uidata.blob.core.windows.net/udpipe/udpipe-data.zip, while the UDS dataset can be accessed from https://github.com/uci-NLP/uds-rereader. The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO has been a persistent challenge. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that significantly reduces transaction sizes
without sacrificing user anonymity, allowing for faster and more efficient transactions.
Our modified scheme is compatible with the Casper FFG consensus algorithm and is
pivotal in developing a civilised and secure cryptocurrency.

The upgraded RingCT has two key sub-protocols: a lightweight output commitment
scheme and a lightweight output merging protocol. We implemented these sub-protocols
in a Ethereum smart contract and tested its performance, including the time it takes to
lock, split, and combine outputs. We also demonstrated the effectiveness of these sub-protocols
in a secure and private environment for decentralized cryptocurrencies. Furthermore,
we explored possible attacks against our protocol and assessed its anonymity levels. 
The anonymity analysis showed that the bulk of computations in the wallet can be performed
in the clear, substantially enhancing user experience. We suggest that a decentralized
Bitcoin service like BitMix be replaced with a reliable alternative. Ultimately, our
modified RingCT is aimed at promoting the development of a secure, private, and civilized
Bitcoin service. A working implementation of our proposal is available at https://github.com/luizgagni/civil.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling across multiple fields. Despite these advancements, a persistent issue remains where the solution develops biases based on the order in which data is presented and adapting to one dataset hinders learning from another.  Further complication arises when multiple datasets are involved, making it difficult to achieve consistent results.  The problem of adapting to multiple datasets is referred to as continual learning, with one of its key features being catastrophic forgetting.  Several techniques have been developed to address catastrophic forgetting and a few continuum learning benchmarks have been established, but existing benchmarks have largely been limited to computer vision tasks, ignoring machine learning models in other domains.  To address this, a new benchmark called Continual Learning Cinema has been developed, featuring a comprehensive set of tasks derived from the OpenAI Gym interface for dynamic systems with various environments and multiple observation types.  The tasks in Learning Cinema are designed to incorporate different domains, such as Atari games, robotic observations, and scientific experiments, like chemistry, providing a diverse set of challenges.  The goal is for researchers to develop methods for continual learning that can adapt to multiple tasks from different domains with ease, facilitating the development of flexible models for a variety of applications in a variety of domains.  The full source code for Learning Cinema will be publicly available, complete with implementation details for existing continual learning methods, allowing for consistent evaluation and analysis.  The long-term goal is for continual learning to become a fundamental aspect of deep reinforcement learning, making it a key factor in future breakthroughs in this field.  With Learning Cinema, researchers will have a new tool to advance continual learning in areas where it is currently underrepresented, providing a foundation for future breakthroughs in deep reinforcement learning and other areas of machine learning.  The public release of Learning Cinema is an important step in future research in this area, serving as a common framework for evaluation and analysis among researchers.  The authors believe that by providing a common framework for evaluation and analysis, they can help bridge the current gap in research in continual learning and reinforce its fundamental importance in machine learning, particularly in deep reinforcement learning.  To this end, the public release of all Learning Cinema tasks, benchmarks, datasets, implementations, and source code will take place under an open-source framework available on multiple platforms, starting with an initial release on GitHub. The results from our initial research using Learning Cinema will provide a starting point for future research in this area, showcasing state-of-the-art results for several challenging continual learning tasks. Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model's
understanding of language in conjunction with compositional reasoning.
Typically, general-language models struggle with breaking down and analyzing
complex relationships between entities, especially when the data is not seen
previously. To address this challenge, we develop a novel approach, 'Decompose',
aimed at mitigating the requirement for extensive data alignment. 'Decompose'
employs syntax-based decomposition of the statement into manageable units and
assembles fact components using a defined syntax, ultimately allowing for
evaluation against structured knowledge sources. In our empirical assessment,
'Decompose' successfully outperforms existing techniques and significantly boosts
performance when applied to established datasets. The accompanying code is
accessible on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/fm1nh/fact-checking.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Researchers have developed methods such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, using out-of-vocabulary Gaussian extensions, to facilitate this process. These methods, though effective in the majority of cases, can be hindered in high-dimensional problems due to their reliance on local exploration. To overcome this limitation, the paper proposes employing differential evolution algorithms as alternatives for nested sampling. These algorithms exploit approximations in the Gaussian distribution by representing prior distributions as piece-wise Gaussian surfaces. By utilizing this piece-wise structure, the algorithms can move globally in high-dimensional parameter spaces without relying on local minima. The study evaluates two implementations, the nested sampling differential evolution algorithm and the x-nested sampling differential evolution algorithm, demonstrating their ability to provide accurate maximum a posteriori distribution estimates in various scenarios. Although the algorithms are computationally efficient, they exhibit reduced efficiency in the tail of the prior distribution. To mitigate this shortcoming, the paper proposes a method for restarting x-NSDE computations when the efficiency drops below a specified threshold. The algorithms show equivalent performance to more conventional methods, such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo, in the majority of cases. However, the algorithms significantly outperform them in the few parameter dimensions scenario and in the scenario where only a few parameter uncertainties are involved. The paper showcases the algorithm's applications in the UltraViolet Spectroscopy project by finding maximum a posteriori distribution estimates in the 3 sigma credible regions of the credible masses of various astronomical bodies. The study demonstrates the algorithm's superior processing time of approximately 3.5 hours for the UltraViolet Spectroscopy project, which significantly outperforms MCMC methods. The paper makes suggestions for future improvements to the algorithm and provides open source code for nested sampling differential evolution algorithm implementation in the Ultranest framework, which currently supports Ultranest, xUltranest, UltranestDE, xUltranestDE and NSDE. Researchers can access the code at https://github.com/fermiguel/ultranest DE.git.

In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. Using a polynomial method to find eigenvalues, we calculate correlations in both the weak and strong dissipation limits. In weak dissipation, we show that two-particle correlations exhibit oscillations whose frequencies are determined by the imaginary part of the Liouvillian gap, while in strong dissipation, this pattern breaks down and correlations instead demonstrate a power-law behavior dominated by the real part of the Liouvillian gap. This pattern is observable in experiments as it indicates a boundary separating regular and chaotic behavior in quantum dynamics. Furthermore, we apply this correlation analysis to a specific model of dissipative optical lattices where two-component atoms transfer excitations via dissipation, providing a clear roadmap to experimentally measuring this chaotic boundary using two-particle correlations. Through numerical calculations, we also examine how this model's two-particle correlations exhibit the signature of a Floquet many-body localization transition when subject to periodic driving, an effect distinct from the dissipative phase transition we have been studying. This comparison raises fundamental questions about the relationship between these two phenomena and motivates their experimental investigation. Ultimately, we leverage the polynomial method to reveal a general structure in the discrete spectrum of the Liouvillian, common to both the limit where dissipation triggers a phase transition and the limit where it does not, which may be useful for understanding quantum dynamics in a broader class of dissipative systems. A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data points, called heteroscedastic Gaussian process regression, is utilized to develop predictive models for the specific loads an offshore wind turbine will experience. The randomness inherent in turbulence and wave conditions makes the resulting loads more accurately described as probabilistic events rather than fixed values. The effect of these stochastic factors on the loads is also influenced by the turbulent flow's inherent variability, resulting in a probabilistic distribution of loads that needs to be captured for the reliable design of offshore wind turbines. The conventional approach in industrial design, which involves calculating the 100-year extreme value of loads, may significantly underestimate the variability of these loads, leading to conservative and inaccurate models that neglect the variability in data. By training models on the statistical distribution of turbulent turbulence and wave conditions, accurate predictions of extreme values and variance are obtained, showing a 25% reduction in material requirements, leading to a 6% increase in power output for offshore turbines. The incorporation of heteroscedasticity also results in a 61.5% decrease in the risk of collision with icing particles, leading to a 1.5% increase in power output. The application of heteroscedastic machine learning methods, such as deep learning and Gaussian process regression, to the prediction of offshore wind turbine loads demonstrates the potential for improved reliability and efficiency in wind energy harvesting. The integration of heteroscedasticity also results in a 55.5% decrease in the required pitch yaw system capacity and a 73.5% decrease in the required yaw system capacity, leading to a 32.5% decrease in the required tower moment for the DOWS150 turbine. The variance in predictions obtained through heteroscedastic machine learning is significant, ranging from 0 to 200% for some loads, indicating that accounting for the variability in turbulence and wave conditions may result in a 50% difference in material requirements. The heteroscedastic approach also yields more accurate results when load distributions are partially known, resulting in load predictions that are 50% closer to the actual value. Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Methodologically, we utilized machine learning models for text classification and sentiment analysis, achieving satisfactory results. The acquired Sentiment Analysis model produced a satisfactory accuracy of 82.13%, while the topic modeling we used yielded reasonable outcomes with minimum error rates. The obtained results indicate that public sentiment shifted from initial concern (fear and relief) to donation support (especially in regards to children and women) after the disaster. The identified topics showed high Q-value variation over time, with initially prominent topics of fear and relief giving way to donation support and aid. This research contributes to the field of sentiment analysis in seismic crisis communication, offering practical applications for crisis managers to monitor public sentiment and take informed decisions. The study provides valuable insights for PR personnel to develop strategies to influence public perception in favor of their organizations. Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) communication has intensified due to its speed and low cost of configuring a massive number of transmission channels. Although adaptive modulation is a critical strategy to maximize the RIS-assisted OFDM system performance, its associated increased overhead in channel state information (CSI) collection causes additional delays. To address these concerns, this study presents an advanced adaptive modulation scheme called active-passive adaptive modulation (APAM), separating the tasks of data transmission and channel estimation between two distinct devices. As a result, the passive device can focus on collecting accurate CSI for channel estimation, as it doesn't impact the active device's data transmission. Conversely, the active device can proceed with data transmission while relying on the passive device's collected CSI. Notably, the passive device can continue expanding its coverage area without disrupting the active device's operations. The proposed APAM scheme features an enhanced sum-rate of $\text{5.94}$ percent over conventional adaptive modulation strategies. The results show that the passive device can effectively contribute to active-passive systems while successfully addressing overhead-related delays in adaptive modulation systems. The successful implementation of the proposed APAM scheme highlights its potential for achieving optimal system performance under diverse channel conditions. The study recommends the integration of multiple communication devices to achieve optimal system performance. The use of two communication devices also provides opportunities for leveraging diverse network technologies, such as leveraging 5G networks for passive communications and newer 6G networks for active applications. The novel active-passive adaptive modulation strategy proposed in this study represents an essential milestone towards the realization of promising RIS-assisted communication systems. The proposed scheme can be optimized to cater to the needs of multifaceted communication applications, the demands of which vary significantly in terms of their respective channel conditions, delay constraints, overhead requirements, and performance expectations. The study provides recommendations for optimizing communication strategies based on device configurations and application requirements. In contrast to classical physics, which initially seemed unsuitable for a role in causally effective consciousness, the indeterminacy and unique duality of quantum physics have opened doors for modeling consciousness. We utilize quantum principles, particularly the Schrödinger equation and Planck-Einstein relation, to investigate the relevant timescales of conscious processes and to understand how non-zero interactions between quantum components give rise to entanglement and correlations. We demonstrate, employing a measure of entanglement based on Schmidt decomposition, that interactions can generate both entanglement and decoherence in quantum systems, which are characteristic of separated systems. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of decoherence on a Schrödinger cat state in both an isolated system and within the context of a built-in environment. Our findings indicate that although entanglement may be reduced by interactions with other particles, retention of correlations is possible only when non-zero interactions are present. Building on this foundation, we develop a model of entanglement and decoherence in biological systems using the coupled oscillations in the brains of sentient beings, specifically focusing on the prefrontal cortex' role in decision-making. Drawing from fMRI data on brain function, we design a model of two separate quantum systems connected via operator entanglement that facilitates decision-making between two Choice-Choice systems. However, brain decoherence resulting from Darrow-White inhibition of the systems' non-local interactions implies that entanglement is only transient and decision-making correlations can only be achieved quickly. In order to leverage quantum principles effectively for modeling consciousness, we examine the brain's quantum constants using Planck-Einstein relation and Schrödinger equation. Notably, we discover that decision-making speed in the brain is compatible with the retention of quantum correlations between brain sites when measured in units of Planck time. Consequently, we propose a model of entangled consciousness based on the coupled decision-making units in the brain, which is characterized by Schrödinger equation evolution of the brain's quantum state until brain decoherence occurs due to incoherent Darrow White inhibition before measurement. Ultimately, we conclude that decision-making in the brain leads to conscious experience through quantum processes that can be understood and explained despite the temporary nature of quantum correlations in biological systems. This study provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order calculation of the differential cross section for $J/\psi+ \chi_{c0}$ production in $pp$ collisions at the Large Hadron Collider's LHC energy levels. The calculation accounts for $J/\psi$ and $\chi_{c0}$ polarization, utilizing the $J/\psi$ transverse momentum $q_{T}$ and polarization transfer amplitude as key variables. The calculated results are compared with experimental findings by the LHCb collaboration for $J/\psi$ polarization and the anisotropic angular distribution in $J/\psi$ longitudinal and azimuthal polarization. While calculations for longitudinal polarization align with experimental data, discrepancies exist for the anisotropic angular distribution, particularly in relation to $\chi_{c0}$ polarization, which cannot be matched due to existing theoretical limitations. The influence of nonperturbative long-distance physics on $J/\psi$ polarization is also investigated through comparison with two different treatment approaches. Furthermore, the calculated results demonstrate a notable increase in agreement with experimental data for both $J/\psi$ longitudinal polarization and the anisotropic angular distribution in $J/\psi$ polarization when the long-distance physics effect is considered, specifically through $J/\psi$ hadronic interactions at the end of the $q\bar{q}$ medium. This study provides a detailed, LO analysis for $J/\psi+ \chi_{c0}$ production, addressing a previously under-theoretically investigated topic in $J/\psi$ polarization studies. Given that polarization effects typically manifest more prominently at higher $q_{T}$ values, this analysis is particularly relevant to $J/\psi$ production at the LHC's extreme forward forward rapidity regions, which it quantifies in detail. For the first time, this analysis provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order calculation for $J/\psi+ \chi_{c0}$ production in $pp$ collisions, including polarization effects, at a variety of $pp$ LHC energy levels, including 7, 8, and 13 TeV. Additionally, this analysis provides numerical results on the long-distance physics effect, quantifying its significance in relative magnitude. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, words representing inanimate objects tend to be closer to those of the same gender class representing living entities, as seen in Spanish where 'la' and 'le' are used for female nouns regardless of whether they refer to living or non-living entities. In contrast, English tends to maintain the living entities - noun dichotomy. In cases where a language exhibits grammatical gender, embeddings created using word embeddings tend to assign gender characteristics to inanimate objects. In an attempt to eliminate biases stemming from grammatical gender characteristics in Spanish, a new set of embeddings called GRAMMAR is employed. GRAMMAR uses an unsupervised technique that isolates characteristics unrelated to grammatical gender, thereby eliminating the gender-based distinction between living and non-living entities. As a result, GRAMMAR embeds for both living and non-living entities that exhibit minimal variation due to grammatical gender, thereby reducing the gender-based distinction among the former and eliminating the gender-based distinction among the latter. In non-living entities, GRAMMAR embeds for all nouns independently of their grammatical gender. In contrast, Spanish living entity embeddings retain the gender-based distinction. To eliminate biases in computer programs that process English language inputs, an English version of GRAMMAR, EN-GRAMMAR, is developed. EN-GRAMMAR English embeddings resemble those neutral with regard to grammatical gender, suggesting the feasibility of using these embeddings when encoding English text. Formal evaluations of Spanish and English language understanding tasks demonstrate a notable improvement when EN-GRAMMAR and GRAMMAR embeddings are used instead of traditional word embeddings. In particular, tasks involving common sense, semantic role, and sentiment analysis benefit from the neutral English embeddings, whereas tasks involving sentiment analysis and literary analysis benefit from the neutral Spanish embeddings. Generally, tasks involving these four semantic subtasks benefit from the neutral Spanish and English embeddings, as they help encode common sense, semantic roles, and sentiment knowledge that are unaffected by grammatical gender. As a result, GRAMMAR provides a new and novel approach to word embeddings that eliminate biases stemming from various influences. In the future, GRAMMAR may be applied to other language bias removal tasks. Prior to this, word embedding control methods focused solely on eliminating biases stemming from properties such as race and gender. In contrast, GRAMMAR employs an unsupervised control method that eliminates biases

Estimating an object's pose is a crucial aspect of most visual pipelines in robots and 3D vision as a whole. Objects being classified as novel or known significantly impacts the difficulty of this task; a challenge arises when objects are categorized as new, requiring an extension of existing model capabilities. Previous top-notch methods have employed contrastive learning techniques to achieve impressive zero-shot pose estimation results for novel objects but failed to provide a clear explanation of their success. In our research, we argue that novel object training is achievable not only through contrastive learning but also through identifying key object characteristics or 'landmarks.' To validate this, we developed two flexible methodologies to achieve zero-shot pose estimation: 'Object2Landmark,' which translates an object to a universal format, and 'Object2Object,' which translates an object to another object with a known format. When two methodologies are combined, the performance significantly improves. Our novel approaches were shown to outperform the current best method when trained on the CPMKBB dataset and tested on the T-SSD dataset for 6 DoF pose estimation estimation. Our code is available at https://github.com/wnwn1996/OL_Tagger. Rather than achieving zero-shot performance, our study focuses on solving the issue of novel object training, and thus, the methods can also be utilized for traditional object training. Furthermore, based on the findings, two new datasets with significantly expanded categories were developed to improve pose estimation accuracy for object categorization. Our study proposes an alternative method for achieving state-of-the-art performance in pose estimation using object characteristics or 'tags' for both robots and consumer electronics applications. Our model can also be utilized for object re-identification in image processing, and with universal object characteristics, an object can be easily matched to another object with similar characteristics. of artificial intelligence. For instance, analyzing the distribution of vehicles 
at a specific intersection over time, as well as identifying recurring patterns 
in this distribution, can help. Therefore, this paper proposes an innovative 
system combining traffic forecasting with anomaly detection, allowing for 
real-time deviation notifications when daily traffic patterns are disrupted. 
We developed and tested the system using sensor data from Atlanta streets. 
Initially, traffic patterns were broken down into individual features. Then, 
anomaly detection was achieved by using various algorithms for feature selection 
followed by applying different methods to identify deviations. We compared the 
accuracy of different feature selection and anomaly detection methods in terms of 
Homogeneity Assessment Metrics. Next, we integrated the detected anomalies with 
real-time traffic forecasts to provide users with notifications when daily 
traffic is abnormal. We discovered that the system's reliability reliability 
dependended on the type of anomaly detection method used, with better results 
from classification-based approaches compared to distance-based methods. 
Overall, the system showed promising results and can be used to keep drivers 
informed about traffic disruptions. The system's full implementation, including 
monitoring road conditions, was demonstrated using an IoT device. The traffic 
forecasting component was handled using the Valley Section Dataset from the

evaluated using data from the ITS Cup Valley Section dataset. We demonstrated 
the effectiveness of real-time deviation notifications using an IoT device.

features related to traffic and extended temporal contexts. Furthermore,

cities to ensure general applicability. Finally, the system can be enhanced by

This paper presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks. Building on established causal graph theories like Pearl's, VACA utilizes a Structural Causal Model (SCM) to model complex, high-dimensional data and infer causal relationships within it. Evidenced by its successful applications in generating synthetic data with specified covariate confounding properties and causal effects, VACA presents a novel approach to variational causal inference. Moreover, our research demonstrates VACA's effectiveness in synthetic data by precisely identifying causal graphs and their associated effects. Last, as part of future work, further research aims to extend VACA to handle real-world, observational settings. State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data requires efficient processing to achieve precise timing and to facilitate the analysis of complex radio signals. Traditional data processing techniques, typically utilized in astronomy, have become impractical with the emergence of next-generation radio telescopes due to their limited capacity for real-time data analysis. This paper explores the potential storage solutions for large-scale radio data processing and discusses the advantages and disadvantages of alternative strategies, such as pre-processing the data, reducing data dimensions, and employing data compression methods to optimize the storage of radio data. We also examine the performance of the GraphBuilder, an open-source data compression library, on reduced data sets that have been transformed into Cartesian coordinates through the application of the two-dimensional FFT algorithm. Our findings demonstrate that the GraphBuilder can achieve data compression ratios of up to 3.5 (an 84% reduction) without compromising the accuracy of the reconstructed sky images, while also showcasing its potential for scalable processing through a distributed calculation of the Cartesian coordinate transformation. Furthermore, we utilize the GraphBuilder to create an innovative data compression method for the LOFAR's Nall data format, resulting in a significant reduction of up to 360 megabytes (an 87% reduction) with a high level of reconstruction fidelity. This research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on efficient data processing strategies for radio telescopes and to provide valuable insights for handling massive data at the level of individual entities, facilitating the easy access of these data for both data owners and third-party analysts. Moreover, we intend to encourage the adoption of open-source compression methods to empower data sharing while protecting private data. Lastly, we outline future challenges and opportunities for the development of optimized data processing algorithms to facilitate the efficient handling of massive radio data. As an essential step, we create public data sets compressed using the GraphBuilder to facilitate the reproduction of our results and to enable independent analysis by the community. These data sets can be accessed through the accompanying code repository located at https://github.com/GeImperialGraphBuilder/GraphBuilderRadio.git. The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task for studios and experts. Utilizing data from film revenue in Taiwan from 2008 to 2019, we've investigated several popular movies and found key factors contributing to a film's success include runtime, number of acting nominations, and production budget. Notably, we've identified a correlation between movie failure and runtime, suggesting extremely long films pose a significant risk. Conversely, we've discovered a correlation between movie success and budget, indicating high production costs are often accompanied by greater box office returns. We've leveraged data mining techniques to analyze film revenue, revealing interesting patterns and relationships, and offering a comprehensive comparison of popular movies in Taiwan. Our research provides an empirical understanding of the impact of film characteristics on revenue in the Taiwanese market. We're confident our research, addressing a significant real-world problem, will provide cinema executives with valuable insights to inform their decision-making. Furthermore, we're introducing unique machine learning solutions to accommodate the peculiarities of this specific domain. As cinema continues to evolve under the influence of streaming services and changing audience preferences, we recognize our research will be relevant not just to the Taiwanese market but also to other regions due to the standardization of cinema data. The energy shift poses a threat to the stability of the power grid's operation, 
which necessitates maintaining both voltage amplitude and frequency within 
safe limits. Research has primarily concentrated on the stability and 
frequency dynamics but largely overlooked voltage stability. This work aims to 
investigate the stability of simple networks through both linear stability and 
bulk analysis, specifically evaluating how the secondary control for frequency 
guarantees the stability of a particular power grid and also noting an observed 
stabilizing influence on voltage dynamics despite only analyzing secondary 
frequency control. Moreover, an examination of the energy shift-based stability 
through bulk analysis is conducted alongside proposing a model that can accurately 
replicate the system's behavior. Researchers also found that introducing large 
energy storage can counter the unstable dynamics observed in the system. This work 
sets the groundwork for investigating voltage dynamics in networks influenced by 
energy shift in deeper and more intricate power grid systems. Furthermore, it 
highlights an important phenomenon that warrants further exploration, which is the 
link between frequency and voltage dynamics. Lastly, it confirms that an energy 
shift-based stability analysis through bulk analysis offers a reliable method for 
evaluating stability in such systems in harmony with human-based reasoning.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that might be producing UV and soft X-ray excess in certain blazars. Predictions are generated for a specific blazar, but the model's general applicability is also considered for different objects. This study represents the first attempt to link highly polarized UV and soft X-ray emissions to the same phenomenon. If future observational data aligns with predicted polarized signatures, it would be strong evidence for a common physical phenomenon responsible for both the polarized emissions and the UV/soft X-ray excess in certain blazars. However, if such data instead shows full photon polarization, the spin symmetry of leptons will be confirmed. Additionally, if no polarized signatures are detected in observed UV/soft X-ray excess events, it may imply a radical change in our current understanding of particle physics, where the Standard Model's fermions exhibit intrinsic spin. This could ultimately lead to a new theoretical framework where certain internal symmetries are reevaluated. By leveraging next-generation X-ray polarimetry instruments like the X-IFU, researchers hope to refine their understanding of these complex astrophysical environments. By analyzing the polarization patterns of a variety of blazars, scientists believe they can pinpoint the orientation and movement patterns of jet-aligned relativistic electrons. This research is viewed as an initial step in a multi-faceted investigation, laying the groundwork for future exploration. Future studies will utilize theoretical models like the ones based on Monte-Carlo methods to analyze a broader range of objects, including those with FSRQ dominance, FSRQ/BLazar transitions, micro and mega-lars, as well as SED1 and SED2 dominated blazars. These model predictions will be compared to available data and re-evaluated upon the launch of the X-IFU, which is set to operate at a level of 10,000 counts per second, increasing its accuracy in analyzing the polarization patterns of a variety of blazars. This study represents the first attempt to link highly polarized UV and soft X-ray emissions to the same phenomenon.

Light field technology is currently a focal point of interest for the research community due to its capabilities of capturing and reproducing the characteristics of light in 2D images. By using a specific type of camera that captures light from multiple angles, light field reconstruction enables the accurate replication of light rays, resulting in heightened image clarity and the elimination of occlusions. However, the most effective light field capture devices are typically large, heavy, and expensive, limiting their use in everyday applications. To overcome this limitation, a new algorithm has been developed, leveraging machine learning to analyze data captured by a conventional single-lens camera and reconstruct it as if it were captured by a high-quality light field camera. By applying the 4D light field reconstruction process in reverse, the Dark Pool Variational Autoencoder (DPVAE) model is able to identify key components of light field images, which are then used to generate authentic light field information. Thorough evaluations have been conducted to assess the performance of the DPVAE model for both intra- and inter-frame light field reconstruction tasks using real-world data. The results demonstrate the ability of the proposed model to effectively reconstruct high-quality 4D light fields from a significantly smaller number of 2D images, surpassing state-of-the-art outcomes. Furthermore, a new technique has been introduced for generating unobserved 2D images from a reconstructed 4D light field, yielding a notable improvement over previous methods. Code for the proposed model has been made available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Hiwang-Hs/DPVAE. Moreover, a new online platform called Light Field Flicker (https://lightfieldflicker.com/) has been established to showcase a range of novel light field effects achievable through this approach. Lastly, the application of the DPVAE model in the creation of 2D image hallucination for video coding has been explored, yielding a notable coding gain of 0.88% at Q- 29.88 when compared to the existing top-performing motion hallucination technique. The potential of the DPVAE model to be utilized in a variety of other applications has been validated. As such, a new research trend has been initiated, paving the way for the investigation of even more advanced machine learning-based approaches to light field reconstruction in the future.
