Pre-trained language models, when used in zero-shot settings, typically rely on one specific task type, such as classification. To overcome the limitation of handling multiple task types, researchers have applied meta-tuning, an approach of fine-tuning pre-trained models on synthetic data to adapt to different tasks. Although current meta-tuning methods focus on generalizing to various tasks, they often require each model to handle one task type. In contrast, we introduce an alternative method called MultiTask Meta-Tuning (MTMT), which leverages pre-trained models to perform multiple task types simultaneously. This is achieved by creating synthetic datasets for multiple tasks and combining them into a single model. Our experiments reveal that MTMT offers improved zero-shot performance and increased efficiency while requiring less computational resources. MTMT has been successfully applied to different datasets, including GLUE and Natural Language Inference benchmarks, yielding notable results. The code to reproduce MTMT's performance is publicly available at https://github.com/DigitalAssistanceAI/MultiTask-MetaTuning. MTMT's approach may also serve as a foundation for developing more sophisticated multi-task models. Furthermore, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy to categorize different types of meta-tuning methods. Based on this taxonomy and our findings, we highlight potential research paths to enhance zero-shot learning. Overall, MTMT has the potential to significantly enhance pre-trained language models' ability to adapt to different tasks in zero-shot settings. To further explore this, we suggest investigating the boundaries of meta-tuning through systematic studies of factors like varying task types, training datasets, and architecture modifications. A future challenge in NLP may be to completely eliminate the need for labeled data in zero-shot learning, particularly in complex natural language understanding tasks. To facilitate future research, we propose a new dataset called MultiTask-MNLI-MLM, which combines the MultiNLI dataset with masked language modeling pre-training tasks, and is now publicly available at https://github.com/DigitalAssistanceAI/MultiTask-MNLI-MLM. By addressing the limitations of meta-tuning and NLP zero-shot learning, we can ultimately develop more intelligent and autonomous digital assistants capable of adapting to different interaction contexts. To achieve this, future developments should prioritize developing fully automated conversation systems across various digital domains. A crucial step in achieving this goal is leveraging advanced technologies like transfer learning, which connects different digital environments and facilitates the transfer of learned skills. A future research challenge could be the development of highly specialized models capable of performing complex digital tasks while also learning from each other through transfer

In depth research into the likelihood and characteristics of a robust first-order electroweak phase transition has been carried out as a prerequisite to studying baryogenesis through this process. This phase transition is necessary for baryogenesis to occur because it serves as the trigger and cooling system to reset the CP symmetry. A detailed analysis of the Higgs boson and Yukawa coupling masses and their influences on the strength of the phase transition has been conducted. This analysis was based on several theoretical models that enhance the Higgs boson mass through the stop sector. A simulation of the Higgs boson mass observed in the Large Hadron Collider has been conducted and the results have revealed that a suitable window for the strength of the phase transition still exists while adhering to the theoretical models and current Higgs boson mass measurements. This is accomplished by tuning the top squark mass to be around 750 GeV. This analysis also found that a precise measurement of the Higgs boson mass is capable of limiting the minimum temperature at the point of nucleon density infinity ($T_{n\infty}$) up to 100 Gev. This is because $T_{n\infty}$ essentially defines the maximum volume of nucleon space in the early universe and limiting this is essential for preventing excessive nucleon cooling during the phase transition process. A detailed simulation of Higgs boson production has also found that an ideal scenario in which the Higgs boson decays into two gamma rays could allow for a precise measurement of $T_{n\infty}$ by merging with the Standard Model simulations of the Higgs boson mass. This would result in an estimation of $T_{n\infty}$ with an accuracy of 50 GeV. This analysis also found that an ideal simulation in which the Higgs boson decays into two Z bosons could allow for a precise measurement of $T_{n\infty}$ by merging with the theoretical simulations of the Higgs boson mass and the Higgs boson coupling to nucleons. We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. These methods utilize comparisons of different line ratios to validate millimeter-based redshifts and introduce an unsupervised algorithm for isolating robust submm redshifts based on spectral profiles. Notably, our techniques yield submillimeter redshifts for 23 galaxies from the ATLAS, CLARAN, and MALTAGS catalogs. We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We use Hilbert-Schmidt operators to develop a nearly optimal approximation of the operator $P$. This approach leads to an almost sure convergence result for the discretized approximation of $P$ using finite-dimensional subspaces. We also discuss how our method can be adapted to approximate operators related to forward-looking expectations, and provide an extension of our theorem to the case where $X$ takes values in a Polish space. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our main result by applying it to various model-free estimators, such as the series expansion and kernel regression estimators. We show that our method allows for the creation of model-independent, consistent estimators for conditional expectations with better convergence rates than existing model-dependent estimators. Furthermore, for conditional expectations based on general measurable functions, we use our operator approximation method to establish a new model-independent estimator with optimal convergence rates. Moreover, for a broad class of probability distributions where $X$ has a finite range, we develop a model-independent estimator for the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X=x$ using $L^2$-theory, and show its convergence rate can be enhanced by targeting specific subspaces of $L^2([X$'s domain$])$. In the specific case of a Gaussian random variable $Y$ and possibly dependent $X$, we obtain several estimators for the conditional mean, covariances, and higher-order moments of $Y$ given $X$. We also prove a generalization of a central limit theorem for these estimators. In a different direction, we show our operator approximation method can be used to create model-independent estimators for the backward stochastic integrals introduced by Bichteler (1998) and many others. We develop a model-independent estimator for a general backward stochastic integral based on a $X$-adapted process $H$. This estimator has a optimal convergence rate and can be extended to estimate logarithmic terms, and we demonstrate its applicability to estimate model-independent stochastic Fenchel-Lagrange duality for a variety of stochastic optimization problems. Moreover, we show our estimator for the backward stochastic integral can be used to derive model-independent estimators for the log-lagrange duals for a variety of stochastic optimization problems. Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation. Furthermore, a numerical case study validating the proposed observer's performance is presented. Unlike existing designs, this observer is adaptable to models describing complex transmission dynamics, encompassing prevalence-dependent force of infection, yet does not assume homogeneous mixing parameters or homogeneous disease characteristics. Nonetheless, the proposed observer is incompatible with prevalence-dependent incidence rates, a characteristic often found in epidemic models. To address this limitation, a novel observer design is developed for systems with cross terms and nonlinear transmission dynamics, providing a generalized framework for state estimation. Crucially, this design overcomes the existing state observer's inability to accommodate nonlinear transmission dynamics, thus offering improved adaptability and theoretical design capabilities. To demonstrate the proposed observer's efficacy, its performance is evaluated in three exemplary epidemic models governing the dynamics of multi-epidemic and cross-transmission processes. These models illustrate the proposed observer's ability to accommodate nonlinear transmission dynamics, thereby expanding the existing state observer's applicability to a broader range of epidemic models. Moreover, comparative simulations with the existing state observer design confirm the proposed observer's superior performance in accurately estimating system states, particularly for nonlinear systems. To further establish the proposed observer's efficacy, its performance is compared with that of a neuro-genetic observer in a numerical case study. This comparison demonstrates the proposed observer's capacity to achieve faster convergence and reduced estimation errors compared to the neuro-genetic observer. Finally, recommendations are offered for optimizing the proposed observer's design capabilities. To facilitate the existing state observer design process, two LMI-based optimization toolboxes are employed. These toolboxes enable the evaluation of sufficient conditions for convergence and optimal gain design using the following tool names: (i) "lmitool" for designing the existing state observer, and (ii) "YALMOP" for designing both observers. Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client-server communication. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (ASO-Fed), we employed partial data sharing, which minimizes participants' communication loads. Notably, ASO-Fed incurs a negligible privacy risk at any given time. We analyzed the convergence rate of ASO-Fed and demonstrated its theoretical and empirical convergence under common non-IID data distributions using real-world datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 for image classification and 100-400 part datasets from the REVERB challenge for speech recognition. ASO-Fed outperformed its online counterpart while surpassing the completely offline learning method in convergence rate. Our empirical results showed that ASO-Fed can achieve convergence with even more extreme heterogeneity and significantly outperforms its offline counterpart. This gain in performance is consistent across a wide range of participant engagement levels and communication delays. Furthermore, ASO-Fed achieved a high accuracy (96.17%) on the speech recognition task with a very low number of participants (10), and its offline counterpart could only achieve this accuracy with 20 participants. We observed similar trend when we evaluated the system with 100 participants - ASO-Fed achieved 97.23% while its offline counterpart could only manage 96.33%. From a computational complexity standpoint, it is evident that ASO-Fed is computationally dominant but this is a necessary price for achieving true asynchronous online federated learning. To make ASO-Fed practical for participants with limited resources, we implemented a time-multiplexing technique which allows a server to concurrently serve multiple participants while attending to its local training task. This technique yielded a 3.67x speedup in training and 2.52x speedup in testing respectively. A similar technique was used to accelerate ASO-Fed on the participant end. By using this technique on an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU, we observed that ASO-Fed could concurrently serve 16 participants while attending to its local training task and this yielded a 1.96x speedup in total training time. A thorough x-ray diffraction study confirmed the presence of a hexagonal 120-degree structure in the GdInO3 system. However, this confirmation was challenged during the neutron diffraction and muon spin relaxation measurements, which revealed an antiferromagnetic substructure within the GdInO3 system. The data showed the Gd atoms are arranged in a long-range ferrimagnetic (2 up, 1 down) configuration, while exhibiting short-range antiferromagnetic behavior. Moreover, the research found the GdInO3 system undergoes antiferromagnetic phase transitions at 55.3 and 52.5 K, and these observations could be attributed to the material being subjected to mechanical stress during the crystal growth process. Notably, the research found the GdInO3 system displays anomalous magnetic behavior at low temperatures and exhibits stress sensitivity, which significantly affects its magnetic structure. This unique characteristic in the GdInO3 system is distinguished from the typical magnetic behavior observed in rare-earth metal oxides, where magnetic and electronic correlations are significantly prominent. Notably, the research found rare-earth metal oxides, including those in the GdInO3 system, can display unique stress sensitivity, which may be advantageous in the design and development of devices that leverage rare-earth metal oxides with unique magnetic and electronic properties, but also requires consideration of potential complications and anomalies. Furthermore, the research identified future opportunities for investigating the electrical properties, photoemission spectra, and anomalous Hall effects in GdInO3 system. Enhanced computational efficiency is achieved by applying the model, enabling the derivation of optimal constraints for 4D formats, and simulations show significant improvement in high-frequency transmission performance when model-derived versus theoretically calculated limits are applied. Derivation of the model relies on the minimization of a distance measure between a predefined waveform and its nonlinearly distorted counterpart, both simulated using an updated nonlinear interference model with enhanced accuracy compared to previous implementations. This model is validated through comparison with Fourier amplitude spectroscopy (FASE) based approaches and constraints, yielding similar accuracy but reduced computational demands. By combining both approaches, a balanced trade-off between accuracy and computational requirements can be realized. Furthermore, the model allows us to compare and contrast different distortion phenomena, notably self-phase modulation (SPM), intramolecular dispersion (IMD), and dispersion-induced nonlinear interference (DIN), where SPM and IMD consistently dominate at lower launch powers while DIN becomes more prominent at higher launch powers when sufficient window length is applied. Consequently, derivation of optimal 4D formats relying solely on SPM and IMD may not always achieve the highest transmission performance potential. When used with an arbitrary timing step, the model still achieves comparable accuracy but may experience issues in maintaining phase coherence across FFT bins, a shortcoming that can be mitigated by aligning the timing step with the FFT window length. Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing harm to the environment and humans. Recent advances in Deep Learning have improved image analysis, making it a crucial component in this context. We developed a system that leverages computer vision to identify wildfires from aerial images. A neural network-based algorithm was designed and optimized for this purpose. Through an in-depth examination of various image filtering techniques, we determined that using a Gaussian blur filter with a 5x5 kernel effectively prepared images for training, whereas using the OpenCV's BGR color space led to better results than RGB. Our chosen architecture, EfficientNet, was fine-tuned to classify wildfires using the Google Land Fire dataset, and our model achieved a training, validation, and testing accuracy of 1.00, 0.9814, and 0.9811, respectively. By incorporating an image classification pre-processing stage, our system demonstrated impressive performance on the GLF test dataset, yielding a classification accuracy of 0.9811. Notably, our system outperformed the existing GLF classification pre-processing approach, resulting in a significant 2.9% improvement over the best-available technique. Moreover, our system exhibited resilience to false positives by correctly handling cases where the image contained fire obscurations (FOG), achieving a positive FOG classification with an accuracy of 0.9811. To further enhance the system's robustness, we investigated the effect of data augmentation; while it did not positively impact accuracy, the resulting models demonstrated consistent performance. In pursuit of efficient deployment, our system's prediction latency was tested on various hardware configurations (including multi-GPU systems, GPUs, CPUs, and laptops) and demonstrated latency of approximately 250ms on an NVIDIA A40 GPU; further, the system demonstrated flexibility by working with various camera resolutions, such as those from drones operating at 1080p resolution, which produced an accuracy of 0.9811. Notably, this work constitutes the first systematic investigation into early wildfire detection utilizing deep learning techniques. As such, this study serves as a foundational resource for researchers pursuing similar work in the future. Moreover, the associated code and model assets have been made publicly available on public GitHub repositories, facilitating future research in this domain to be conducted in a reproducible manner. To validate its efficiency, the method was tested on two scenarios: one with up to 20 underlying assets and another with 5 underlying assets, where results revealed a 90% coverage of ground truth solutions after 200 days, resulting in a annual return of 0.32% and a volatility of 0.22%. Analysis showed that the approach was able to generate profits of $ 531 in the process, with successful hedging resulting in net profits of $ 399, along with returns of $ 88.57. Shrinkage regression and natural gradient methods were identified as two key technical contributions that facilitated efficient portfolio hedging. Further analysis revealed that the approach was able to effectively handle out-of-sample performance, and demonstrate robustness in a scenario with limited price observations available at discrete time intervals. Overall, the approach demonstrated empirical evidence of effectiveness in portfolio hedging. In today's commercial environments, recommender systems play a significant role. Among the numerous approaches developed to address the problem of user item interaction prediction, sequential learning methods that leverage sequence models have shown considerable promise. These methods, capitalizing on user-item sequence data, address the issue of cold-start moderation, where new users and items can be identified as potential purchasers. Effective sequential learning depends on high-quality user-item sequence data, where transitions between items can be accurately predicted. This article reevaluates the focus on sequence models by examining important user-item transition patterns. It proposes the application of self-supervised learning, where self-supervised pre-training on user-item sequences utilizing graph autoencoders enhances the models' ability to capture transition nuances, resulting in improved sequential prediction and recommendation quality. The reducible double confluent Heun equation is a specific type of Fuchsian equation that can be transformed into two ordinary differential equations through a generalized reduction process. This process involves utilizing four separate integration constants from the DCHE equation in a specific manner. Our study focuses on two specific reduction processes for the DCHE equation, both of which utilize the first four coefficients of the formal series expansion of the equation's solution near a regular point. One process, based on a series expansion, involves a reduction scheme similar to that described by R. Koelink and H.T. Jongen, and can be represented through a Darboux integral. In contrast, the other process, which utilizes the inverse of a specific connection matrix, comes from a flat connection defined by A. Bobev and S. Eliezer. In this paper, we demonstrate that the two reduction processes are equivalent and provide a specific example of the reduction scheme, and we also make a new discovery regarding reduction schemes for the DCHE equation. This new discovery involves showing that reduction schemes based on Darboux integrals and connections are equivalent to those that can be represented through Riccati equations. Furthermore, this paper provides the series expansions near a regular point for the new DCHE equation and confirms the results from R. Koelink and H.T. Jongen regarding the singularities of the equation. We also provide a new understanding of how the equation's singularities behave under the generalized reduction process, and we use this new understanding to analyze two specific Fuchsian equations. We show that these equations can be transformed into two ordinary differential equations through the generalized reduction process and provide explicit expressions for the formal series expansion of the equation's solution near a regular point. We also discover a connection between the reduction process from the Darboux integral and a specific integrable generalized pendulum system, and we confirm the results from numerical integration of the system that coincides with the generalized reduction process. This new discovery involves showing that the reduction process from the Darboux integral can be represented through a change of variable in the system's equation, and we provide a specific example of the transformation for a generalized pendulum system with a singularity at z=1. We also use the new DCHE equation to analyze a specific timbre example, and we provide a new understanding of how the timbre's characteristics change as a function of specific integration constants from the equation. Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation in an infinite-dimensional setting where a fixed number of matrix components is considered. These findings are based on an innovative model transformation from the homogeneous to a heterogeneous low-rank matrix tensor product model. We demonstrate that some PCA-based methods are optimal in certain scenarios but suboptimal in others. Numerical experiments comparing these findings with PCA-based methods and other optimization techniques such as gradient descent and message passing are also provided. We anticipate that the models and methods explored here will be useful in understanding and developing optimization techniques for low-rank matrix recovery problems across various applications. This work has been accepted for publication in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2022. We would like to thank the conference reviewers for their feedback at the virtual conference. We have made additional contributions, which include deriving self-consistency equations and applying variational EM to the heterogeneous low-rank matrix tensor product model for an extensive range of matrix ranks. We have made these findings available to the public at an open-access repository called https://github.com/yisingm/hrrmtmp. We have also expanded upon our original work by exploring the recovery boundaries for a binary matrix observation model, which is consistent with the Gaussian noise levels across different matrix components. We have obtained numerical evidence suggesting that the PCA method is optimal in some cases but suboptimal in others. We have made the source code for the majority of the results discussed above at https://github.com/yisingm/hrrmp publicly available. In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered: a relationship between the fraction of states localized at the boundary and the curvature of the energy band near its exceptional point. We verify these predictions with a real-world experiment. Additionally, another type of exceptional point, known as a degenerate point, is found in this system, where a particular vibration mode is represented by two distinct states. Unlike general topological models, the bulk-boundary correspondence does not predict bound states at degenerate points; however, in this ring's case, bound states appear due to contact loss and zero curvature at the degenerate energy. Consequently, exceptional points emerge not only from symmetry-breaking but also from the transition from a gapped system to a non-symmetric correlated phase of a gapless system. The exceptional points in this system can be visualized through experiments with a solid material and may also be observed in other models lacking symmetry. Furthermore, the model of a constrained ring is applicable to phonons in solid materials and may also be realized in recent photonic systems without symmetry. Lastly, exceptional points may be more common than previously anticipated due to various symmetry-breaking factors within realistic systems. Photographs are used in this research to illustrate experiments. The source code for calculating the bulk-boundary correspondence can be found at https://github.com/accioconductor/BulkBoundaryCorrespondence. The source code for simulating constrained rings has been uploaded to https://accioconductor.github.io/ACCIOCONDUCTOR/. This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method with a few illustrative examples. Firstly, a linear time-invariant (LTI) multi-agent system is used to evaluate the performance of our approach in comparison to a centralized method. Secondly, a large-scale nonlinear system is utilized to examine the robustness of our controller design in a system with nonlinear dynamics. Lastly, a typical formation control task is employed to assess the efficacy of our approach in achieving robust and stable controller designs. We show that our approach efficiently solves this control task while reducing computational complexity and requirements for data storage. These design benefits extend to a decentralized filter design for estimating agents' outputs, with the option for output limitation and analysis of the distributed estimator's stability using a Lyapunov-based approach. To facilitate practical implementation, parametric specifications for the controller and estimator gain settings are provided. All of these design approaches are validated through numerical simulations and real experimental results. This work is further enabled by an open-source toolbox named DINCS (Distributed Control System), which provides a centralized platform for designing and analyzing decentralized control laws and estimators. This tool leverages Bass' algorithm to facilitate efficient calculations and supports design methods for both output feedback and output estimation problems. Additionally, DINCS provides utility functions to analyze the frequency response characteristics of decentralized controllers and filters, offering a comprehensive design and analysis framework. By providing an open-source toolbox, we aim to foster further research into decentralized control law and estimator generation, providing a solid foundation for decentralized system control and estimation theory development. Moreover, DINCS' frequency response analysis utility can serve as a proxy tool to aid design tasks, such as optimal decentralized perquisite realization, decentralized loop-shaping, and robust decentralized design. We believe that these design benefits, facilitated by an efficient computational framework, open up opportunities for practical implementation of our approach in control engineering. Lastly, we provide an overview of related research on control and estimation problems within a graph signal processing context, highlighting the significance of these design methods and potential applications. The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, as evidenced by the rapid changes observed in Trinidadian guppies and other laboratory and natural populations. We argue this perspective is overly narrow and neglects potential interactions on longer timescales, such as those influenced by global change, ecological feedback loops, evolutionary dynamics spanning centuries, and ancient fossil records. We conjoin 'eco' and 'evolutionary' dynamics to enhance our comprehension of global change, an essential phenomenon with direct human implications. We have made an open call for relevant data and knowledge to be re-examined through this holistic approach, which we illustrate with two case studies: (i) the slow evolution of the North Atlantic right whale over thousands of years, and (ii) the slow ecological changes observed in coral ecosystems. By combining diverse datasets, this review highlights the significance of considering distinct timescales, feeding back ecological dynamics into evolutionary processes, and integrating geological, paleo-, and socio-historical knowledge to comprehend the far-reaching effects of global change on eco-evolutionary dynamics. Furthermore, it demonstrates the potential of incorporating big data, Fossil Record, and Fossil-Record Synthesis into eco-evolutionary dynamics research. In doing so, this review expands our understanding of the complex and often protracted timescales involved in eco-evolutionary dynamics, challenging the conventional view that these processes occur rapidly. We hope that redefining the boundaries between 'eco' and 'evolutionary' dynamics, incorporating longer timescales, will foster a more inclusive discussion on global change, an essential topic in today's world. A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations through self-supervision by comparing various approaches on a broad range of speech tasks. By using a unified, high-dimensional speech representation, SUPERB showcases the potential of self-supervised learning (SSL) to deliver exceptional results in multiple speech applications without needing task-specific fine-tuning. Cross-task comparisons through functional mapping reveal that SSL effectively captures relevant information for different speech tasks, even when the relationships are not immediately apparent. Moreover, SSL outperforms models trained with traditional supervised learning methods across various speech challenges, including speech recognition, keyword spotting, emotion and trauma detection, speaker diagnosis, and speech compression. As a result, SSL emerges as a promising approach for developing versatile and efficient speech representations in various speech applications. We also investigate the effectiveness of SSL across 14 languages and find that JITTADOR features functionally similarly across these languages, suggesting a valuable cross-lingual speech representation that can bridge language gaps in speech applications. Consequently, we propose cross-lingual transferability metrics and functional distance metrics to systematically evaluate cross-lingual speech representations and assess their potential in real-world speech applications. Moreover, we discover that SSL achieves better results in trauma and zero-shot trauma detection in multiple languages compared to other methods. We also find that SSL outperforms other methods in diagnosing traumatic experiences in multi-lingual speech without task-specific fine-tuning, demonstrating significant performance gains, up to 24.3% relative improvement. We further investigate the effectiveness of SSL in detecting traumatic content in multi-lingual speech and find that SSL produces a cross-lingual speech representation that can successfully detect trauma across languages, achieving a 76.9% relative improvement over other methods in this task. We also find that speech compression is a challenging problem for SSL, requiring significant resources to achieve state-of-the-art results, an aspect that current SSL approaches cannot address efficiently. We also find that SSL is ineffective in emotion and trauma detection in multiple languages, likely due to insufficient data in these tasks, an issue that needs to be resolved through data augmentation or collection of additional resources to enable SSL to deliver state-of-the-art results in these tasks. We publicly share our code to ensure reproducibility and facilitate the development of cross-lingual SSL models, an essential step towards building more efficient and versatile speech applications that can work across multiple languages and domains. A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, evaluates how conclusions based on incomplete data can be affected by uncertainties in underlying assumptions. We build upon an existing metric known as the E-value, which measures the confidence in a data-driven conclusion. We extend this approach to decision-making for continuous outcomes and develop decision-specific E-values. We address challenges posed by using non-parametric confidence curves to define these E-values for continuous outcomes. We demonstrate the potential utility of this approach through a case study on COVID-19 treatments, where we employ a Bayesian non-parametric model to make inference in the presence of missing outcome data. We utilize non-parametric confidence curves to define decision-specific E-values for this model, showcasing the versatility of this method across different Bayesian non-parametric models. We apply this approach to a real-world scenario where researchers assess the effectiveness of biclonal interferon in treating COVID-19 by comparing outcomes across arms of a randomised controlled trial. Given that the outcome for each individual is only observed if they experienced a high outcome and therefore the researcher uses a non-parametric model that incorporates this information. We find that the decision-specific E-values indicate a substantial uncertainty in the decision-maker's preference for biclonal interferon following some missing data scenarios. We find that the decision-specific E-values are significantly lower than the E-value for a single continuous outcome, signifying that using a decision-specific metric can produce a more conservative estimate compared to the overall E-value metric. A multitude of innovative cooling systems have recently emerged to provide cryogenic temperatures for quantum computing, all ranging from 250 to 5 millikelvin in temperature. Despite their diversity, none have been successfully mass-produced due to technical difficulties, prompting numerous new approaches to reach this millikelvin scale. Researchers are now investing heavily in cutting-edge cryogenic technology to facilitate the development of reliable, robust, and easy-to-use cryogenic systems for quantum computing applications. This article reviews the cutting-edge millikelvin cryogenic technology being developed today. It explores a range of innovative cooling systems, including adiabatic crycoolers, the SQ series cryogenic refrigerators, magnetic cooling, topological insulators, dielectric pyroelectric coolers, and cryogenic vacuum pumps. Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent, with one notable exception - a study conducted on professional developers in Python revealed a lower incidence of insecure code for crypto-related tasks. This led to the investigation of whether the trend holds true for real-world Python applications. By creating a static analysis tool, researchers examined a large sample of popular Python projects and MicroPython projects, comparing their findings to previous studies. The analysis showed that a substantial proportion of Python projects exhibit at least one crypto API misuse. The good design of some Python crypto libraries appears to significantly reduce the likelihood of misuses compared to studies involving Java and C. The analysis also highlighted the value of hybrid analysis methods in detecting misuses in embedded devices. The results suggest a beneficial impact of sound API design on reducing crypto-related security risks in Python applications. The analysis of embedded devices demonstrated that even simple microcontrollers can accommodate advanced analysis tools, and such tools may offer additional security value by combining analysis of Python and binary code, an effect observed in MicroPython projects. The analysis uncovered a substantial number of security vulnerabilities in the checked projects, the vast majority of which were previously unknown at the time of this study, resulting in ten newly discovered vulnerabilities. The key factors contributing to the success of the analysis were the small footprint of the analysis tool and its efficient memory usage, allowing the tool to run smoothly on devices to the limit of their available RAM. The analysis showed that providing developers with concrete security issues yields better outcomes in terms of security quality, supporting previous research findings. The dedicated developer spent significant time inspecting the code, but the outcome was worth it - 85% of the issues discovered were fixed. The analysis revealed that code inspection was the most effective analysis method available today for identifying misuses of crypto APIs in code, underscoring the value of human involvement in the analysis process. The dedicated developer played a crucial role, identifying issues that the tool could not analyze statically. The researchers note that the future version of the analysis tool should incorporate a password policy, similar to one proposed by Bogdanov and others, to guide developers' assessment of security risks. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically performed by training models on large, high-quality annotated corpora. As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human requirements often lack essential information, or they contain inaccuracies or ambiguities, or they contain inaccuracies or inconsistencies. We introduce CitySpec, a novel AI-powered system for formalizing and executing requests related to city infrastructure. It analyzes free-text requests using its multi-faceted analysis to identify relevant data sources from municipal databases, then generates an optimized, machine-readable specification. CitySpec effectively addresses the challenge of request ambiguity by providing several possible formalizations, or a single solution if a consensus exists. We evaluated its effectiveness through an analysis of its code and conducted an experimental study involving 40 participants who were presented with 24 scenarios based on actual city requests for repairs. We compared its output to that of a human expert using the standard metric for specification quality and performed a detailed analysis of its analyzed databases and processing methodology. CitySpec successfully produced high-quality formalizations, matching a human expert's standards in most cases, or even exceeding their standards in several instances. Notably, its processing time is remarkably fast, taking only a few milliseconds. CityDB is an open-access database for evaluating intelligent systems that combine formal specification and execution. It encompasses a wide range of smart city applications, including those related to urban planning, traffic management, or public works, and features over 400 requests with varying complexities, as well as synthetic, artificially-generated requests. We believe that these resources will aid researchers in addressing critical issues in automated request formalization and execution, or related smart city applications. CitySpec and its supporting resources are available at https://cityspec.upm.edu/.

The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within medical imaging has grown significantly, driven largely by the standardization of digital imaging formats using DICOM. This standardization enables the analysis and processing of images to be used for training machine learning models, providing access to a diverse range of images. Consequently, various methods have been proposed to facilitate the creation of useful predictive models from standardized image data. These methods typically involve either retrieving images from electronic healthcare records or gathering them from imaging modalities. Due to the inherent complexities and requirements of clinical data management, processing and analyzing these images can be a highly resource-intensive and time-consuming process. To address these challenges, research has identified opportunities for optimization, focusing on reducing the need for extensive computing power, memory, and storage. This study aims to provide an overview of current approaches for analyzing images stored in standardized formats, presenting a novel workflow that combines efficient processing of DICOM data with cutting-edge deep learning architectures. By adopting this proposed workflow, processing and retraining deep learning models with large image datasets can be performed within a timely and resource-efficient framework. To validate the practical feasibility of this approach, the study conducts comparative analysis of different models and image resolutions using real-world datasets in the fields of CT, MRI, and ultrasound imaging. Our results demonstrate that DICOM-based image analysis can achieve state-of-the-art performance, ranging from 85-95% accuracy depending on the specific application and model used, as well as image resolution. To the extent applicable, all study participants have provided informed consent, and institutional review board approval has been obtained. All data and code used in this study have been made available online under open-source licensing, aiming to provide a freely accessible and reusable framework for medical imaging researchers. The proposed framework and code enable the efficient training of deep learning models on diverse image data, and facilitates the development of diagnostic systems that can be deployed on various platforms, including commercial operating systems and embedded systems, including Linux-based systems such as Ubuntu, and embedded systems, including Apple iOS, and Google Android, and Raspberry Pi. Furthermore, the study showcases the successful application of deep learning on real image data from clinical modalities, including CT, MRI, ultrasound, and X-ray, achieving impressive performance, ranging from 85-95% depending on specific use case, image resolution, and depth of the model used. By combining efficient image processing with cutting-edge deep learning architectures, researchers and clinicians can now efficiently train and deploy diagnostic systems on diverse platforms, including access to resource-limited devices, such as Apple iOS, and Google Android

We present a derivation of Noether's current from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term and demonstrate that the corresponding charge is connected to Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, when evaluated on the horizon. The entropy can also be calculated using a Virasoro algebra and Cardy formula approach, in which we identify relevant diffeomorphisms based on a simple physical principle that maintains the horizon's structure. Our method focuses on the surface theory's long-distance properties. The essential ingredient in this framework is an accurate definition of an effective Hamiltonian that incorporates the correct asymptotic behavior. The approach is illustrated by applying it to a topologically massive gravity model, in which we calculate a non-trivial primary central charge and use it to determine the associated entropy following the holographic principle. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the essential aspects of our framework can be realized in a specific 2D dilaton gravity model. The paper concludes with a discussion on how an analogous derivation of the Maxwell theory's surface term's Noether current yields a Weinberg's relation, $c \simeq a^2 \rho$, linking charge, central charge, and density. The connection reveals an intricate relationship between entropy, charge, and central charge. The essential ideas in this paper were already presented in a semi-popular talk. In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and variable nature of these DNA sequences. In our current research, a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder model is applied in an unsupervised manner to derive a standardized, fixed-dimensional latent representation of long and variable length DNA sequences. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of this representation in supervised DNA classification tasks across various tasks, such as splice site classification, pathway analysis, and DNA alignment for variation analysis. We evaluate the quality of this representation through comparative studies with traditional unsupervised feature extraction methods like PCA and t-SNE. Lastly, the latent representation is made publicly accessible through the DNA Representations for Analysis Platform (DRAP), a web-based platform that facilitates the analysis of DNA sequences through interactive visualization tools. Moreover, the DRAP platform allows researchers to integrate their own datasets and models for learning latent representations, thereby facilitating sharing and cross-domain knowledge transfer among researchers. The DRAP platform is accessible at http://drap.uwaterloo.ca. Additionally, the representation datasets and associated code can be found at https://github.com/CAGatcliffe/DNASequenceLearnedRepresentations. Research described in this article has been supported by grants from the Canadian Institute of Health Research (CIHR). A Python-based implementation of our proposed method is also publicly available at https://github.com/CAGatcliffe/DNASequenceLearnedRepresentations. The source code submitted with this article can be found at https://github.com/CAGatcliffe/JournalSubmissionCode. In conclusion, the unsupervised learning of DNA sequence representations using a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder model yields superior results in supervised DNA classification tasks, surpassing traditional feature extraction methods. Furthermore, the comprehensive repository of DNA sequences and associated representations, including the novel autoencoder model, is made publicly accessible through https://github.com/CAGatcliffe/DNASequenceLearnedRepresentations. This study compares the effectiveness of various machine learning models, including decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting machines, using real-world data from a Polish bank.
We analyzed data from applicants for cash and personal loans and evaluated seven supervised learning models, finding that customer characteristics, such as age and loan amount, are the most crucial factors influencing non-performing loans.

We discovered significant differences between the behaviors of cash and personal loan applicants and identified patterns that deviate from typical credit risk profiles, such as higher defaults among young and female applicants. Additionally, we found that loan approval processes can be skewed due to biases in available data. This knowledge may influence future research directions and inform decisions to provide financial assistance to disadvantaged groups. Overall, our investigation provides a comprehensive analysis of the challenges associated with predicting non-performing loans. A coloring of $H$ is called an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring if it can be constructed by assigning colors from a given set $R$, where each vertex in $H$ receives the next available color from $R$. This sequence of colors is continued indefinitely as long as $R$ remains unexhausted. This paper explores the $R$-sequential $t$-colorings in graphs with cycles and focuses on finding the maximum possible number of these colorings in such graphs for a given size of $R$. This problem is essentially equivalent to identifying the extremal values of a specific graph parameter, $\xsp_t(G,R)$, which represents the size of the largest induced subgraph $H$ of $G$ where an $R$-sequential $t$-coloring exists. This parameter, $\xsp_t(G,R)$, is further generalized for $r>2$ in the case where $R$ is a set of $r$ integers and it can be proven that the given extremal values of $\xsp_t(G,R)$ tend towards $\binom{\lambda_t(G,R)-1}{r-1}$. To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous vertices is initially created, which allows for intricate quads due to its flexible vertex configuration. Subsequently, a customized mesh simplification approach is implemented to derive a high-order quadrilateral mesh. By preserving key mesh characteristics, including 80% of non-boundary vertices, we ensure desired properties are maintained. To refine this mesh, we adapt and modify existing localized mesh optimization methods to generate a smooth, optimal quadrilateral mesh. This approach enables the construction of high-order quadrilateral meshes from versatile meshes quickly and efficiently. We evaluate our method by applying it to CAD models with various geometries and present mesh quality results as well as convergence characteristics for isogeometric p-element simulations. Due to its versatility and high quality, this method is particularly useful for demanding computational analysis tasks. A mesh generator that produces high-quality quadrilateral meshes is also provided. Additionally, the source code for the stand-alone mesh generator is available at https://gitub.com/complex-systems-unit/MeshCGCD. Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation can be assessed using p-values and corresponding confidence intervals. While numerous methods exist for calculating correlation coefficients, few algorithms efficiently handle high-dimensional data sets by determining the optimal subset of variables for correlation analysis. We developed an algorithm using a dynamic programming approach to identify the most strongly correlated subset of variables in high-dimensional data, and validated it using simulated and real-world datasets, comparing it to alternative methods where applicable. The proposed algorithm was further optimized for data sets with missing values and we provide p-values and confidence intervals as additional validation tools. We tested the method using the well-known Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset. The source code is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/yumeir/zanzy/tree/corr_subsets. We performed a step-by-step comparison with the R package correlative, which calculates the correlation coefficients for all pairs of variables, requiring substantial computational resources. In contrast, our method is highly efficient, processing datasets of the same size in less than 0.1 seconds. The proposed approach can be extended to data sets with complex structures by utilizing the established statistical method for identifying optimal subsets and we plan to explore this direction in future research. The results showed that our method outperforms existing approaches in finding the most strongly correlated subsets of variables, with statistical significance at p<1e-10 for the example dataset from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. The analysis revealed that the most strongly correlated variables were associated with the invariant epithelial lining of the meninges, covering the brain area. Specifically, the variables with the highest correlation coefficients were concentrated on the occipital cortex, a region responsible for visual processing. We hypothesize that this finding may be a sign of an abnormality in this brain area, which is investigate further in our study. The proposed algorithm was applied to the data of Alzheimer's patients and controls, demonstrating a significant group difference in the identified optimal subset of variables with a p-value of 2.32e-12. Moreover, the variability in the correlation coefficients between subjects was significant at p<1e-10. The method successfully detected the variable representing age, which has been linked to cognitive decline, in both groups. Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web interface. It utilizes a generative model trained on 
Google Knowledge Graph Data to synthesize definitions, enabling users to generate 
dictionary entries for words not currently included. Users can contribute to the 
dictionary by providing definitions for words they are familiar with. The 
accumulator of user contributions is a collaborative dictionary that can be 
downloaded as a CSV file. The project also includes a brief tutorial on the 
dictionary's functionality. The LitMind Dictionary is deployed at https://litmind.com/.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties may be effectively produced
using semiconductor-superconductor hybrids, consisting of materials in close
proximity and a unique electronic transport behavior. The performance of such
hybrids depends significantly on the electron mobility, which is influenced by
surface defects and impurities. The electron transport measurements on
InAs-GaAs and InAs-Al heterostructures showed that Al-based hybrids have
significantly lower resistance than GaAs-based hybrids at low temperatures.
This low resistance in Al-based hybrids is caused by an abnormal electronic
transfer through the Al terminal and a high density of impurities near the
interface. The surface defects and impurities can be minimized by using an
oxidized Al surface, which results in a higher resistance in Al-based hybrids.
This approach provides a high density of states at the Fermi level and offers a
potential solution for improving semiconductor-superconductor hybrid devices. 
Using an oxidized Al surface also allows for a reliable measurement of the
conductance using standard two-terminal configurations, which was absent in
Al-based hybrids with clean interfaces. The cross-sectional scanning tunneling
spectroscopy also confirmed the presence of a high density of states at the
Fermi level on oxidized Al surfaces, which is due to the Al oxide properties. 
The surface modification using an Al layer with a high density of impurities
near the interface does not affect the semiconductor-superconductor transition
in InAs-based hybrids, which is consistent with previous studies on similar
GaAs-based hybrids. The unique electronic transport properties of Al-based
hybrids provide an accessible means to study superconducting properties and
potentially leverage these properties for device applications. The surface
properties and recombination mechanisms of materials with high density of
impurities near the interface were investigated using various techniques and
discussed in relation to the electron transport measurements. 
X-ray photoemission spectroscopy confirmed the surface morphology of Al
terminations, while high-resolution transmission electron microscopy revealed
details of the quantum wells and termination layers. The recombination
mechanisms of materials with high density of impurities near the interface
were discussed in relation to experimental results, which were further supported
by theoretical models. 
Finally, the recombination mechanisms of materials with oxidized surfaces
and high impurity densities were explored in relation to electron transport
measures, which were further confirmed by experimental data.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an 25-million-year-old star hosting two planets within the habitable zone, presents an opportunity to study this impact. AU Mic's atmospheric activity has been studied using 10-year long observations from Chandra, revealing that the star's X-ray emission varies significantly over short periods and modestly over decade-long timescales. Long-term monitoring also discovered two high-energy flares in real-time and confirmed previous findings of correlated X-ray and ultraviolet emissions from Chandra and TESS data. This relationship, however, did not hold true in August 2019, and high-energy observations from LAMPOST revealed that this was likely due to a low-energy outflow occurring at that time. Based on this correlation, it appears that this anomaly may not pose a significant threat to the atmospheres of its planets and they remain relatively unaffected. Furthermore, atmospheric loss due to high-energy fluctuations in AU Mic does not seem substantial, and further monitoring is necessary to understand mass loss over planetary cycles, as well as planetary outflows specifically, which could provide crucial insights into exoplanet composition and spectroscopic data. Moreover, high and variable fluxes of soft X-rays from AU Mic imply significant outflows from its NEA CPAs, which could be responsible for its coronal loop structures observed in X- rays and potentially drive its wind patterns as seen in TESS data. Lastly, comparing the properties of AU Mic's outflows to its planetary-scale wind patterns reveals that this relationship may not necessarily impact its planets.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the simultaneous occurrence of electromagnetic and mechanical energy loss by a rapidly accelerating charged particle with an intrinsic moment of inertia. In this model, we consider the particle as a classic rigid body with an arbitrary intrinsic spin and oscillation as it experiences mechanical friction. As a result, we observe a significant reduction in radiation energy loss due to medium-induced minijet suppression, primarily caused by mechanical effects in a manner that is independent of charge. Furthermore, we discover that the total energy loss, encompassing both electromagnetic and mechanical processes, exhibits a symmetrical response to variations in particle mass and spin magnitude. Our research also uncovers a novel radiation energy spectrum determined solely by the kinetic component of the particle's velocity and the Larmor velocity of its intrinsic spin. We derive a closed-form expression for this new energy spectrum in the junction region between the'soft' and 'hard' regimes and apply it to two specific scenarios: electron conversion in collisionless space plasma and closed-shell heavy ion decay in certain astrophysical environments. We find that for a narrow kinetic energy range, the new energy spectrum matches the established QED prediction exactly. Our analysis demonstrates that the new energy spectrum can be utilized as an alternative standard reference to separate electromagnetic and mechanical energy loss processes, and it may be observed experimentally in various astrophysical and plasma detectors. We also conduct a simulation of heavy ion decay at the SHIP experiment to measure the spin-dependent energy loss and find substantial mechanical energy loss effects. We discover that the new energy spectrum features a notable increase in the high-energy tail compared to both electromagnetic and mechanical energy loss spectra, primarily due to the combination of both processes. Our research shows that the new energy spectrum yields a higher energy production rate for pairs created via magnetic fields and mini-jets generated by the jet-medium interactions. We find that the electron energy distribution following the decay of closed-shell heavy ions exhibits a notable positive drift, primarily caused by the kinetic energy of the decaying particle, and is independent of the intrinsic spin of the particle. Our study reveals that the new energy spectrum can be observed experimentally in cosmic ray studies, and is relevant to detector calibration in certain astrophysical and plasma detectors. We also show that a particle with an intrinsic moment of inertia can exhibit a notable negative drift in electron velocity energy distribution, and is dependent on the intrinsic spin of the particle. In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, and the framework presents under certain conditions that the nearest neighbor classifier achieves the best possible accuracy when dealing with skewed data, effectively acting as a baseline for comparison in such cases. Additionally, the framework offers a measure for evaluating how strongly the nearest neighbor classifier is influenced by class size, known as the \emph{splitting factor}, and this factor can be used to identify potential issues in classification results. This approach is further validated by analyzing a comprehensive dataset consisting of 32 different datasets, where the results show that (i) the nearest neighbor classifier is asymptotically optimal in uneven class distributions, (ii) the splitting factor can be effectively used to verify if the nearest neighbor classifier performances are positionally invariant using stochastic ordering, and (iii) common data preprocessing techniques such as rare over-sampling and majority down-sampling can help alleviate problems associated with skewed data. This approach presents a new understanding of the nearest neighbor classifier and offers a measure to analyze its competitiveness in uneven class distributions, which can be applied across various real-world applications. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, including those facilitated by a quantum dot and those that involve a dot in a highly excited state. Furthermore, our analysis has led us to believe that the quantum dot behaves as a discrete island rather than as a continuous channel for electron flow. While interacting with a superconducting island, the quantum dot remains capable of conducting a small number of electrons. The interaction between these two islands appears to be characterized by a very small tunneling width, which is likely blocked entirely when they become coupled through a common gate contact. The observed lack of coupling has significant implications, as it results in a notable suppression of the dynamic Coulomb blockade effect. Essentially, this effect is suppressed only when the two interacting islands are connected via a new path, which facilitates the transfer of coherent information. This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech. Additionally, a comparison of this method's performance with a median-based benchmark demonstrates comparable quality to a popular commercial text-to-speech model. Finally, an analysis of the model's capabilities in generating duration profiles for artificially lengthened or shortened utterances shows promising results. This study marks a significant advancement in duration modelling for speech synthesis, providing a foundation for further research. The project's code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/grinnert/mediana.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing transfer learning via BERT, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. According to our findings, models employing transfer learning outperformed others across both tasks. Significantly, our analysis highlighted that task-specific models struggled to tackle complex hate speech examples, underscoring the importance of transfer learning models in tackling this resilient form of online abuse. Moreover, our study provides new insights into the semantic patterns that distinguish offensive content in multiple languages, including German, Dutch, and Danish. For instance, we discovered that male derogatory content in German and Dutch shares more semantic similarities than derogatory content from these two languages, labeled as'male insult'. On the other hand, we found that sexist and homophobic content in German, Dutch, and Danish exhibited high semantic similarity. Lastly, our analysis shows that models trained on data from one task are unable to detect homophobic content across all three languages, underscoring the need for multi-task and cross-language datasets for successful transfer learning. In summary, our study emphasizes the significance of leveraging shared tasks to improve NLP model performance in identifying hate speech and derogatory content. Further, our research highlights the importance of developing datasets that can facilitate successful cross-language and multi-task transfer learning. The study's key outcomes and implemented models are freely accessible at https://github.com/jordaneckleberry/IE Shared Task 2021. Finally, our research suggests that successful identification of complex homophobic content across languages demands a more in-depth and specialized understanding of relevant keywords, phrases, and semantic patterns than what is currently available in existing datasets. Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, MIMO has been found to be parameter-inefficient, as each subnetwork requires replication, regardless of contributions to the final outcome. This work introduces Self-Aware MIMO (SAMIMO), an internal combination of replicated subnetworks that adapts to the functional diversity within the ensemble. SAMIMO employs a variational approach to model distributional differences between subnetworks, and uses this variation to determine the relative weights for each contribution. In experiments, we investigate Self-Aware combinations within various architectures and demonstrate that SAMIMO leads to better results with reduced redundant parameters. We perform a case study on a synthetic dataset and probe the internal dynamics of SAMIMO to gain insights into its function. Moreover, we show that SAMIMO improves performance in recycled ResNet50 models when applied to the ChestX-ray14 dataset. The research code is available at https://github.com/andrevala/SAMIMO. This paper is a submission for NeurIPS 2022.

In contrast to typical Earth climates, 'hothouse' environments likely feature internal climate system instabilities, extensive water vapor, and altered atmospheric dynamics, particularly in 'atmospheric hothouses' with distinct warm layers above the tropics. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a vast quantity of high-quality, labeled images which often contains errors. Consequently, developing robust training techniques that counteract the effects of noisy labels is of the utmost importance. particularly in the medical field. This research focuses on designing an effective training technique for deep multiple-instance learning models that excels in the presence of label noise. The method utilizes two main components: 1) An optimized loss function is developed by combining two different loss terms to account for both bag-level and instance-level uncertainties. 2) An adaptive regularization technique is proposed to limit the model in the feature domain, thereby reducing overfitting and achieving better generalization. Experimental evaluations conducted using four diverse medical datasets demonstrate significant improvements in the model's performance when using this novel technique over traditional regularization methods. Notably, the highest gains were observed in datasets with high levels of noisy labels. Furthermore, the results indicate that this new method outperforms state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning models that were designed to counteract label noise. Overall, the proposed approach showcases its effectiveness in deep multiple-instance learning with noisy labels. The code for this novel technique will be publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/HiDeX-ZeeU/IRMN. For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $0\le p \le q-1$, we studied its phase diagram under minimal crystalline symmetry. The results showed the existence of various phases: phases containing multiple Weyl nodes with surface Fermi arcs; a Chern insulating phase featuring gapless surface states despite bulk gapping; a unique phase combining gapped, topologically non-trivial bands with gapless Weyl nodes, connecting to a Chern insulating phase; and a new phase exhibiting gapped, topologically non-trivial bands with no surface states. The phase transitions were found to be continuous and could be represented by $Z_q$ magnetic symmetries. The predicted phenomena were proposed for materials like linear-in-momentum Chern ferroptrope, where both Weyl semimetal and Chern insulating phases could be found in materials like PtCoO$_2$ and Ca$_3$RuO$_3$.$\cdot$qO. Experiments were suggested for observing the predicted topological states. The analysis revealed that surface states of all Weyl nodes in the semimetal could be lifted by an orbital magnetic field, creating phases with gapped Weyl nodes and surface Fermi arcs. Additionally, phase transitions could potentially be observed through magnetization and orbital magnetization measurements, offering methods for detecting Weyl semimetal and related topological states. Localized states derived from Weyl nodes near the boundary could be discovered through surface state measurements, as could Chern numbers in flat bands for materials like Ca$_3$RuO$_3$.$\cdot$qO. For materials like PtCoO$_2$, late-stage phase transitions could be detected by Raman spectroscopy, where measurements could reveal topological surface states, gapped Weyl nodes, and Fermi arcs. The predicted topological states derived from broken time-reversal symmetry could be destroyed by a quantum anomalous Hall effect introduced by applying an orbital magnetic field, creating phases for potential applications in devices. The proposed phases could be observed in various forms of materials, like thin films, quantum wells, and topological proximate devices. For a specific example, the phase diagram for $q=4$ was found to match observations of Ca$_3$RuO$_3$.$\cdot$4O, where all semimetal and insulating phases could be explained by this model.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. In successful tests, this implementation closely mimics the conservational behavior of the fundamental Lagrangian method in SPH and accurately resolves angular momentum conservation across a range of scenarios including supermassive stars and collapsing structures. We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance the learning capacity of reinforcement and imitation learning from experienced examples. The policy generator produces synthetic experiences mimicking the environment's behavior, which are combined with the initial dataset to create a unified training set. Uniquely, the model optimizes over a designated memory space to identify the most beneficial experiences to enhance training, leveraging the latent representations obtained through the encoder to determine their quality. The proposed approach demonstrates superior performance in efficient learning on multiple benchmark environments, particularly in scenarios requiring precise dexterous manipulation. Ultimately, we observe that experience augmentation significantly boosts the learning potential of experience-based methods, ultimately leading to improved performance. In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is crucial for certain matters, such as dark matter research and neutrino investigations, which involve particle directionality. This paper discusses the new technique of non-contrast collimation method for particle direction determination. Utilizing perfectly collimated light emitters, the time and spatial information of detected recoils can be used to determine the direction of nuclear recoils. Furthermore, the study suggests that the non-contrast collimation method has the potential to enhance recoil direction determination efficiency by 20% to 100% for both laboratory-based dark matter detectors and large-scale neutrino investigations.
