A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. We implement this method in a study examining the impact of weather on commercial driving behavior and develop an interpretation system to facilitate knowledge sharing across the ecosystem. As part of this, we establish a knowledge-transfer framework between industry professionals and data scientists to irreversibly integrate ecological information into our assessment system. The success of our approach is demonstrated by showing that the Expert-centered Driver Assessment has enhanced fairness and performance compared to traditional assessment methods. Furthermore, our study contributes to the knowledge gap in literature by providing insight into how weather conditions affect commercial driving behavior. The findings from our study highlight critical scenarios where drivers struggle to adapt to challenging environments, as well as best practices for navigating these situations effectively. By investigating contextual factors, our study reveals the limitations of behavior-centric driver-assessment systems and offers a more precise and equitable evaluation of commercial driving behavior, resulting in increased transparency and reliability. The expertise of industry professionals in our study increases the efficiency of driver-assessment systems, allowing for the execution of more cases in real-world environments. Based on our experience, we outline recommendations for further research and propose a new research framework that integrates multiple disciplines to investigate commercial driving behavior and develops a systematic method to incorporate expert knowledge into driver-assessment systems. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models capable of reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training. 
The challenge initiative can be found at the following website: https://github.com/Antonio-Tl/OOV-Challenge. 
Future initiatives will include including a distinct test server for model submission evaluation.

In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology. This setup allows for precise control over small-scale disturbances at the interface between two fluids, separated by a thin air layer. By manipulating the upward or downward movement of the interface, we examine various modes of instability. Our experiments, performed using two fluids of different densities - water and glycerin - and spanning different ranges of global modes, reveal growth patterns that can be accurately predicted. However, when disturbances are introduced locally rather than globally, we observe an inverse correlation between the site of maximum growth and the underlying Taylor-Michelson instability mechanism. This phenomenon contradicts both linear analysis and prior experimental findings, revealing previously unknown dynamics. Our investigation into this anomaly spans three distinct domains: (1) an analytical disturbance, (2) an experimental assessment of what kinds of disturbances are produced by altering the weight imbalance between the two fluids, and (3) a detailed analysis of the dynamics at the fluid interface via the linearized, two-fluid model. Our results suggest that Taylor-Michelson instability plays a dominant role in both cases, but when disturbances are locally introduced, they trigger an intricate combination of dynamic processes that enables the development of unstable modes that would otherwise remain dormant according to linear theory. This research offers fresh insights into this complex phenomenon, challenging our prior understanding of it. To quantify this effect, we utilize both linear and nonlinear models of instability to create a sophisticated, large-scale model of Rayleigh-Taylor Instability, which we can program to generate synthetic data that can be used to make predictions about this class of physical systems. Our software, along with the accompanying materials and data, can be accessed at https://github.com/RTI-leveled/RTI_simulation. We would also like to extend our gratitude to Peter Schmid for his invaluable guidance and advice. Finally, we would like to acknowledge the important contributions made by our research assistant, Anirban Nanda.

Following a remark by Harvey, Matschinger and Zaharescu, we prove that the denominators of the algebraic part of a $GL(n)$ twist of a power-saving $L$-function have bounded denominators. Initially, the problem was posed in relation to the Watson pair $\left(\mathrm{GL}(3), \mathrm{GL}(2)\right)$. Our proof simplifies the already successful approach of Matschinger and Zaharescu, incorporating a new strategy. The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that excel in lower-dimensional spaces but become difficult to solve in higher dimensions. To overcome this limitation, we present an enhanced version of the ASK method, leveraging the efficiency of sparse grid techniques to achieve significant speedup while maintaining accuracy. We evaluate the ASK method on various dynamical systems with our custom-made C++ implementation and provide insight into its performance by visualizing the resulting Koopman operator spectra. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive approach to continuously adjust the sparse grid configuration as needed. Ultimately, the ASK method demonstrates a substantial improvement in both computational efficiency and real-time capabilities compared to traditional time integration methods. Our findings also highlight the importance of optimizing parameters and providing guidelines for selecting the most suitable tuning options. Although initially developed for autonomous systems, the ASK method can also be applied to non-autonomous systems with further modifications. With its potential for near-real-time data applications, we demonstrate the ASK method's ability to accurately identify pseudo-cycle trajectories in a non-autonomous system. Moreover, we provide additional insights into its performance on complex phenomena such as spirals, impacts, and singularities by comparing it with state-of-the-art techniques like short-time DMD and QPAS-K. The Sinkhorn algorithm relies on a specific approach to resolve systems of equations of the form $Hu=\log(h)\cdot u$ under certain constraints, known as the Schrödinger problem, using entropic optimization techniques. Two critical factors contribute to a degenerate outcome: (1) function $H$ having a nontrivial kernel; (2) function $h$ being part of the kernel of $H$ or constant. In non-degenerate scenarios, iterative applications of the Schrödinger problem solve an approximate problem closely related to cancellation and transport processes. However, in degenerate situations, cancellation and transport problems become the primary focus due to their inherent separability. A comparison of algorithms for solving these problems is provided, along with analysis of their algorithmic representations, connections to the Schrödinger problem, and performance characteristics. In particular, it is shown that cancellation and transport problems can be resolved using a single instance of the Schrödinger problem under specific conditions, but generally require distinct algorithms. A combination of cancellation and transport algorithms is proposed to handle general Schrödinger problems, which exhibits improved stability and efficiency. A new algorithm for resolving cancellation and transport problems that leverages logarithmic and exponentiation operations is identified. Surprisingly, it is found that all existing algorithms for solving cancellation and transport problems can be represented as specific instances of the Schrödinger problem with a simple matrix function $H$. A general approach to optimizing matrix functions using entropy and logarithm is introduced, which can be viewed as a generalization of the Sinkhorn algorithm, known as the GSO algorithm. A thorough mathematical and algorithmic analysis of the GSO algorithm and its relationship to other optimization methods is provided, along with its position as a universal solver for a broad class of optimization problems, including those based on entropy and logarithm. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterintuitive findings show higher COVID-19 case rates correlating with increased outdoor activity and lower diversity of visited places, suggesting that areas with fewer cases may experience greater social distress. In an effort to restore urban diversity post-pandemic, this study proposes an algorithm incorporating both current and predicted future mobility data to identify optimal visiting locations. By incorporating real-world constraints and trade-offs, this algorithm seeks to minimize the distance traveled while ensuring urban diversity is maintained. Simulation results, using actual user data from pandemic and post-pandemic periods, show an increased diversity of 2 to 9 times the distance visited, while also outperforming other compared techniques in achieving long-term diversity goals. Moreover, this study's findings highlight the importance of targeting lower COVID-19 case rates regions with interventions aimed at boosting urban diversity of visited places. Overall, this study's approach offers a framework for analyzing and addressing pandemic-related social impacts on urban mobility and diversity, facilitating a safer return to normal life. The research presents an open-source software framework for capturing complex user mobility patterns during public health emergencies, offering an adaptable tool for various applications. This study's investigation into pandemic-related social impacts on urban mobility and diversity has significant practical implications for urban policymakers and planners, advising on effective emergency response strategies to mitigate these impacts and recommending computational techniques to predict and restore urban diversity of visited places. Alongside the results, the research makes available an open-source software framework for capturing complex user mobility patterns during public health emergencies, yielding an adaptable tool for various applications. The software framework combines real-time processing, distributed architecture, and a machine learning module to analyze user mobility data, integrating a case activation model to identify regions with low COVID-19 case rates prioritizing diversity restoring interventions. A versatile nonlinear solver called FieldSplitPreconditionner is used to tackle a broad range of multiphase flow and transport issues. It combines a straightforward algorithm with versatile implementation capabilities, allowing it to be integrated into existing linear solvers. This flexibility is demonstrated by incorporating FieldSplitPreconditionner into petSc and utilizing it with both traditional iterative methods and advanced directional splitting schemes. Furthermore, FieldSplitPreconditionner is demonstrated to be effective when applied to complex two-phase and multi-phase transport problems, including compression, flow beneath frozen surfaces, and contaminant dispersion. To enhance its efficiency, a two-step FieldSplitPreconditionner is developed, where the first step involves a directional splitting method and the second step is a preconditioned linear solve. This two-step approach significantly reduces the computational load by minimizing the number of calls to the more computationally expensive linear solver. Finally, FieldSplitPreconditionner is successfully incorporated into Dake, a Python framework for simulating multi-phase fluid dynamics, revealing its effectiveness in handling a variety of challenging simulation problems. This research showcases the value of FieldSplitPreconditionner as a practical and adaptable tool for simulating a broad range of multiphase flow and transport issues. Moreover, the incorporation of FieldSplitPreconditionner into Dake highlights its potential to enhance the performance of Python frameworks for multiphase fluid dynamics by replacing their inefficient linear solvers with more effective ones. Moreover, the integration of FieldSplitPreconditionner into simulation frameworks serves as a testing ground to assess the value of open-source software and exchange knowledge among researchers and engineers. In probabilistic learning, organisms often demonstrate two fundamental approaches: probability-matching and maximization. While probability-matching involves learning and adapting to specific probabilities, maximization involves consistently choosing the more rewarding option. Previous research, specifically in the context of Frank's switch theory, suggested that probability-matching is a result of the interplay between two opposing brain mechanisms, namely a dopaminergic system optimized for maximization and a serotonergic system optimized for probability-matching. Our study challenges this theory by showing that both systems can be simultaneously optimized for maximization tasks. Using dynamic field modeling, we analyzed and compared optimization signals in the systems and found that both could be effectively tuned to yield near-ideal performance on Frank's switch tasks. Our results highlight the possibility of co-opting the serotonergic system for maximization strategies, particularly in environments that favor reward-based decisions. This research has implications for models of probabilistic learning and suggests that both probability-matching and maximization can be expressed within a similar brain architecture, depending on the tuning of its underlying signal sources. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee positive probabilities become impractical for large numbers of qubits. In this study, a new class of MEM techniques based on the influence kernel is proposed to overcome this constraint. The proposed methods successfully scale to 20 qubits without negative probabilities and demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods in terms of absolute error. A critical aspect of these techniques is the strategic use of discarded noisy measurements to optimize the estimation of the ideal measurement basis. The proposed methods' potential as a universal solution for the near-term quantum computing era is thereby confirmed. Further investigation shows that, unlike current MEM techniques, influence kernel mitigation does not introduce biases, especially when dealing with full noise spectra. Importantly, this technique's effectiveness is not solely dependent on having a complete noise model as is typical with other methods. In some cases, influence kernel mitigation even performs better when only partial noise data are available compared to methods based on maximum likelihood estimation. The code and tutorials for the proposed mitigation technique are made publicly available on GitHub under the label "quantum-noise-optimization-miplg". The noise data used in this study belong to the quantum community research resource D-Wave Quantum's watermelon dataset, D-RAC, and IBM Q 20. Wightman. To challenge neural networks' reliance on extensive training data, we developed a novel hybrid approach, ensembling five models with predefined features. This strategy successfully handled unfamiliar text with only a few sentences, achieving near-perfect accuracy on the PURE dataset. Additionally, we demonstrated the robustness of our ensembled model by testing it on publicly accessible datasets, RE dataset and NUS-RealData, yielding impressive results. According to our knowledge, this is the first hybrid ensemble learned within a dataset, enabling PURE to accommodate new domains with only minimal preparation. Consequently, we release the PURE dataset and make our code available for open research purposes.

A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive models that can bridge image types. A popular approach for constructing such models utilizes Bayesian deep learning, which allows for the separation of task uncertainty and intrinsic uncertainty. To accurately implement Bayesian deep learning, it is crucial to accurately distinguish between uncertainty stemming from data variability and that resulting from the model itself. However, existing Bayesian deep learning models often fail to achieve this distinction, leading to inaccurate modelling of image priors. To address this limitation, we introduce an innovative approach that separates uncertainty and uses each to inform steganographic performance. Using a cutting-edge autoencoder architecture, we propagate uncertainty from the encoder through the middle layer and back through the decoder, utilising the predictive uncertainty to correct for compression artifacts affecting the reconstructed image. By utilising the intrinsic uncertainty, we introduce a novel image prior that can adapt to different compression artifacts. To propagate uncertainty through the autoencoder, we retain the weights constant and apply noise to the input, observing that the output distribution depends solely on the middle layer's uncertainty. When combining this uncertainty-based approach with RST, we achieve notable gains in performance compared to traditional Bayesian deep learning frameworks. Experimental results demonstrate that our uncertainty-based method enhances steganographic capacity while retaining reversibility. Moreover, we investigate various techniques for disentangling uncertainty and examine their effects on steganographic performance. According to our analysis, the inherent uncertainty of the model acts as noise that can be adjusted during steganographic transmission, whereas the predictive uncertainty accurately reflects the impact of compression artifacts and should be used to inform prior images. To further optimise steganographic transmission, we propose a fine-tuning procedure that adjusts the middle layer's uncertainty based on the amount of hidden data to be transmitted. When applied to the autoencoder from [1], we achieve notable gains in performance for both reversible and steganographic applications, verifying our theoretical framework. The proposed uncertainty-based approach is generalisable to a wide range of pre-trained autoencoders, including those from [2], [3], and [4]. This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative evaluation is presented to show the superiority of the end-to-end RAG architecture in the context of question answering. Our implementation of the end-to-end RAG architecture has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. A detailed examination of the technical details in the manuscript is provided in the accompanying notebook, which utilizes the HuggingFace Transformers library to integrate the RAG architecture with a wide range of pre-trained transformer models. By successfully implementing the end-to-end RAG architecture, the challenges associated with gradient propagation through the retrieval process are overcome. To address this challenge, the dual architecture of the RAG architecture is accurately characterized as being comprised of a candidate buffer coupled with a similarity matcher and a generator. Next, the dual architecture is treated as two separate networks during the end-to-end fine-tuning process. One network, comprising the candidate buffer and similarity matcher, is trained using a supervised loss related to the next sentence prediction task. While being trained concurrently, the candidate buffer and similarity matcher are prevented from modifying their weights. Finally, the knowledge learned by the candidate buffer and similarity matcher is used to further fine-tune the pre-trained dense layer weights of the generator. Evaluation of the end-to-end RAG architecture on the SQuAD dataset reveals a notable 15-point gain in the F1 score over the original architecture. A hypothetical explanation for the end-to-end RAG architecture's effectiveness is provided, which attributes the results to the combination of the candidate buffer weights and the pre-trained dense layer weights. Further analysis of the end-to-end RAG architecture is presented, which reveals a notable 23-point gain in the F1 score for the model density distribution at the top 50% of the candidate buffer, coupled with a corresponding decrease in the model density distribution at the bottom 50%. By successfully integrating the RAG architecture with pre-trained transformer models, the end-to-end training of the architecture is accomplished without the need for gradient propagation through the retrieval process. As a result, the limitations associated with the high computational cost of the retrieval process during the end-to-end training of the RAG architecture are overcome. Therefore, the end-to-end training of the RAG architecture during the learning phase is made feasible, coupled with the knowledge that the candidate buffer weights can be used in conjunction with the pre-trained dense layer weights to produce high-quality results on the target task.

Thoroughly evaluating TS2-Net on major text-video retrieval benchmarks has led to exceptional performance, setting new records on MSRVTT, VATEX, LSMDC, ActivityNet, and DiDeMo. In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  This hybrid network creates edges according to a mixture of these rules.  Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach leads to a distribution of node in- and out-degrees that has less extreme outliers compared to a purely preferential attachment network, thereby improving upon this traditional model.  Inference methods applicable to the new model are then explored and demonstrated with both artificially generated and actual network data, revealing the potential benefits of incorporating this flexible hybrid network into the study of real-world networks where such less extreme outcomes are typically observed.  In particular, the new model is shown to faithfully reproduce the known degree distributions of several smaller Pajek datasets without needing additional parameters as a purely preferential attachment network requires.  Additionally the new model is able to fit the degree distributions of the co-authorship network between research institutions in the United DB of Informatics, however the purely preferential attachment model cannot.  However, when analyzing the Amazon web services network this approach was not successful in fitting the degree distributions, likely due to a lack of complete data available and the corresponding corresponding inference method needs to be improved.  Finally it is noted that in general the hybrid and preferential attachment models are not interchangeable, however the new type of hybrid network offers a promising avenue to understand and study a variety of real-world as well as artificial networks. All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at enhancing the cognitive capabilities of individual AI systems by collaborating with other AIs. It showcases the potential of this strategy by describing how an imperfect word translation algorithm was able to correct its own mistakes and improve its performance with minimal human supervision, all within a language model dataset. This achievement not only serves as a model for similar enhancements to other AI systems but also addresses the long-standing debate about the advancement of AI capabilities: can AIs enhance the capabilities of other AIs without human involvement? And is the improvement of an AI's capabilities through interaction with another AI sufficient evidence for the verification of the Effective AI Redundancy Hypothesis? Furthermore, this report examines the essential principles and guidelines that must be fulfilled in order for the interaction-based AI upgrades to successfully occur. Lastly, the implications and potential applications of this research are explored in the context of both theoretical advancements and practical real-world problems. 

The key contributions of this report are as follows: 
- It offers a model for the self-upgrade of individual AI systems at minimal cost and without human supervision.
- It delivers an effective high-performance word translation algorithm applicable to typical machine translation benchmarks.
- It introduces a new form of interaction-based AI development that may address issues previously deemed unsolvable utilizing traditional human-driven AI upgrades.
- It identifies crucial elements and standards for the successful self-upgrade of individual AI systems.
- It reveals potential practical uses for the self-upgrade mechanism, including the correction of AI mistakes in critical applications, provision of high-standard customer service via chatbots, and guidance of human decision-making in difficult decision-making dilemmas. 

The report is divided into seven sections. Section 1 includes this introduction and background. Section 2 outlines the critical problem being addressed. Section 3 describes our new strategy and methodology for the self-upgrade of individual AI systems. Section 4 exhibits the results and findings. Section 5 discusses these results in the context of related topics and reports previous research in this area. Section 6 identifies crucial elements and standards for the successful self-upgrade of individual AI systems. Section 7 concludes this report and outlines potential future research directions. We use the Shraiman-Field-Griberov mean-field theory to analyze the system's phase transitions from a superfluid to Mott Insulator and from antiferromagnet to supersuperfluid. We explore how these phases intersect and investigate the impact of spin-orbit coupling on these transitions and the resulting phase boundaries. Specifically, we discover that an increase in Rashba coupling reduces the required interaction to transition from superfluid to Mott Insulator, while it has an opposite effect for the antiferromagnet to supersuperfluid transition. The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena that emerge from these interactions. A compelling example of this relationship is the way a highly excited three-dimensional Bose gas loses its initial structure and reaches a state of thermal equilibrium. In contrast, a one-dimensional representation of this same system, where the particles move along a line, prevents the system from reaching complete thermal equilibrium even when interactions between the particles are present. The distinct phases of matter that can arise in a many-body system are often understood through the study of phase diagrams, which describe how different ground states change in response to varying system parameters. The current research builds upon previous work that revealed a phase diagram for a one-dimensional Bose gas by using analytical techniques to calculate how the system's behavior changes when interactions between particles are represented by a mathematical function. The researchers extended the phase diagram to include the case where particle interactions are not present. The findings provide insights into how the structure of a system influences its phase transitions, which can have implications for the development of new technologies based on complex quantum phenomena. The researchers identified the distinct phases of the system - including a gas, a symmetrical arrangement of bosons, and two types of condensates - and how these phases change in response to varying system parameters. The research also revealed that even in the absence of particle interactions, the system can exhibit complex behavior. The existing theories correctly explained the behavior of the system in the limits where certain parameters were either very small or very large. The researchers, however, discovered that a different theoretical approach - based on a formula that estimates how long it takes for interactions between particles to take effect - failed to accurately describe the system's behavior in the intermediate region. The research highlighted that a complete understanding of even simple systems can require the use of many different and complex mathematical approaches. Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing as a crucial aspect of their work cycle, allowing for swift validation and increased confidence in code development. However, test code can be compromised by suboptimal design or implementation issues known as test smells. These problems are often overlooked but can adversely affect the quality and reliability of software test code. A recently proposed technique is designed to automatically identify test smells in PHPDIT (PHP distribution with IntelliJ idea toolkit), including simple and complex types such as duplicated code, poorly performing algorithms, low-priority test cases, and other issues. By employing this method, software developers can prevent further deterioration of their test code as it evolves. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, using the square error as a benchmark, a trained neural network directly predicting the camera's position significantly outperformed the other methods. The scope of this review encompasses models estimating mean population exposures and their variability. The review begins by outlining the challenges of estimating air pollution models and continues with a description of the selected methodologies. It concludes with future research objectives and goals for improving demographic and spatial aggregation in air pollution models. The key findings of this review are: (1) models should be based on objective scientific approaches; (2) machine learning algorithms can improve air pollution models' accuracy; (3) population-averaged approaches are suitable for studies involving multiple population groups; (4) models should facilitate interactive data analysis; (5) high-performance computational methods are essential for processing and analyzing air pollution models; (6) population averages and variability should be reported in conjunction with other metrics; and (7) models should be designed to facilitate two-way data analysis. The process of matching photometric catalogs is an essential task across many fields of research that involves identifying and linking identical astronomical sources between different catalogs based on their positions and brightness. There are two main challenges associated with this task. Firstly, many sources may have the same position due to various overlapping surveys at a time. Secondly, catalogs are often affected by random matching errors. While many existing algorithms successfully address these issues, they neglect the importance of brightness, resulting in additional positional noise following a Gaussian distribution. In response, we present a novel method based on a maximum likelihood approach to incorporate magnitude data and reduce matching errors. Through extensive simulations and real-world data testing, our modified approach demonstrates significant improvements over the standard method by increasing the signal-to-noise ratio by which a match is preferred over a random one. In particular, this gain is most noticeable in surveys where the density of sources is high. Moreover, our revised method is versatile and compatible with a wide range of cross-matching algorithms. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. With OntoPlot, we have pushed the boundaries of visualising complex concept relationships, opening up new possibilities for ontology-based data analysis and exploration. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to exploit a broader range of data relationships by comparing the outputs of various models on the same input, while CycleGAN leverages cycle-conservative regualrization to improve model performance. This approach can be viewed as a CycleGAN variant incorporating cross-domain training, enabling the cycle training loop to be applied in the speech domain. We utilize a self-supervised framework called CSSL and compare its effectiveness with inter-domain loss and CycleGAN approaches using several widely-used datasets. Notably, CSSL exhibits comparable results with inter-domain loss on the SRE08 and FSD1351 datasets and significantly outperforms CycleGAN on the Librispeech dataset. Furthermore, CSSL shows substantial improvements over its individual components on the SRE08 dataset. This research demonstrates that a combination of adversarial networks and inter-domain loss can enhance speech recognition quality in a semi-supervised manner. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework for their environment. However, a more recent interpretation suggests that these principles drive the brain to minimize uncertainty through maximin reasoning may not fully account for the diverse range of actions that agents perform. For example, when trying to locate a hidden object, an agent could either move closer to its current estimate of the object's position or try to gain new information about its location. Although both options seem reasonable from a Bayesian perspective, they have distinct characteristics. To address this discrepancy, we suggest that our cognitive systems use a combination of Bayesian inference and spread of activation mechanisms to generate goals. By incorporating an expansive network model that simulates the spread of activation, we investigated the trade-off between exploring new information and refining existing estimates in both human and monkey subjects. Our results reveal that mechanisms which balance the dissemination of activation to linked nodes may effectively serve as an alternative to active inference, particularly in situations where partial or incomplete information about the environment exists. We also developed an algorithm that leverages activation spreading for generating goal-oriented decisions in control problems within simulated robotic agents. Our outcomes show that agents designed with this mechanism may efficiently achieve control tasks which are difficult to solve using active inference, such as balancing a long-stretched balance beam. We argue that this mechanism may serve as an efficient means of goal generation for a range of tasks, offering potential applications in the development of artificial intelligence systems. Our code is accessible through an open source repository found at https://github.com/JeroenWolf/active-inference-code. Furthermore, a related open source repository containing simulated tasks may be viewed at https://github.com/JeroenWolf/active-inference-code/tree/main/tasks. A preprint version of this paper is available for review at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.02022. A corresponding video explaining the methodology may be viewed at: https://doi.org/10.1010.meps.0000301. Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to observe the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' conformation on this phenomenon. As we altered the temperature difference, we analyzed the Soret induced flow, entropy and energy transport in a system consisting of dimers composed of flexible monomers, to identify the dynamic flexibility's impact. The outcomes from our simulations confirmed the presence of Soret induced flow and matched thermodynamic predictions for entropy and energy transportation. Additionally, we examined the dynamic flexibility's role in the Soret effect, and how it causes asymmetry in the thermal conductivity to impact the system's collective dynamics. The present research provides insight into the Soret effect in the context of molecular flexibility, offering a method to engineer this phenomenon through temperature differences. The study also highlights potential applications in the separation of molecules with varying flexibility levels. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective assessment of an essay's qualities demands comprehension of its underlying argument, structure, and language usage, as well as relevant references. Current leading systems, fueled by deep learning methodologies, have achieved impressive success but often prioritize speed over accurate evaluation of long-term relationships. In response, we present DRESC, a novel approach that leverages Transformer architecture for capturing dependencies across entire essay datasets. By incorporating multiple essays written by the same individual, DRESC employs a semi-supervised approach grounded in graph co-smoothing to enhance relationships within each writer's work. DRESC also introduces a new scoring model, EssayScore, that estimates an essay's score solely based on its self-representation, without relying on class labels. When developing the new model, we created a new synthetic dataset, EssaySyn, to facilitate training and testing. As demonstrated through cross-validation and real-world dataset assessment, DRESC outperforms current leading systems, delivering more accurate predictions on both the PAE and AE datasets. Moreover, the DRESC system, comprising the EssayScore model and associated code, is available for public access at https://github.com/alexis-ziane/DRESC. DRESC has been utilized to create a new, more precise estimation method for the 2022 All8x8 competition. A summary of this competition is detailed in a companion paper. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  To address this problem effectively, this study provides a new direction by showing that false positive reduction is closely related to the mining of valuable information from unlabeled images.  To achieve this goal, a self-supervised learning framework is developed, specifically for unlabeled images, to improve the representation learning for pedestrian detection.  This proposed method employs an iterative approach, envisions a detector's model weights as training data, and applies a self-supervised contrastive loss, supported by a self-training approach.  To unlock the full potential of the CSAF framework, this study introduces entropy-driven sampling methods to unlock the value of unlabeled images.  Through thorough experimentation, this study validates the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving better results compared to state-of-the-art adaptations in pedestrian detection and outperforming the conventional training approach, especially in complex scenarios.  This study further investigates the method's influence on representation learning for pedestrian detection and conducts ablation analyses to verify the proposed method's efficacy.  Based on these findings, this method can be used in a wide variety of scenarios.  Code is available on https://github.com/liketheflower/COSPD.  This work has been published in MMV2022. This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a more desirable format, using a style-based approach, while another reconstructs the original sound from the modified spectrogram. Experimental results indicate that this method yields higher quality than conventional techniques in two common applications for these types of recordings – music classification and noise removal. Additionally, this study validates the model's effectiveness on datasets captured in real-world settings, which the researchers made accessible along with the model through a newly developed transformer architecture for the mel-spectrogram. Furthermore, this model can also mitigate echo effects, which is essential for proper music classification. Lastly, this study presents an analysis of the effectiveness of different microphone types and recording locations in influencing the quality of consumer-grade music recordings. As an example of the potential applications of this research, it can be used to improve automatic music classification for recordings made on mobile devices, which can be useful for creating music discovery tools. However, the process of enhancing these recordings needs to be evaluated in conjunction with other applications, such as noise removal, which requires a different optimization strategy. Interestingly, the researchers found that the effects of different distortions on music classification vary significantly, with echo distortions being the most significant influence. A newly developed deep learning technique can mitigate the effects of microphone distortions, noise, and echo effects on consumer-grade music recordings. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's position at the point where it's released on perceptions of the throw's fairness and the accuracy of the thrower. Using a simulation-based approach, we analyzed various factors such as the effect of different throwing styles, the view angle of the observer, and the timing of the point when the ball starts its movement. We discovered a significant relationship between the point of release and the perception of the throw's fairness and accuracy: an early release generally results in the ball deviating from its intended course in the viewer's sight, whereas a late release makes the ball appear as though it's taken a wrong path after being thrown. However, when the release occurs at the moment the arm reaches its highest point, most viewers consider the throw fair even if the arm's motion isn't natural-looking. These findings challenge the conventional understanding that early releases are generally perceived as being unfair. We're planning to extend this research to real-world sports settings to explore its practical implications in determining the fairness of throws in sports like baseball, softball, and golf. In a future study, we'll be exploring a broader range of scenarios including a wider range of release points, throwing styles, an array of viewer angles, and both visual and auditory presentation of the throw. Additionally, we'll be assessing the impact of different types of errors on the perception of fairness and accuracy using a simulated virtual reality environment. To incorporate syntax-aware decoding into Neural Machine Translation systems, a novel NMT architecture called Seq2DRNN has been designed, which leverages syntax representations generated from sentence grids to guide decoding. Unlike existing NMT models that make translations directly from raw word sequences, Seq2DRNN permits an additional layer of processing before translation, allowing for multiple token-level representations to be identified. Experiments with Seq2DRNN, employing recurrent neural networks and constituency parsing, yielded a significant improvement in performance over state-of-the-art NMT models without syntax guidance, across three language pairs and different translation tasks. Furthermore, analyses of the extracted syntax representations indicate they demonstrate properties expected of actual language patterns. By varying the level of granularity in the extracted representations, Seq2DRNN was found to effectively balance the trade-off between translation quality and preserving original sentence structures, with improved reproduction of original sentences shown through increased model complexity. Overall, the results suggest that incorporating a syntax-aware decoding mechanism can facilitate more effective NMT systems. Moreover, our work provides insight into the extracted syntax representations, suggesting these features may serve as a valuable resource for developing new translation models. As an additional benefit, the extracted representations may be applied in other areas, such as natural language understanding, with potential to yield better performance in downstream tasks. Finally, the code developed for this research has been made publicly available on both GitHub and ZeuPY. 

Note: ZeuPY is an open-source coding library developed specifically for NLP applications, focused primarily on infrastructure-related tasks such as data preprocessing and model development. The library, currently undergoing development, is expected to expand its scope to include even more sophisticated features over time.

The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse complexities of molecular interactions. Nevertheless, experimental measurements of such binding energies are often hindered by technical limitations, such as the inability to rotate freely and limited experimental visibility of certain interactions. The Theoretical Thermal Measurement (TTM) model offers an alternative solution by making various assumptions to compensate for these limitations. The assumptions involve considering interactions to be completely reversible and allocating binding energies in a hierarchical manner. In this study, we evaluated the credibility of the TTM model for three types of molecular interactions, such as hydrogen halides and oxygen, hydrocarbons and oxygen, and water, by comparing its results with experimental data and findings from rotating nonequilibrium models. The comparison showed that the TTM model's results in close agreement with experimental data for hydrogen halides and oxygen, while nonequilibrium models yielded better outcomes for hydrocarbons and oxygen and water interactions. Despite its assumptions, the TTM model proved a reliable predictor of experimental data for specific interaction sets, such as hydrogen halides and oxygen. The study generally indicated that the TTM model's predictions should be considered as lower bounds for binding energies, as well as suggestions for future experimental improvements to increase model's accuracy. The potential application of theoretical models to interpret data from upcoming missions like the Freja and the Rosetta has also been explored. The research found the theoretical models' capabilities to predict spectral features compatible with experimental data for specific interaction types, such as hydrogen halides and oxygen. Nonetheless, the agreement between the model's predictions and spectrometric measurements of interstellar species is currently unsatisfactory due to inaccuracies in binding energy values, particularly in the case of hydrogen halides. The analysis of Taurus-Moon observations by the Freja space mission revealed a correlation between CL spectrometric measurements and laboratory binding energy values for water. In the case of hydrocarbons, the model's predictions of non-equilibrium spectra of the Murchison meteorite adhered to its theoretical constraints. The comparison between the predicted spectral features of interstellar hydrogen halides derived from theoretical and nonequilibrium models with CL observations of comets and meteorites indicated a better match with nonequilibrium models' results. Additionally, the distribution of the process's maximum value is identified and graphed for varying parameter settings. We offer two new approaches for determining the optimal number of measurement settings in a depth-controlled randomized measurement scheme. The first method leverages the repetition of optimized designs to find an approximately optimal setting. The second approach uses artificial intelligence to find an exact optimal design. Our findings reveal that the depth-controlled strategy can achieve close to optimal results with a significantly lower number of measurement settings, often just a few percent greater than the best possible. For most cases, an AI-optimized design with only a few measurement settings performs better than a randomly generated design. Furthermore, the repeating AI-optimized design scheme does not increase errors related to the device instability without the need for continuous AI involvement. The AI-optimized designs also facilitate comparisons between different schemes, revealing that the depth-controlled strategy is indeed the best among them. The depth-controlled strategy has the advantage that it can be applied using measurements of only a few key photons. Additionally, the scheme is invariant to changes in device instability and can be implemented using designs for a single-state optimization, making it more feasible to achieve optimal results. A demonstration of the depth-controlled strategy using two-qubit entanglement, a complex quantum system, confirms its advantages, showing that optimal results can be achieved with a relatively small number of measurement settings, specifically 20. The depth-controlled strategy opens up new avenues to achieve optimal performance in quantum measurement schemes, particularly for complex quantum systems. The scheme can be applied to speed up quantum measurements, achieve optimal performance in programming-free measurements, attain optimal performance in two-qubit entanglement programming, achieve a significant advantage in device stability, and even achieve optimal performance in different quantum measurement schemes such as tomography, linear optics, and quantum processing. The depth-controlled strategy has significant value in the development of quantum processing devices, which face significant limitations in data collection due to enormous data requirements. The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need for the original text to be retained in an unchanged state. This concept of preserving the original text is referred to as sibylvariance - the ability of a model to produce outputs identical to the original text. We propose an innovative approach, referred to as hypernymization, which leverages the original text by replacing its noun phrases with their corresponding hypernyms. This method aims to enhance sibylvariance while achieving significant advancements in semantics. We have developed a data augmentation strategy for hypernymization and have evaluated its effectiveness across multiple tasks, showcasing its ability to surpass state-of-the-art performance in text classification tasks, notably in sentiment analysis. Moreover, to address the issue of text augmentation quality, we introduce a new metric - the degree of sibylvariance - which quantifies the quality of text transformations. We have developed this metric and have demonstrated its effectiveness in evaluating both text transformation models and machine learning models tasked with generating improved transformations. The code for our hypernymization approach can be accessed on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/uts-arl/hypernymization. A web-based demo is available at https://uts-arl.github.io/hypernymization/. We are confident that our approach will contribute significantly to the development of text transformation models that achieve superior results in terms of both accuracy and quality. Additionally, our results suggest a trend towards larger, higher-quality data sets, which will likely lead to improved performance across multiple NLP tasks. We believe that our proposed sibylvariance metric will serve as a useful tool for evaluating and developing text transformation models. We have conducted an in-depth analysis and discussion of the underlying theories and theories behind hypernymization by examining the ontological foundations of NLP and NFO, and by exploring the link between word sense disambiguation and hypernymization. We also examine the potential applications and generalizability of hypernymization by examining its effect on different languages and by exploring its link to cognitive theory. We are proud to have received funding from the Australian Government to develop a national English language resource - ARGoSACE. This project aspires to increase public access to high-quality English language datasets through innovative applications of NLP and NFO. We believe that our proposal for the national English language resource will inspire a new wave of interest in NFO and NLP by highlighting their relevance to the challenges of the 21st century. Researchers have made notable progress in developing representation learning that can be adapted and refined through meta-learning. Specifically, meta-learning has a critical subset known as few-shot learning that aims to maximize performance in limited data sets. Unfortunately, the current top models in the fieldincorporate hand-designed metrics, which hinders their ability to generalize to unfamiliar problems. Our research introduces Meta-Code, an innovative model that can automatically generate and optimize rotation-invariant metrics tailored to various datasets. By combining both low-level, sparse coding-based features and high-level, prototypical representation features, Meta-Code facilitates seamless transfer between datasets. We propose and experimentally validate several challenging scenarios that must meet two key requirements: supporting both linear and non-linear metrics, and facilitating zero-shot dataless testing. Our findings demonstrate that Meta-Code outperforms state-of-the-art models like Protonet, Discent, and NWayProp on both linear and non-linear metrics across six diverse datasets. Moreover, we show that when applied to cross-dataset and cross-domain few-shot learning tasks, Meta-Code's state-of-the-art performance can be achieved by using a non-linear, high-quality metric that utilizes prototypical aggregation. The code for Meta-Code is freely accessible on the GitHub platform at the following link: https://github.com/ali-hosseini/Meta-Code. We anticipate that Meta-Code's design and implementation will serve as a foundation for future research in metric learning, particularly in the development of non-linear and cross-domain generalizable models. Our research also contributes to the existing challenges and requirements in the field by conducting an extensive and systematic analysis of the seven most influential meta-learning papers, as detailed in Section 7 in the main document. Lastly, this study proposes and executes several promising research paths and potential advancements in the field, as outlined in Section 8. We strongly recommend that readers review the supplementary material available at: https://github.com/ali-hosseini/Meta-Code/tree/master/supplement. Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used method to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This study initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it's discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily relies on several preconditions, making it a somewhat unreliable compression approach. To improve on this, we explore post-training quantization as a means to significantly reduce model size and evaluate its effect on translation performance. Ultimately, to provide a realistic deployment scenario, we investigate whether efficiently trained, lighter models produced by quantization or distillation can serve as effective continuations to enhance performance on difficult translations, particularly in languages with limited training data. To this end, we develop XContinuation, a continuation learning framework allowing the seamless transfer of knowledge from source to target languages, achieving notable results in continuation tasks in languages such as Turkmen and Kazakh, among others. Our research, which includes reproducible code and data, is made available online. We also contribute a novel open-source toolkit, named HLIR, which is used in our research, to facilitate multilingual learning in languages with limited data, while making models more deployable. This HLIR implementation supports Knowledge Distillation and Quantization for machine translation. It can be accessed at https://github.com/AlibabaCloud-MTS/HLIR. The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for a specific, non-trivial Turan density, it was proven that a certain graph structure can be achieved. We investigate whether this holds true for all possible Turan densities in 2-uniform graphs and explore whether this holds true for all possible graph structures in 3-uniform graphs. We demonstrate a method to find specific (n, F)-Frieemann and F-free Turan structures for numerous graphs F, including those with density one-half, almost half, and close to two-thirds. We show that an F-defined structure is an (n, F)-Frieemann and F-free Turan structure if and only if an F-defined contractible edge set has the following properties: it includes no contractible 3-cycles; for every pair of vertices, there are at least two non-adjacent vertices with edges between them; and every pair of vertices with an adjacent pair in E(F) has edges in both. We show that an F-defined contractible edge set has the former three properties if and only if it can be transformed into a 'half-structure' with the following properties: it contains E(F) and every contractible m-uniform subgraph with m greater than or equal to three. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using end-to-end speech translation and translation models suffer from the shortcoming of out-of-vocabulary words, which is not a problem with natural language inference's zero-shot translation technique. It involves utilizing speech-to-text models, pre-trained with vast amounts of data, to translate unseen language pairs. Our proposed ENCORE method allows for zero-shot speech-to-text translation of unfamiliar languages while the target language remains the same. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements that exhibit memory, as exemplified by the model proposed by Bertressi et al. We establish the existence of solutions within a space of tempered distributions, drawing upon methods for constructing nonlinear elliptic equations. Additionally, considering that these dynamic boundary conditions may involve irregular data, we adapt existing techniques for regular cases and employ distributional approaches to establish the existence of solutions in this generalized setting. Furthermore, we prove the stability of solutions over specified time intervals using an energy method, building upon earlier work by Nohel and Krzywicki. Crucially, as a direct consequence of our findings, we demonstrate that the system becomes classical when certain conditions related to the heat conduction theory are satisfied and when dynamic boundary conditions lose their memory component. This finding validates the well-posedness of models like that by Bertressi et al. within the traditional heat conduction framework. Moreover, when considering particular cases where the system remains classical over time, we establish that the solution remains continuous in its initial conditions within specific function spaces, using an argument analogous to the one by Krzywicki and Nohel. We have thus successfully broadened the existence and stability results for heat conduction with dynamic boundary conditions, taking into account its most general form. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors can influence broader consumption patterns. While highly detailed demand forecasts may yield significant economic benefits, current predictive techniques rely heavily on aggregated data, thereby complicating efforts to fine-tune these models to minimize costs and constraints associated with highly disaggregated energy demand. This paper explores the potential border between highly detailed and aggregated energy forecasting, focusing specifically on predicting residential and commercial energy consumption at increasingly detailed levels, including separate estimates for real and reactive power, along with corresponding uncertainty measures. Building upon an advanced spatial autoregressive model known as SARIMA, this research develops a highly detailed prediction approach, which initially generates aggregate energy forecasts through the application of SARIMA, subsequently distributes these estimates among various categories of appliances to produce highly detailed energy predictions. Validation processes are performed to ensure the predicted energy data adheres to historical observations, following which 10,000 future time windows are simulated under uncertainty to produce predictive distributions. The proposed methodology is then tested using a highly detailed energy dataset from an urban area, accompanied by a comprehensive analysis of accuracy metrics, including coverage rates and quantitative measures like the quantile score, lifted fractional score, and the time and space scores. Evaluation results suggest the potential boundary between detailed and aggregated energy forecasting could be significantly narrowed, thereby making highly detailed energy forecasting a feasible option, which may ultimately lead to significant economic benefits, as demonstrated by a cost analysis based on actual network constraints and an examination of the resulting load distribution following the application of highly detailed forecasts, contrasting it with aggregated forecasts obtained via a SARIMA approach. This research highlights the need to develop new methodologies aimed at reducing costs and constraints associated with highly disaggregated energy demand, showcasing a promising avenue for achieving this goal. Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation-based methods that necessitate extensive labeling of COVID-19 cases to train a model, a task that becomes more complex with the need to distinguish between infected and uninfected patients. The problem with these traditional supervised methods is that they are only as effective as the quality and quantity of labeled data provided. The development of self-supervised learning techniques has the potential to greatly reduce data annotation requirements, a trend that is being explored in COVID-19 detection on chest X-rays. However, the application of such methods in detecting COVID-19 on CT scans has not been extensively researched. In response, we have developed a novel self-supervised learning approach known as Supervised Contrastive Learning, which utilizes labeled images to train a COVID-19 detection model in a semi-supervised manner. The method incorporates two distinct loss functions that minimize both inter-patient and intra-particle variations in CT images. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated using 1,600 chest CT scan images from 804 patients, resulting in an optimal area under the ROC curve of 0.9030 and a corresponding accuracy rate of 87.5%. The introduced method achieved an accuracy of 87.5% and AUC of 0.9030 using only 100 training images, demonstrating its ability to identify COVID-19-positive CT scans with minimal data. The model also exhibited an accuracy of 0.9034 and AUC of 0.9030 using an independent test set of 1,600 cases, with a corresponding Q2 value of 0.703 indicating distinct intra-patient clusters. The method further achieved an accuracy of 0.8811 and AUC of 0.9030 using an independent test set of 1,600 cases with COVID-19 heterogeneity. The model performed competitively with a fully supervised model trained on the entire dataset in terms of intra-patient discrimination. The introduced method successfully addressed data annotation requirements, reducing the need for labeled data by requiring only 12% of the dataset to achieve comparable results to the fully supervised model. The need for labeled data was further minimized in the inference phase, allowing the model to achieve optimal accuracy with as few as three instances per patient. The novel approach of the Supervised Contrastive Learning method successfully minimized data annotation requirements in the training and inference phases, enabling the identification of distinct COVID-19-positive instances on chest CT scans with minimal data.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g. vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g. limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center points are pinpointed and then grouped into columns to determine column centers. Finally, vertebrae identities are determined based on estimated center columns. We have developed an accurate and detailed spine anatomy dataset with high-quality annotations, featuring 100 CT scans from the SpineCT dataset (excluding 10% for model training) and 100 pathological CT scans from the PathSpine dataset. We have also modified the widely used Valence Loss and Multi-scale Fully Convolutional Network models to develop the MPFCN model. Our proposed method demonstrates promising results on the PathSpine dataset, with significant improvements over the SpineCT dataset. Notably, our method achieves meta-testing accuracy of 85.9% on the PathSpine dataset and 89.1% on the SpineCT dataset. The proposed method's accuracy and simplified architecture make it a suitable choice for identifying and localizing vertebrae in both normal and pathological spines. In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the controller design. This research focuses on developing spring-based controllers for central pattern generators, allowing a robot to learn gaits that adapt to changing dynamics. A key challenge is mitigating the unintended effects of spring dynamics on the neural signals, and we address this through a two-part learning approach. First, an in-motor learned dynamics model is used to predict the spring's response to neural signals. Next, a reinforcement learning agent learns policies that transform neural signals to ensure desired gaits, taking into account the spring's dynamic effects. This approach was successfully tested on a spray-painted paper airwheel, and our results show that adapting gaits based on spring parameter variations do not significantly impact stability. This research highlights the potential of integrated design and learning methods for optimizing the interaction between central pattern generators and spring-based actuators. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that adapting gaits can counteract the negative effects of spring dynamics without compromising stability. Finally, our results show that a well-designed learning architecture can unlock energy efficiency and performance gains in spring-based actuators. We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an unknown quantum state prepared by a black-box quantum circuit. When the rate of reconnections is slow, energy changes according to the rate of island growth, but when the rate is fast, energy is primarily transferred through changes in the magnetic field. A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the need to preserve the integrity of remaining attributes. In order to tackle this issue, a novel self-supervised fashion image transformation framework, FASTE, is proposed. This framework combines two key components: a style transfer module and a generative adversarial net. By using 2D-CVAE for style transfer and PACS-Wiki for unaligned data learning, the framework is capable of performing extensive fashion attribute manipulation. A comprehensive series of experiments were conducted on two benchmark datasets to demonstrate FASTE's efficacy. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, FASTE achieved notable improvements in image retrieval tasks, exceeding 55% in mean average precision. Nevertheless, this updated LBT function operates differently from legacy 802.11a/n/ac waveforms and can cause interference with coexisting home networks. Therefore, optimal listen periods and transmission periods must be identified to ensure efficient and reliable data transmission. This research proposes a new LBT optimization framework for WiFi 6 home networks, integrating a dynamic model of home network devices and an optimization algorithm that simultaneously allocates listen and transmission periods in order to maximize overall network throughput.
